subjective.answer: First, I open the Executions list. If there is a failed execution, the schedule worked and I debug the failing node, often an HTTP Request error or an expired credential. If there is no execution at all, the trigger did not fire. Then I check that the workflow is active or published, and that my latest changes were saved and published, since unpublished edits do not apply. Next, I confirm the trigger is a Schedule Trigger and not a Manual Trigger. I check the timezone in Workflow Settings and the instance timezone, because the run may have happened at a different hour than expected. On self-hosted, I check that the n8n instance or container was actually running at that time. Finally, after fixing, I watch the next scheduled run in Executions to confirm.
keyPoints: Check Executions list first
Failed run versus no run tells you where to look
Confirm workflow is published with latest changes
Check trigger type and timezone
On self-hosted, confirm the instance was running

subjective.question: An API returns 40 records and you need one email containing a summary of all of them. How do you build this in n8n?
subjective.answer: Because nodes run once per input item, sending the 40 items straight to an email node would send 40 emails. So I combine them first. One option is the Aggregate node, which collects a field, or all item data, into a single item holding a list. After that, an Edit Fields node or an expression can turn the list into readable text, for example joining titles with line breaks. Another option is a Code node, where I loop over all input items in JavaScript and return one item with a formatted summary, such as counts and totals. Before combining, I usually use Edit Fields to keep only the fields I need. Then the email or Slack node receives one item and sends one message. I test with pinned data, then check one live production run.
keyPoints: Per-item execution would send 40 emails
Aggregate node combines items into one
Code node can build a custom summary
Format text with Edit Fields or expressions
Only one item should reach the send node

subjective.question: An API returns 100 records per page and gives a 'next' URL in each response. How do you fetch all pages in n8n with the HTTP Request node?
subjective.answer: I use the Pagination option built into the HTTP Request node rather than building a loop by hand. Under Options I add Pagination and pick the mode that matches the API. Here the response contains the next URL, so I choose that mode and set the next URL with an expression such as {{ $response.body.next }}. If the API used page numbers or offsets, I would use the mode that updates a parameter in each request, for example page = {{ $pageCount + 1 }}. Then I set 'Pagination Complete When', for example when the next field is empty or a specific status code comes back. I also set a maximum number of pages as a safety limit, so a buggy API cannot loop forever. I may add a short interval between requests to respect rate limits. Finally, I test with a small page size and check the total item count.
keyPoints: Use the HTTP Request node's built-in Pagination option
Choose a mode: next URL in response, or update a parameter
Use $response and $pageCount in expressions
Define a clear completion condition and a max page limit
Respect rate limits with an interval between requests

subjective.question: Your workflow calls a third-party API that sometimes fails with timeouts or 429/5xx errors. Which HTTP Request node and node settings help make it reliable?
subjective.answer: First, in the node Settings I turn on Retry On Fail. I set a sensible number of tries and a wait time between them, so short glitches recover on their own. Second, for many items I use the Batching option to control items per batch and the interval, which keeps me under the rate limit and avoids 429s. Third, I set a Timeout in Options, so a hanging call does not block the run. Fourth, I decide what should happen on failure with the On Error setting. 'Stop Workflow' is right when the data is critical. 'Continue' (using an error output) lets me route failed items to a logging or alert branch. I store credentials in n8n credentials, never in plain headers. Finally, I check failed runs in the Executions list and add an error workflow for alerts.
keyPoints: Retry On Fail with tries and wait time
Batching to respect rate limits
Timeout option for hanging calls
On Error setting: stop vs continue with error output
Credentials stored securely, failures monitored

subjective.question: Explain the difference between $json, $('Node').item, $('Node').first() and $input.all() in n8n expressions. When would you use each?
subjective.answer: $json is the JSON of the current input item, which comes from the node directly before. I use it for most field mappings. $('Node name').item reaches back to an earlier node. It uses item pairing to return the item linked to the current one, so it is right when a later node has dropped a field I still need, such as an ID. $('Node name').first() always returns the first item of that node, whatever the current item is. It suits single values like a token or a config row. $input.all() returns every input item as an array. I use it when one operation must see all items, for example building a summary text with map and join in a node set to Execute Once. The common mistake is using first() where item is needed, which gives every item the same value.
keyPoints: $json = current item from previous node
$('Node').item uses item pairing to earlier node
first() returns a fixed first item
$input.all() returns all items as an array
Wrong choice causes repeated or mismatched values

subjective.question: A public Webhook node will receive order events from a partner. How do you secure it?
subjective.answer: A production webhook URL is reachable by anyone who knows it, so I add several layers. First, I set Authentication on the Webhook node. Options are Basic Auth, Header Auth or JWT Auth, and a shared secret header is the usual choice with partners. Second, I set the HTTP Method to exactly what the partner sends, usually POST, so other methods are rejected. Third, if the partner publishes fixed IPs, I use the IP allowlist option. Fourth, if the partner signs payloads, I verify the signature in the workflow and stop invalid requests early with an IF node, returning an error response. I also use a hard-to-guess path, validate required fields before any writes, and never echo sensitive data back in the response. On self-hosted n8n, I put it behind HTTPS with a reverse proxy.
keyPoints: Webhook Authentication: Basic, Header or JWT
Restrict the HTTP method
IP allowlist where possible
Validate signatures and payloads early
Serve over HTTPS

subjective.question: What does this Slack message expression do, and which node setting must be on for it to send a single summary?

code.code:
Daily report: {{ $input.all().length }} tickets
{{ $input.all().map(i => `• ${i.json.title} (${i.json.priority})`).join('\n') }}

subjective.answer: The first line counts all items that reached the Slack node and prints, for example, 'Daily report: 12 tickets'. The second line takes every input item, turns each one into a bullet line with its title and priority, and joins them with newlines into one block of text. On its own, though, the Slack node still runs once per item. With 12 items you would get 12 identical full summaries. To send one message, I enable Execute Once in the Slack node settings. The expression still reads all items through $input.all(), but the node runs only once. Another option is to use an Aggregate or Code node before Slack to collapse the items into one. I would also handle empty results, for example with an IF on the count, so the team does not get an empty report.
keyPoints: $input.all() reads every input item
map and join build one multi-line text
Nodes run per item by default
Execute Once, or an Aggregate node first, gives one message
Handle the zero-items case

subjective.question: A company wants new rows in a SaaS tool to trigger processing. n8n has an app trigger for that tool, but you could also use a Schedule Trigger plus an HTTP Request. How do you choose?
subjective.answer: I prefer the app trigger when it covers the event I need. It handles authentication, registers webhooks or polls for me, and tracks what it has already seen, so I get only new records without writing de-duplication logic. A Schedule Trigger plus HTTP Request makes sense in other cases. Examples are when the app trigger does not offer the event or fields I need, when I need a fixed batch time such as a 9 AM digest, or when I want full control over the query, filters and pagination. The cost is that I must handle 'only new since last run' myself, for example by filtering on a timestamp or using the Remove Duplicates node's option to remove items processed in previous executions. I also weigh speed against batching. Webhook-based triggers are near real time, while schedules suit reports.
keyPoints: App triggers handle auth and new-item tracking
Schedule + HTTP gives control and fixed timing
Schedule approach needs your own de-duplication
Real-time events vs batch digests
Check whether the trigger exposes the needed event

subjective.question: Your scheduled workflow fetches 'recent orders' every hour and posts them to Slack. People complain the same orders appear in many posts. How do you fix it?
subjective.answer: The API returns a rolling window, so overlapping hours repeat records. There are two clean fixes. One is to ask only for new data: pass a time filter in the HTTP Request, for example created_after = {{ $now.minus({hours: 1}).toISO() }}, so it matches the schedule interval. This is simple but can miss or repeat records if a run is late. The more robust fix is to de-duplicate across runs. The Remove Duplicates node has an operation that removes items processed in previous executions, keyed on a value such as the order ID, so each order passes only once. I then send only the remaining items, often aggregated into one message with Execute Once. Finally, I make sure the IF or empty-result check skips posting when there are no new orders, and I review a few executions to confirm it works.
keyPoints: Rolling window causes overlap
Filter by time based on the schedule interval
Remove Duplicates across previous executions by unique ID
Aggregate into one message
Skip posting when nothing is new

subjective.question: An IF node's true branch ends in a Slack alert and the workflow then continues. On days when no item matches, later nodes never run. Why, and how do you handle it?
subjective.answer: In n8n, a node that receives zero items does not run, and nothing flows past it. If the true branch is empty, every node after it on that path is skipped. The run still shows as successful, which is why this is easy to miss. There are a few fixes. I can enable the Always Output Data setting on the node that may return nothing. It then outputs one empty item, so the chain continues, but downstream nodes must handle an empty item safely. Often a better design is to keep work that must always happen off the conditional branch. For example, place it before the IF, or run it from the false branch too. If I need to bring branches together again, I use a Merge node with the right mode. I test both cases with pinned data, one with matches and one without.
keyPoints: Zero input items means the node does not execute
Run can show success while steps are skipped
Always Output Data emits an empty item
Restructure so must-run steps are not conditional
Test both paths with pinned data

subjective.question: How would you use pinned data to test edge cases in a workflow that starts with a Webhook or a slow API call?
subjective.answer: First I run the trigger or the API node once with real data, then pin its output. Manual test runs then reuse that output, so I don't need to resend webhooks or wait for slow or rate-limited APIs. Pinned data is editable, so I change it to create edge cases: an empty field, a string instead of a number, a missing priority, a very long text, or zero items. With each version I run the workflow and check that the IF, Switch and Edit Fields nodes behave correctly. I keep the data free of real personal information. Pinned data applies only to manual executions in the editor; production runs always use live data. So before relying on the workflow I unpin and run a real test. After publishing, I check the first production executions to confirm real data matches what I pinned.
keyPoints: Pin real output once to avoid re-triggering
Edit pinned data to simulate edge cases
Covers empty, wrong-type and missing fields
Pinned data affects only manual runs, not production
Unpin and verify with live data before relying on it

subjective.question: Case study: Finance wants a Slack post at 7:30 AM IST, Monday to Friday, with USD/INR and EUR/INR rates from a REST API that needs an API key. If the API fails, #ops must be alerted. It must run without anyone opening the editor. Design the workflow.
subjective.answer: I would start with a Schedule Trigger using a Custom (Cron) rule of 30 7 * * 1-5. Then I set the workflow Timezone to Asia/Kolkata in Workflow Settings, because otherwise it fires in the instance timezone. Next comes an HTTP Request node that uses a Header Auth credential for the key, so the secret is encrypted and not exported. I turn on Retry On Fail with a few tries and a wait between them. An Edit Fields node picks out only the two rates and formats them. Because the API returns a single item, the Slack node sends one message. If it returned many items, I would add Aggregate first. For failures, I set the HTTP node's On Error to 'Continue (using error output)' and connect that output to a Slack alert in #ops. An error workflow is the alternative. While building, I pin one real response. Then I publish and check Executions the next morning to confirm an automatic run.
keyPoints: Cron 30 7 * * 1-5 with workflow timezone Asia/Kolkata
HTTP Request with a stored credential and Retry On Fail
Edit Fields to shape the data, one item gives one Slack message
Error output or error workflow routed to #ops
Publish, then verify in Executions

subjective.question: This Docker Compose setup has two bugs. Scheduled runs fire 9.5 or 10.5 hours late, and the Webhook URLs show localhost. Explain both and fix them.

code.code:
services:
  n8n:
    image: docker.n8n.io/n8nio/n8n
    ports:
      - "5678:5678"
    environment:
      - N8N_HOST=n8n.example.in
    volumes:
      - n8n_data:/home/node/.n8n

subjective.answer: Both problems come from missing environment variables. GENERIC_TIMEZONE is not set, so the Schedule Trigger uses the default America/New_York. That zone is 9.5 or 10.5 hours behind IST, depending on US daylight saving, which explains the two different delays. I would add GENERIC_TIMEZONE=Asia/Kolkata, and usually TZ=Asia/Kolkata as well, so the container's system time matches. A workflow-level timezone setting still overrides this per workflow. For webhooks, n8n sits behind a reverse proxy and builds URLs from its internal address. So I would add WEBHOOK_URL=https://n8n.example.in/. Then the Production and Test URLs show the public HTTPS address that partners can actually reach. After changing these, I recreate the container and confirm the new URL in the Webhook node. Then I re-publish any workflow whose URL I had shared, check that the proxy forwards /webhook/ paths, and watch the next scheduled run in Executions.
keyPoints: The default instance timezone is America/New_York
Add GENERIC_TIMEZONE (and TZ) set to Asia/Kolkata
A workflow timezone overrides the instance setting
WEBHOOK_URL makes n8n show the public URL behind a proxy
Recreate the container and verify URLs and the next run

subjective.question: Compare the Switch node's Rules mode and Expression mode. Which would you use to route leads to five regional teams, and which to route by a computed value?
subjective.answer: In Rules mode, each output has its own conditions, such as region equals 'South'. It is easy for a teammate to read. It also supports a fallback output for items that match nothing, and an option to send an item to every matching output. For five regional teams with clear field values, I would use Rules mode, with a fallback output so leads with an empty or unknown region are not lost. In Expression mode, you set the number of outputs and write one expression that returns the output index. Counting starts at 0. This suits routing based on a calculation, for example a lookup object that maps 40 city names to team numbers, or a round-robin based on a lead ID. It is compact but harder to read. I would also make sure the expression can never return an index outside the outputs I defined.
keyPoints: Rules: per-output conditions, readable, with fallback and 'all matching' options
Expression: one expression returns a 0-based output index
Rules mode suits clear field values like region
Expression mode suits computed or lookup-based routing
Always handle unmatched or out-of-range items

subjective.question: Sales wants a daily Slack post with total revenue per region, from an API returning 300 order items. Would you use the Aggregate node or the Summarize node, and how?
subjective.answer: The Summarize node fits better for the maths. It works like a pivot table. I would choose Sum on the amount field and set 'Fields to Split By' to region. The output is one item per region with the total, for example 5 items for 5 regions. The Aggregate node does not calculate anything. It only collects field values, or whole items, into lists inside a single item. So after Summarize I would add Aggregate, using All Item Data, to combine the 5 region items into one item. Then the Slack node runs once and the message can list every region with an expression. Another option is to build the text with $input.all() and turn on Execute Once on the Slack node. Either way, I would check that amount is numeric. If the API sends strings, I would convert them first so the sums are correct.
keyPoints: Summarize computes sum, count, average and similar, grouped by fields
Aggregate only collects values into lists in one item
Summarize, then Aggregate gives one item and one Slack message
An alternative is $input.all() with Execute Once
Make sure amount is numeric before summing

subjective.question: A colleague used Merge in 'Combine by Position' to join customers with their invoices. Some customers now show other people's invoices. Explain why, and what you would use instead.
subjective.answer: Combine by Position pairs item 0 of Input 1 with item 0 of Input 2, then item 1 with item 1, and so on. It knows nothing about the data. If the two APIs return records in a different order, or one customer has no invoice, every pair after that point shifts, and customers get the wrong invoices. This is a silent data bug, not an error, which makes it dangerous. When both sides share a key such as customer_id, I would use Combine by Matching Fields on that key instead. I would choose 'Enrich Input 1' if every customer must appear, or 'Keep Matches' if only customers with invoices matter. If one customer can have several invoices, I would check that the output shape is what I expect. Position mode is only safe when both lists come from the same source in a guaranteed order with equal counts.
keyPoints: Position mode pairs items by index only
Different order or missing records shift every later pair
The result is wrong data with no error
Use Combine by Matching Fields on a shared key
Choose the output type: Enrich Input 1 or Keep Matches

subjective.question: Put these steps in order for safely changing a published scheduled workflow, and explain why the order matters: publish; edit nodes; pin real data from a past run; watch the next executions; test the changed nodes against pinned data; do one test run with live data.
subjective.answer: My order is this. First, pin real data from a recent run, or from a fresh test of the trigger and HTTP nodes. Then I have realistic input without hitting the API again and again. Second, edit the nodes. Third, test the changed nodes against the pinned data, including edge cases I add by editing the pin. Fourth, unpin and do one test run with live data, because production ignores pins and the live API may have changed. Fifth, publish, since in current n8n your edits do not reach production until the workflow is published again. Sixth, watch the next scheduled executions in the Executions list. The order matters because each step removes one risk before the next. Pins make testing fast and repeatable, the live run catches real-world differences, and publishing comes only after both pass. Watching Executions is the only proof that the schedule still works.
keyPoints: Pin real data before editing
Test edits against pins, including edge cases
Unpin and run once with live data
Publish so the changes reach production
Confirm with the next executions

subjective.question: Spot the mistake: an HTTP Request node fetches /customers/{{ $json.id }}, and an IF node after it checks whether the status code equals 404 to create missing customers. The workflow stops with an error whenever a customer is missing. Why, and how do you fix it?
subjective.answer: By default, the HTTP Request node treats any non-2xx response as a node error. A 404 stops the workflow before the IF node ever runs, so the 'missing customer' branch can never be reached. Also, without the Full Response option, the output would not include the status code for the IF node to check. To fix it, I open the HTTP node's options. I turn on 'Include Response Headers and Status', so the output contains statusCode, and I turn on 'Never Error', so a 404 passes through as a normal item. The IF node can then check statusCode equals 404 and send those items to the create branch. The body now sits under a body field, so later expressions must be updated. Another option is On Error set to 'Continue (using error output)', with the error output wired to the create step. I would still let real failures like 500s reach an alert rather than treat them as 'missing'.
keyPoints: The node errors on non-2xx responses by default
The IF node never runs on a 404
Enable Full Response (status) and Never Error
Or use the error output to handle failures
Do not treat 500s as 'not found'

subjective.question: A form tool calls your Webhook and times out after 10 seconds. Your workflow takes about 40 seconds to update the CRM. Submissions show errors to users, but the data does arrive. How do you redesign it?
subjective.answer: The caller waits for a reply, and n8n only replies when the workflow ends, which is too late. The data arrives because the workflow keeps running after the caller gives up. Users still see an error, and the form tool may retry, which creates duplicates. I have two options. If the caller only needs a simple acknowledgement, I set the Webhook node's Respond setting to Immediately, and it gets a quick success reply. If it needs a custom reply, such as JSON with a reference number, I set Respond to 'Using Respond to Webhook Node'. Then I place that node right after basic validation, before the slow CRM steps. The workflow continues after responding. Either way, I would make the CRM step idempotent, for example by checking whether the email already exists. That way, any retries already sent do not create duplicates. I then test with the Test URL, publish, and confirm response times in Executions.
keyPoints: The reply was sent only when the workflow finished
Respond Immediately for a simple acknowledgement
Place Respond to Webhook before the slow steps for custom replies
The workflow keeps running after the response
Guard against duplicate retries

subjective.question: Troubleshoot: a Merge node set to Combine by Matching Fields on customer_id returns zero items, although you can see matching IDs in both inputs. What is likely wrong?
subjective.answer: The most common cause is a type mismatch. One source sends customer_id as the number 1042, and the other sends it as the string "1042". Merge compares values strictly, so they do not match. I would open both input panels and look at the field type icons, or switch to the JSON view to see the quotes. Other causes to check are hidden spaces, different letter case in text IDs, and different field names, such as customer_id versus customerId. Different names need the 'Fields to Match Have Different Names' setting. To fix the type mismatch, I can turn on the Merge option Fuzzy Compare, which treats 3 and "3" as equal. The cleaner fix is to normalise the key first with Edit Fields, for example {{ String($json.customer_id).trim() }} on both branches. Then I rerun with pinned data from both inputs to confirm the matches.
keyPoints: Number versus string IDs do not match strictly
Check types in the input panel or JSON view
Also check spaces, letter case and field names
Use the Fuzzy Compare option or normalise with Edit Fields
Re-test with pinned data on both inputs

subjective.question: Spot the mistake: a Switch node routes tickets with rules priority equals 'High', 'Medium' and 'Low', plus a fallback output. Almost every ticket goes to the fallback. The API documentation shows values like 'HIGH' and 'high '. What is wrong and how do you fix it?
subjective.answer: String comparisons in the Switch node are exact by default. 'HIGH' and 'high ' with a trailing space are not equal to 'High', so they fall through to the fallback. The fallback output is doing its job here. It revealed the bug instead of silently losing tickets. To fix it, I would turn on the Ignore Case option on the Switch conditions. That handles 'HIGH' and 'high'. Ignore Case does not remove spaces, though. So I would also normalise the value, either in an Edit Fields node before the Switch with {{ $json.priority.trim().toLowerCase() }}, or directly in the rule's value expression. Then the rules compare against 'high', 'medium' and 'low'. I would keep the fallback connected to an alert or a review queue, so genuinely unknown priorities are still seen. Finally, I would edit pinned data to include messy values and test that each one routes correctly.
keyPoints: String comparison is exact and case-sensitive by default
Turn on the Ignore Case option
Trim and lowercase values to handle stray spaces
Keep the fallback output wired to review
Test messy values with edited pinned data

subjective.question: Case study: one workflow must send the same report at 9 AM IST to Bengaluru and at 9 AM London time to the UK team, all year. A teammate suggests one workflow with two Cron rules in UTC. What is the problem, and what would you build?
subjective.answer: The timezone is a workflow-level setting, so one workflow can only run its schedules in one zone. Fixed UTC rules work for India, because IST has no daylight saving: 9 AM IST is always 03:30 UTC. London, however, switches between GMT and BST. A rule at 09:00 UTC is correct in winter but arrives at 10 AM London time in summer. Someone would have to edit it twice a year. I would build two small trigger workflows. One has its timezone set to Asia/Kolkata and the other Europe/London, and each has a Schedule Trigger at 9 AM. Both call one shared report workflow through the Execute Workflow node, passing a parameter such as the team or channel. The report logic lives in one place, so changes are made once, and each schedule handles daylight saving automatically. I would publish all of them and check both teams' runs in Executions.
keyPoints: The timezone is set per workflow, not per trigger
IST has no daylight saving; London does
Fixed UTC rules drift by an hour for London
Use two trigger workflows with their own timezones
Share the logic through a sub-workflow

subjective.question: An HTTP Request node returns a single item, {"data": [ ...50 orders... ]}. The next IF node seems to run only once, and the Slack summary says '1 order'. What is happening and how do you fix it?
subjective.answer: n8n runs nodes once per item. Here the API returned one JSON object, and the 50 orders sit inside an array field called data. To n8n, that is one item, so the IF node evaluates it once and any count of items is 1. The fix is to turn the array into separate items. I would add a Split Out node after the HTTP Request and set 'Fields To Split Out' to data. Each order then becomes its own item. The IF node will check every order, and later nodes will run per order. If I want a summary afterwards, I would add Aggregate or Summarize before Slack to bring the data back into one item, so Slack sends one message instead of 50. I would always check the item count shown on the node output, not just the JSON, when an API wraps results this way.
keyPoints: Nodes run once per item
An array inside one item counts as one item
Use Split Out on the data field
Aggregate again before a single summary message
Check item counts in the output panel

subjective.question: Spot the mistakes in this Edit Fields node in JSON mode, which is meant to output name, email and a tags array.
subjective.answer: There are three problems. First, name is a string, but the expression is not inside quotes, so the result is invalid JSON, such as "name": Ravi, and the node errors. Second, email is quoted, which works until a value contains a double quote or backslash. Then the JSON breaks again. Third, tags is wrapped in quotes, so the array becomes a single text string instead of staying a list, and downstream nodes cannot loop over it. The safest pattern is to let JavaScript produce valid JSON values: "name": {{ JSON.stringify($json.name) }}, "email": {{ JSON.stringify($json.email) }}, "tags": {{ JSON.stringify($json.tags) }}. There are no surrounding quotes, because JSON.stringify adds them and escapes special characters, and it keeps arrays as arrays. For simple shapes like this, I would usually switch to Manual Mapping instead. You set each field's type, such as Array for tags, and avoid quoting bugs entirely.
keyPoints: An unquoted string expression gives invalid JSON
Quoted values break on special characters
Quoting an array turns it into a string
Use JSON.stringify() without surrounding quotes
Manual Mapping with typed fields is simpler

subjective.question: Troubleshoot: a scheduled report workflow runs twice at each scheduled time, and Slack gets duplicate posts. List the likely causes and how you would check each.
subjective.answer: I would check four things. First, duplicate workflows. Someone may have duplicated the workflow and published both copies, so I search the workflow list for similar names and check which ones are published. Second, the trigger itself. A Schedule Trigger can hold several trigger rules, and two rules might resolve to the same time. There might also be two Schedule Trigger nodes on the canvas. Third, the infrastructure. On self-hosted setups, two n8n main instances pointing at the same database, such as an old container that was never stopped, will each fire the schedule. In queue mode, triggers should run only on the main instance, not on workers. Fourth, an external caller. A cron job or another workflow might be calling a webhook in the same workflow. The Executions list helps here. It shows how each run was triggered and its exact start time, and two runs a few milliseconds apart point to two instances.
keyPoints: Duplicated workflows that are both published
Overlapping trigger rules or two Schedule Trigger nodes
Two main n8n instances sharing one database
External calls to a webhook in the same workflow
Use Executions timestamps to narrow the cause

subjective.question: For this week's task, compare running it on n8n Cloud and on a self-hosted n8n on your laptop or a VPS. What practical differences affect whether the schedule and webhooks work?
subjective.answer: On n8n Cloud, the instance is always on, webhook URLs are public HTTPS out of the box, and updates and backups are handled for you. You still must set the workflow timezone, for example Asia/Kolkata, and keep within your plan's execution limits. Self-hosted gives you full control and no per-execution pricing. However, the schedule only fires while n8n is running. A laptop that sleeps or shuts down simply misses runs. There is no automatic catch-up, so there are just gaps in Executions. Webhooks on a laptop are not reachable from the internet without a tunnel, and a VPS needs a domain, TLS, a reverse proxy and WEBHOOK_URL set correctly. You also set GENERIC_TIMEZONE yourself, and you handle updates, database backups and the encryption key. For a reliable daily schedule during learning, Cloud or a small always-on VPS works. A laptop is fine for building, but not for the checkpoint.
keyPoints: Cloud is always on, with public HTTPS webhooks
Self-hosted schedules fire only while the instance runs
Laptop webhooks need a tunnel; a VPS needs a proxy and WEBHOOK_URL
Timezone setup: workflow setting or GENERIC_TIMEZONE
Self-hosting adds maintenance: updates, backups, encryption key

subjective.question: Spot the mistake in this Schedule Trigger Cron expression, meant to run once at 8 AM IST on weekdays. Fix it and say what else to check.

code.code:
Schedule Trigger
Trigger Interval: Custom (Cron)
Expression: * 8 * * 1-5

subjective.answer: The first field is minutes, and * means every minute. So this runs every minute from 08:00 to 08:59 on weekdays, which is 60 runs and 60 Slack posts each morning. The fix is 0 8 * * 1-5: minute 0, hour 8, any day of the month, any month, Monday to Friday. n8n also accepts an optional leading seconds field, so be careful when copying six-field expressions from other tools. Two more checks are needed. First, timezone. The expression is read in the workflow's timezone, or the instance timezone if none is set, so set Asia/Kolkata in Workflow Settings. Otherwise 8 AM may mean 8 AM New York time. Second, publishing. A changed schedule only reaches production once the workflow is published. Then I would confirm a single run at 08:00 in Executions. For a simple daily time like this, the Days or Weeks interval with hour and minute fields avoids cron mistakes altogether.
keyPoints: * in the minute field means every minute
Correct expression: 0 8 * * 1-5
Watch for the optional seconds field
Set the workflow timezone to Asia/Kolkata
Publish and verify a single run in Executions

steps.overview: This step explains how data moves through an n8n workflow. Data travels as a list of items, and each item holds JSON. You will learn to read that data with expressions, reshape it with looping, splitting and aggregating nodes, and drop into the Code node when no built-in node fits. Level 1 and Level 2 knowledge checks test these ideas heavily, and they are the base for every real workflow you build.
objectives: Describe the n8n item structure (an array of objects with a json key and an optional binary key) and how nodes process items.
Write expressions with {{ $json }} and $('Node Name') to reference fields from the current or any earlier node.
Choose between automatic per-item processing, Loop Over Items, Split Out, Aggregate and Summarize for a given data shape.
Write a Code node in 'Run Once for All Items' and 'Run Once for Each Item' modes that returns valid n8n items.
Transform a CSV of orders into per-customer totals using both a no-code path (Summarize) and a Code node path.

concepts.explanation: An item is the unit of data in n8n. Each node receives and outputs an array of items. Each item is an object with a json key for structured data and an optional binary key for files. For example, a CSV with 50 rows becomes 50 items after parsing.

Most nodes run once for every incoming item automatically. If 50 items reach a Gmail node, it sends 50 emails. This is why you rarely need a manual loop in n8n. The node setting 'Execute Once' forces a node to run only for the first item.

An expression is JavaScript written inside {{ }} in a parameter set to Expression mode. {{ $json.email }} reads a field from the current item of the node's direct input. Expressions can call methods such as {{ $json.name.toUpperCase() }}. They also support n8n helpers like $now and $today (Luxon dates) and $jmespath.

$('Node Name').item.json.field gets the item in that node that is linked to the current item, using paired items. $('Node Name').first(), .last() and .all() give fixed positions or every item. The older $node["Node Name"].json syntax still appears in old workflows. The current $() syntax is the one to learn.

n8n tracks which input item produced each output item. This tracking is what lets .item find the matching item in an earlier node. Built-in nodes keep the links for you. A Code node that builds brand-new items can break them, which causes paired-item errors downstream.

This node splits incoming items into batches of a set size. It sends each batch through the 'loop' output, and when all batches are done it sends the combined results through the 'done' output. Use it for rate limits, very large datasets, or nodes that only process the first item. Do not use it for normal per-item work.

Split Out turns an array field inside one item into many items. Aggregate does the opposite and collects field values from many items into one item. Summarize works like a pivot table: it groups by 'Fields to Split By' and calculates Sum, Count, Average, Min, Max and similar values.

The Code node runs JavaScript or Python when built-in nodes cannot express the logic. 'Run Once for All Items' (the default) gives you every item through $input.all(). 'Run Once for Each Item' runs the code per item and exposes $json. The node must return items, which means objects with a json key.

keyFacts: Data between nodes is always an array of items, and each item looks like { json: {...}, binary?: {...} }.
{{ $json.field }} reads only from the node directly connected before the current one. Use $('Node Name') to read from any earlier node.
$('Node').item uses item linking. Use .first(), .last() or .all() when you need a fixed position or every item.
Code node default mode is 'Run Once for All Items'. $json is only available in 'Run Once for Each Item' mode.
In the Code node, $input.all(), $input.first() and $input.item read the node's input data.
Loop Over Items has two outputs: 'loop' for each batch and 'done' after every batch has been processed.
The Extract From File node parses CSV, XLSX and JSON files from binary data into items. CSV values usually arrive as strings.
On self-hosted n8n, the Code node can use external npm modules or Node built-ins only if they are allowed through NODE_FUNCTION_ALLOW_EXTERNAL or NODE_FUNCTION_ALLOW_BUILTIN.

example.caption: Code node (JavaScript, Run Once for All Items): per-customer order totals from parsed CSV items

pitfalls: Adding Loop Over Items for simple per-item work. Nodes already iterate over every item, so the extra loop only adds complexity.
Forgetting that CSV values are strings. Summing '120' and '80' gives '12080' unless you convert with Number() or set the field type in an Edit Fields (Set) node.
Using $json to read data from a node that is not the direct parent. It silently reads the wrong data; use $('Node Name').item.json instead.
Returning plain values or a single object from the Code node instead of an array of { json: {...} } items. This causes errors or unexpected output.
Building new items in a Code node and then using .item references downstream. This can raise paired-item errors; use .first() or .all(), or keep the item links intact.
Printing an object inside a text expression. It shows [object Object]; use JSON.stringify() or select a specific field.

workflow.title: CSV of orders to per-customer totals

steps.label: Trigger and load the file
steps.detail: Start with a Manual Trigger, then read the CSV with Read/Write Files from Disk (self-hosted), HTTP Request or a Google Drive download.

steps.label: Parse CSV into items
steps.detail: Use the Extract From File node with the CSV operation so that each row becomes one item with header-named fields.

steps.label: Clean and type fields
steps.detail: Use Edit Fields (Set) with expressions such as {{ $json.customer.trim() }} and convert the amount to a number.

steps.label: Group and sum
steps.detail: Use a Summarize node split by customer with a Sum of amount, or use the Code node shown in the example.

steps.label: Reference earlier node data
steps.detail: Add context such as the file name with {{ $('Read Orders CSV').first().json.fileName }} to prove you can reach any earlier node.

steps.label: Write results out
steps.detail: Send the per-customer items to Google Sheets, Postgres or a new CSV with Convert to File.

steps.label: Verify with pinned data
steps.detail: Pin the parsed CSV output, re-run the downstream nodes, and check that the totals and item counts match your source file.

project.title: orders-to-customer-totals
project.summary: A self-hosted n8n project that reads a CSV of orders, turns each row into an item, cleans the fields with expressions, groups them per customer with Summarize, and ranks the results in a Code node. docker-compose.yml runs n8n with file access, data/orders.csv is the input, workflows/customer-totals.json is the importable workflow, src/rank-customers.js is the Code node source, and README.md explains how items, per-item execution, expressions and paired items work in each node.
project.run:
docker compose up -d
docker compose exec n8n n8n import:workflow --input=/workflows/customer-totals.json
# open http://localhost:5678, create the owner account, open 'Orders to Customer Totals', click 'Execute workflow'

files.code:
# Runs a single self-hosted n8n instance for this lesson
services:
  n8n:
    image: docker.n8n.io/n8nio/n8n:latest   # official n8n image
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - "5678:5678"                          # editor UI at http://localhost:5678
    environment:
      - GENERIC_TIMEZONE=Asia/Kolkata        # timezone used by schedule nodes
      - TZ=Asia/Kolkata
      # Read/Write Files from Disk may only touch this folder
      - N8N_RESTRICT_FILE_ACCESS_TO=/files
    volumes:
      - n8n_data:/home/node/.n8n             # credentials, workflows, settings
      - ./data:/files                        # orders.csv is read from here
      - ./workflows:/workflows               # used by the import:workflow CLI

volumes:
  n8n_data:

# orders-to-customer-totals

Step 3 hands-on task: turn a CSV of orders into per-customer totals.

## Run
1. `docker compose up -d`
2. `docker compose exec n8n n8n import:workflow --input=/workflows/customer-totals.json`
3. Open http://localhost:5678, set up the owner account, open the workflow, click **Execute workflow**.

## What each node teaches
| Node | Concept |
|------|---------|
| Read Orders CSV | Output is 1 item with binary data (`data`), not JSON rows yet |
| Extract CSV | 1 file becomes 10 items. Each item is `{ json: {...} }`, all values are strings |
| Clean Fields | Per-item execution: expressions run once per item. `$json.amount` is the current item. `$('Extract CSV').item` uses paired items to find the matching earlier item |
| Total per Customer | Summarize groups items by `customer`, giving `sum_amount` and `count_order_id` |
| Rank Customers | Code node for logic nodes cannot do: share %, rounding, sorting. Uses `$('Clean Fields').all()` to read an earlier node |

## Expected output (3 items)
| customer | orders | total | share_pct |
|----------|--------|-------|-----------|
| Kiran Foods | 3 | 3000 | 49.6 |
| Asha Traders | 4 | 2000 | 33.1 |
| Rahul Stores | 3 | 1049.25 | 17.3 |

`all_orders` is 10 on every row. Note " Asha Traders " was trimmed, so it joined the right group.

## Checkpoint exercises
- In Clean Fields add `source_row = {{ $('Extract CSV').item.json.order_id }}`. This is referencing an earlier node.
- Replace Summarize with Aggregate ("All Item Data") and see 1 item with an array.
- After Extract CSV add Loop Over Items (batch size 3) to process rows in batches, e.g. for rate-limited APIs.
- Use Split Out on the Aggregate array to get items back.

## Tips
- `$json` = current item. `$('Node').item` = paired item. `.first()`, `.last()`, `.all()` work on any earlier node.
- Code node must return an array of `{ json: {...} }` objects.

revision.examFocus: This step maps to the data-handling parts of the n8n Level 1 and Level 2 courses. It covers the item data structure, expressions, referencing earlier nodes, splitting, merging and aggregating items, and the Code node. The knowledge checks usually show a short workflow or a snippet of expression or code. You then pick the output, the correct syntax, or the node that fits the job. Read every expression carefully. A single wrong reference ($json vs $('Node')) or mode (all items vs each item) is often the whole question.

compare.difference: $json reads only the current input item from the directly connected parent node. $('Node Name').item follows item linking back to the matching item in any earlier node.
compare.chooseA: Pick $json when the field comes from the node wired straight into the current one.
compare.chooseB: Pick $('Node Name').item.json when the field lives two or more nodes back, or on a different branch that has already executed.

compare.difference: .item depends on paired-item links and gives the item that matches the current one. .first() and .all() ignore links and use fixed positions.
compare.chooseA: Use .item when each output item must line up with its own source item, such as the same order or the same row.
compare.chooseB: Use .first() for a single config or token item, and .all() when you need every item. Also use them when links were broken, for example after a Code node created new items.

compare.difference: Split Out turns one item that holds an array into many items. Aggregate combines many items into one item with an array field. Summarize groups items and calculates values such as sum, count, min, max or average, like a pivot table.
compare.chooseA: Choose Split Out when an API returns a list inside one item and you need to process each element.
compare.chooseB: n/a

cues.cue: field from a node that is not directly connected
cues.pick: $('Node Name').item.json.field
cues.why: $json only sees the direct parent's output, so it would silently read the wrong data.

cues.cue: total per customer / count per category / group by
cues.pick: Summarize node (Group By + Sum or Count)
cues.why: It does grouped calculations without code and returns one item per group.

cues.cue: API rate limit, process N records at a time, wait between calls
cues.pick: Loop Over Items with a batch size, plus a Wait node inside the loop
cues.why: This is the real use for batching. Plain per-item work needs no loop.

cues.cue: one item contains an array of line items
cues.pick: Split Out on that array field
cues.why: It turns array elements into separate items, so later nodes run once per element.

cues.cue: logic no built-in node can do, e.g. custom maths across all items
cues.pick: Code node in 'Run Once for All Items' mode
cues.why: You get every item through $input.all() and can return any number of new items.

cues.cue: output shows [object Object]
cues.pick: JSON.stringify() or a specific sub-field
cues.why: A text expression converts an object to a string unless you serialise it or pick one field.

cues.cue: sum looks like '12080' instead of 200
cues.pick: Number() or set the field type to Number in Edit Fields (Set)
cues.why: CSV values arrive as strings, and + joins strings together instead of adding them.

cues.cue: paired item / 'can't determine which item to use' error
cues.pick: Switch to .first() or .all(), or keep item links intact in the Code node
cues.why: .item needs links that new items built in code do not have.

scenario.situation: A shop uploads a daily orders CSV with columns order_id, customer_email and amount. You read the file and use Extract From File to get one item per row. The manager wants one result per customer with the total amount spent. A colleague's draft uses Loop Over Items around a Code node that adds amount values with +, and the totals look far too large. What is the simplest correct fix?
reasoning: Spot the string trap first. CSV amounts are strings, so + joins them together ('120' + '80' = '12080'). That explains the 'far too large' totals.
Drop Loop Over Items. There is no rate limit or batch need, and nodes already process every item.
Look for a built-in node before writing code. Grouping by customer and summing a field is exactly what Summarize does.
Make the amount numeric. Set its type to Number in an Edit Fields (Set) node, or confirm that Summarize treats it as a number.
Reject a per-item Code node. It sees one row at a time and cannot build totals across rows.
scenario.answer: Use Extract From File, then Edit Fields (Set) to make amount a Number, then Summarize with Group By customer_email and Sum of amount. This removes the needless loop, fixes the string-concatenation bug, and returns one item per customer without any code.

memoryAids: Neighbour vs Name: $json reads your direct neighbour. For anyone further back, call them by name with $('Node Name').
Split spreads, Aggregate gathers, Summarize counts. One-to-many, many-to-one, many-to-groups.
Loop only for Limits: use Loop Over Items only when rate Limits, batch Limits or nodes that handle one item at a time force you to.
cheatSheet: Every node receives and returns an array of items. Each item keeps its fields under json, and files go under binary.
Most nodes run once per input item automatically, so check this before adding any loop.
Use $json for the direct parent and $('Node Name').item.json for any earlier node.
Use .first(), .last() or .all() when item links are missing or you need a fixed item.
Choose Code node 'Run Once for All Items' for cross-item maths. Use 'Run Once for Each Item' (where $json works) for per-row edits.
The Code node must return an array of { json: {...} } objects, even when there is only one result.
Wrap a CSV string field in Number() before adding it, or set its type in Edit Fields (Set).
Summarize handles grouped totals, counts and averages without code.
Use Split Out when an array inside one item should become many items.
Loop Over Items has two outputs: 'loop' runs per batch, 'done' fires once at the end. Connect the last node in the loop back to its input.
Use JSON.stringify() to print a whole object in text, otherwise you get [object Object].
Self-hosted only: npm or built-in modules in the Code node need NODE_FUNCTION_ALLOW_EXTERNAL or NODE_FUNCTION_ALLOW_BUILTIN.
selfCheck: I can write an expression that reads a field from a node three steps back, and explain why $json would fail there.
I can predict how many items each node outputs in a chain of Extract From File, Split Out, Summarize and Code.
I can write a Code node in 'Run Once for All Items' mode that returns correctly shaped items.
I can explain when Loop Over Items is truly needed and when it only adds complexity.
I can fix a paired-item error by choosing between .item, .first() and .all().
I can turn a CSV of orders into per-customer numeric totals without any string bugs.

objective.question: In n8n, what is the shape of the data that one node passes to the next?
options: An array of items, where each item has a 'json' key and an optional 'binary' key
A key-value map indexed by node name
A CSV string that the next node parses
A single JSON object with all fields merged
objective.explanation: n8n always passes an array of items, and each item looks like { json: {...}, binary?: {...} }. It is never a single merged object, a raw CSV string or a map keyed by node name.

objective.question: Your workflow is Webhook → HTTP Request → Slack. In the Slack node you write {{ $json.email }}, but email was only in the Webhook body. The result is empty. Why?
options: $json reads only from the node directly connected before the current one, which is HTTP Request
The Webhook node must be pinned before you can use its data
Slack nodes do not support expressions
Expressions cannot read webhook data
objective.explanation: $json refers to the current input item, which here comes from HTTP Request. To read the Webhook field, reference that node by name. Expressions do work in Slack, and pinning is not required.

objective.question: Which expression correctly reads the email field from the matching item of an earlier node called 'Webhook'?
options: {{ $node.Webhook.email }}
{{ $input.Webhook.json.email }}
{{ $('Webhook').item.json.email }}
{{ $json('Webhook').email }}
objective.explanation: $('Node Name').item uses item linking to find the item that matches the current one, and .json.email reads the field. The other forms are not valid n8n syntax for this purpose.

objective.question: A 'Get Settings' node returns one item that holds an API region. A later node processes 200 order items and every order needs that same region. What is the most reliable expression?
options: {{ $('Get Settings').first().json.region }}
{{ $json.region }}
{{ $('Get Settings').all().json.region }}
{{ $('Get Settings').item.json.region }}
objective.explanation: .first() always returns the first item at a fixed position, so all 200 orders get the same single setting. .item depends on item linking, which may not map 200 items to one. $json reads the wrong node. .all() returns an array, so it has no .json property.

objective.question: What is the default mode of the Code node when you add it to a workflow?
options: Run Once per Batch
Run Only on First Item
Run Once for All Items
Run Once for Each Item
objective.explanation: The Code node defaults to 'Run Once for All Items'. The only other mode is 'Run Once for Each Item'. The other two options are not real Code node modes.

objective.question: A learner pastes 'return { total: $json.price * $json.qty };' into a new Code node and it fails. What is the best fix?
options: Switch the mode to 'Run Once for Each Item', or rewrite the code to loop over $input.all()
Add a Loop Over Items node before the Code node
Use Python instead of JavaScript
Rename $json to $data
objective.explanation: $json only works in 'Run Once for Each Item' mode. In the default all-items mode you must read items with $input.all() and return an array. Adding a loop or changing the language does not fix the mode problem.

objective.question: In 'Run Once for All Items' mode, which return statement gives valid output?
options: return $json;
console.log($input.all());
return $input.all().map(i => ({ json: { id: i.json.id, ok: true } }));
return 'done';
objective.explanation: In all-items mode the node must return an array of items, each with a json object. A plain string is not valid. $json is not available in this mode. console.log returns nothing to the next node.

objective.question: The Loop Over Items node has two outputs. What do they do?
options: 'success' and 'error' for error handling
'first' for the first item and 'rest' for the others
'loop' gives each batch for processing; 'done' fires after every batch has been processed
'true' and 'false', like an IF node
objective.explanation: Loop Over Items sends each batch out of 'loop' and, once all batches are processed, sends the combined result out of 'done'. It has no true/false, success/error or first/rest outputs.

objective.question: An API accepts at most 50 records per request and rate-limits you. You have 1,000 items. Which design fits best?
options: Use Aggregate to put all 1,000 into one item
Use Split Out on the items
Use Loop Over Items with batch size 50, add HTTP Request plus a Wait node on the 'loop' branch, and connect them back to the loop
Send all 1,000 items to HTTP Request with no changes
objective.explanation: Loop Over Items processes controlled batches, and a Wait node spaces out the calls to respect the rate limit. Sending everything at once ignores the limit. Aggregate creates one huge payload. Split Out is for splitting arrays inside an item.

objective.question: Each order item has a lineItems array with several products. You need one item per product for the next node. Which node should you use?
options: Split Out
Merge
Summarize
Aggregate
objective.explanation: Split Out turns an array field inside an item into separate items. Aggregate and Summarize do the opposite and combine items. Merge joins data from two inputs.

objective.question: You have one item per order with customer and amount fields. You need total amount per customer with the least custom code. Which configuration is right?
options: Summarize with a Sum aggregation on amount and 'customer' in Fields to Split By
Split Out on customer
Loop Over Items with batch size 1
Aggregate with 'All Item Data'
objective.explanation: Summarize works like a pivot table. Sum on amount, grouped by customer through 'Fields to Split By', gives per-customer totals. Aggregate only collects items into one item without grouping. Split Out and Loop Over Items do not calculate totals.

objective.question: After Extract From File reads an orders CSV, your Code node does 'totals[c] = (totals[c] || 0) + item.json.amount' and returns '0120.5045'. What went wrong?
options: The Code node does not support decimals
JavaScript objects cannot use customer names as keys
CSV values usually arrive as strings, so + concatenated text instead of adding numbers
Extract From File rounds numbers
objective.explanation: CSV values usually arrive as strings, and in JavaScript 0 + '120.50' gives the string '0120.50'. Convert the value first, for example with Number(item.json.amount). The other options are false.

objective.question: An HTTP Request node downloads orders.csv as binary data. Which node turns it into one item per row?
options: Convert to File
Aggregate
Extract From File
Split Out
objective.explanation: Extract From File parses CSV, XLSX and JSON files from binary data into items. Convert to File does the reverse. Split Out and Aggregate work on JSON items, not binary files.

objective.question: On a self-hosted n8n instance, a Code node using require('lodash') fails with a 'module not allowed' type error. lodash is installed on the server. What must the admin do?
options: Add lodash to the NODE_FUNCTION_ALLOW_EXTERNAL environment variable and restart n8n
Set NODE_FUNCTION_ALLOW_BUILTIN to lodash
Switch the Code node to Python
Enable the module in the workflow's Settings tab
objective.explanation: External npm modules are blocked unless listed in NODE_FUNCTION_ALLOW_EXTERNAL. NODE_FUNCTION_ALLOW_BUILTIN is only for Node built-ins such as crypto. Workflow settings and changing language do not grant module access.

objective.question: Your Code node collapses 10 order items into 3 customer-total items. A later node uses {{ $('Orders Sheet').item.json.region }} and shows a paired item error. What is the most sensible fix?
options: Change $( ) to $json
Increase the batch size in Loop Over Items
The 3 new items do not link clearly to single original items, so use .first()/.all() or carry the region into the Code node output
Delete the Code node and use Split Out
objective.explanation: .item relies on item linking, and items created by grouping have no clear one-to-one link back to the source. Carry the field through, or use a fixed position or .all() logic. $json reads the wrong node, and batch size is unrelated.

objective.question: A CSV column header is 'Customer Name' (with a space). Which expression reads it correctly from the current item?
options: {{ $json["Customer Name"] }}
{{ $json.Customer_Name }}
{{ $json->'Customer Name' }}
{{ $json.Customer Name }}
objective.explanation: Field names with spaces or special characters need JavaScript bracket notation. Dot notation breaks at the space. n8n does not rename the field to Customer_Name, and -> is not valid expression syntax.

objective.question: A workflow reads 200 orders and ends with a Slack node that posts 'Daily orders processed'. The team gets 200 identical Slack messages. What is the simplest fix without changing the message?
options: Wrap the Slack node in a Loop Over Items node with batch size 1
Add {{ $json }} to the message text
Set the Slack node to 'Always Output Data'
Turn on the 'Execute Once' setting on the Slack node
objective.explanation: Execute Once makes the node run only once, using the first input item, so it sends one message. A loop still sends one message per item. Always Output Data only controls empty output, and adding $json just changes the text.

objective.question: This Code node runs in 'Run Once for Each Item' mode. The input is two items: {qty: 2, price: 50} and {qty: 1, price: 30}. What is the output?

code.code:
const j = $input.item.json;
return { json: { ...j, lineTotal: j.qty * j.price } };

options: Two items, each with its original fields plus lineTotal (100 and 30)
Two items holding only lineTotal, with the original fields removed
An error, because per-item mode must return an array
One item: {lineTotal: 130}
objective.explanation: In per-item mode the code runs once per item. Returning one object with a json key is valid. The spread copies the original fields and adds lineTotal. The node never sums across items.

objective.question: An earlier node 'Orders' output three items with amount 100, 250 and 50. What does this expression return in a later node?

code.code: {{ $('Orders').all().map(i => i.json.amount).reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0) }}

options: A paired item error, because .all() needs item linking
100, the amount of the paired item
objective.explanation: .all() returns every output item of the node, without using item pairing. map pulls the amounts into an array, and reduce sums them to 400. .item would return only the paired item.

objective.question: In 'Run Once for All Items' mode, a Code node builds new items from input items. Why might you add pairedItem to each returned item?
options: It tells n8n which input item each output came from, so later .item references to earlier nodes resolve correctly
It makes the node process items in parallel
It keeps binary data attached to each item
It is required, or the Code node fails to run
objective.explanation: pairedItem records item linking. Later nodes can then use $('Earlier Node').item and get the correct record. It is not mandatory, and it does not affect parallelism or binary data.

objective.question: A Filter node sometimes lets zero items through. The workflow then stops, and the final 'Log Run' node never executes. You want 'Log Run' to always run. What setting helps?
options: Set the workflow timeout to a higher value
Enable 'Retry On Fail' on the Filter node
Enable 'Execute Once' on the Log Run node
Enable 'Always Output Data' on the Filter node
objective.explanation: When a node outputs no items, downstream nodes do not run. Always Output Data makes the node emit one empty item, so the chain continues. Downstream logic must then handle that empty item.

objective.question: Three items each have an email field. You add an Aggregate node with 'Individual Fields' and choose the field email. What is the output?
options: One item with email set to an array of the three values
One item with a data field containing all full items
One item with email set to the count 3
Three items, unchanged
objective.explanation: Aggregate in Individual Fields mode collects the chosen field from all items into one array on a single item. 'All Item Data' would put whole items into a list. Counting is a Summarize operation.

objective.question: An HTTP Request node downloads a PDF invoice. Where does n8n keep the file inside the item?
options: In item.binary, under a property such as 'data', alongside item.json
Only on disk, with no reference in the item
In a separate execution called the binary run
As a base64 string inside item.json.file
objective.explanation: An item has a json part for structured data and an optional binary part for files. The binary part is keyed by a property name, 'data' by default. Metadata such as the file name and MIME type sits there, and json stays separate.

objective.question: You need today's date as 2026-03-15 in a file name. Which expression is correct?
options: {{ $now.toFormat('yyyy-MM-dd') }}
{{ $today('yyyy-MM-dd') }}
{{ new Date().toFormat('yyyy-MM-dd') }}
{{ $now.format('YYYY-MM-DD') }}
objective.explanation: $now is a Luxon DateTime, so you format it with toFormat and Luxon tokens (yyyy-MM-dd). format() with Moment tokens does not exist on it. A native Date has no toFormat, and $today is a value, not a function.

objective.question: You have to turn a downloaded orders CSV into per-customer totals with as little custom code as possible. Which node order is correct?
options: HTTP Request (download file) → Summarize → Extract From File (CSV) → Edit Fields (Set)
HTTP Request (download file) → Edit Fields (Set) → Extract From File (CSV) → Summarize
Extract From File (CSV) → HTTP Request (download file) → Summarize → Edit Fields (Set)
HTTP Request (download file) → Extract From File (CSV) → Edit Fields (Set) with amount typed as Number → Summarize (Sum of amount, split by customer)
objective.explanation: The binary file must exist before you can extract rows, and the rows must exist before you set field types. Amounts must be numbers before Summarize adds them. The other orders either try to parse a file that has not been downloaded yet or try to summarise binary data that has no rows.

objective.question: A Loop Over Items node has Batch Size 10 and receives 100 items. Only the first 10 items reach the HTTP Request node inside the loop. Then the workflow ends. What is the most likely cause?
options: The last node inside the loop is not connected back to the input of Loop Over Items
Loop Over Items only works with the Code node
The HTTP Request node needs 'Execute Once' enabled
Batch Size must equal the total item count
objective.explanation: Loop Over Items sends the next batch only when the loop branch feeds back into its input. Without that connection it emits one batch and stops. Batch Size, Execute Once and the Code node have nothing to do with this.

objective.question: Branch A has 500 order items, each with customerId. Branch B has 80 customer items, each with id and tier. You need every order enriched with the customer's tier. Which Merge node setup fits?
options: Combine → By Position
Choose Branch → Input 1
Combine → By Matching Fields, with customerId (input 1) matched to id (input 2)
Append
objective.explanation: Matching on the key joins each order to its customer, much like a SQL join. Append just stacks the two lists. By Position pairs item 1 with item 1 regardless of customer. Choose Branch throws away one input.

objective.question: A Slack message field contains this text. The Slack post shows 'Customer: [object Object]'. What is the fix?
options: Switch the Slack field from Expression to Fixed mode
Use {{ $json['customer'] }} instead
Select a specific field such as {{ $json.customer.name }}, or use {{ JSON.stringify($json.customer) }}
Wrap the field in quotes: '{{ $json.customer }}'
objective.explanation: Putting an object into a text template converts it to the string '[object Object]'. Either pick a primitive field or serialise the object. Quotes and bracket notation still return the same object. Fixed mode would print the braces as literal text.

objective.question: This Code node is in 'Run Once for All Items' mode. It fails with an error about not returning items. Why?
options: Number() is not available in the Code node
You cannot change item.json in place
$input.all() is only valid in 'Run Once for Each Item' mode
There is no return statement, so the node produces no valid output
objective.explanation: The loop updates the items but never returns them. Adding 'return $input.all();' or returning a mapped array fixes it. Number() and $input.all() both work in this mode.

objective.question: An Edit Fields (Set) node adds a field amountNum = {{ Number($json.amount) }}. After it runs, customer and orderId have disappeared and only amountNum remains. What is the cause?
options: Edit Fields always replaces the whole item, and nothing can change that
The 'Include Other Input Fields' option is off, so only the fields you set are output
The node must be in JSON mode to keep fields
Number() deletes the other fields it does not use
objective.explanation: Edit Fields outputs only the fields you define unless you turn on 'Include Other Input Fields' and choose to include all fields or selected ones. JSON mode does not change this, and Number() does not touch other fields.

objective.question: Some CSV rows have no address object. This expression then fails with 'Cannot read properties of undefined'. Which replacement is safest?

code.code: {{ $json.address.city }}

options: {{ $json['address.city'] }}
{{ $json.address.city.toString() }}
{{ $json.address?.city ?? 'Unknown' }}
{{ $json.address.city || 'Unknown' }}
objective.explanation: Optional chaining stops at the missing address, and ?? supplies a default value. With || the code still evaluates address.city first, so it still throws. 'address.city' as a single key looks for a field literally named with a dot. Calling toString() fails in the same way as the original.

objective.question: A workflow gives correct totals when you click 'Execute workflow' in the editor. After you activate it, the scheduled runs produce totals from a different set of orders. Nothing else changed. What should you check first?
options: Whether the Code node is in the wrong mode
Whether expressions are disabled in production
Whether a node has pinned data: pinned data is used in manual runs but ignored in production executions
Whether the Schedule Trigger uses UTC
objective.explanation: Pinned test data makes manual runs repeatable, but production executions fetch live data. So the two can differ. Expressions and the Code node behave the same in both kinds of run.

objective.question: In a Code node set to 'Run Once for All Items', you need the region from the 'Orders Sheet' item that is linked to each input item. Which line goes in the gap?
options: $('Orders Sheet').itemMatching(i).json.region
$json.region
$('Orders Sheet').first().json.region
$('Orders Sheet').item.json.region
objective.explanation: In 'Run Once for All Items' mode there is no single current item, so .item cannot be used. itemMatching(index) follows the item links for a given input index. first() always gives the same row for every item, and $json is not defined in this mode.

objective.question: A designer puts Loop Over Items (batch size 50) → Edit Fields → Summarize (sum amount by customer) → back to the loop. The 'done' output goes to Google Sheets. The sheet shows several rows per customer with partial totals. What is the design mistake?
options: Google Sheets must be connected to the 'loop' output
Edit Fields cannot be used inside a loop
The batch size is too small for Summarize
Summarize runs inside the loop, so it totals each batch separately. It should run once on the full set after the 'done' output, or the loop should be removed
objective.explanation: Each pass of the loop gives Summarize only 50 items, so you get one total per batch. Since nodes already process every item, this task needs no loop at all. Changing the batch size or rewiring Sheets does not fix the per-batch grouping.

objective.question: You must call an API once per order for 2,000 orders. The API allows about 10 requests per second. You want the simplest reliable design. Which is better?
options: Loop Over Items with batch size 1 and no Wait node
The HTTP Request node's built-in Batching option, with items per batch and a batch interval
Execute Once on the HTTP Request node
A Code node that calls the API in a for loop
objective.explanation: The HTTP Request node can throttle itself, so you need no extra loop wiring. A loop without a Wait node does not slow the calls down. Execute Once would send only one request. A hand-written loop in code is harder to maintain and to retry.

objective.question: You need total sales per customer per month. Each order has an ISO date string such as '2026-03-15T10:20:00Z'. What should you do before the Summarize node?
options: Add an Edit Fields node with month = {{ DateTime.fromISO($json.date).toFormat('yyyy-MM') }}, then split by customer and month
Use Split Out on the date field
Sort the items by date, and Summarize will group the months automatically
Nothing: Summarize can group by part of a date string
objective.explanation: Summarize groups by exact field values, so you need a month field first. Luxon's DateTime is available in expressions. Split Out is for arrays, and sorting does not create groups.

objective.question: The orders CSV export sometimes repeats the same orderId on two rows, and the customer totals come out inflated. Which change fixes it cleanly?
options: Change the Summarize aggregation from Sum to Max
Turn on 'Always Output Data' in Extract From File
Add Loop Over Items with batch size 1
Add a Remove Duplicates node that compares orderId, placed before Summarize
objective.explanation: Removing duplicate orderIds before you aggregate means each order is counted once. Max gives a different metric, not a corrected sum. The other two options do not affect duplicate rows at all.

objective.question: An If node sends paid orders to 'Send Invoice' (true branch) and unpaid orders to 'Send Reminder' (false branch). Inside 'Send Reminder' you use {{ $('Send Invoice').item.json.invoiceId }} and get an error. Why?
options: 'Send Invoice' did not run for these items, so there is no data or item link to reference
invoiceId must be read with $input instead
The If node removes item links
Expressions cannot reference nodes by name
objective.explanation: A node can only read data from nodes that ran earlier on its own path. 'Send Invoice' is on the other branch. Reference a node that is upstream of both branches instead. The If node keeps item links intact.

objective.question: After Summarize gives one item per customer with the total, you need only the 3 customers with the highest totals. Which is the better approach?
options: A Merge node in Choose Branch mode
A Sort node (total, descending) followed by a Limit node (max items 3)
A Code node that loops with Run Once for Each Item
A Filter node on total > 1000
objective.explanation: Sort and Limit express 'top N' directly, and both are easy to read. A fixed threshold can return more or fewer than 3 customers. In 'Run Once for Each Item' mode the code cannot compare items with each other.

objective.question: This Code node is in 'Run Once for Each Item' mode and receives 4 items. What happens?
options: It throws an error, because $input.all() is forbidden
It returns 4 items, each with its own amount
It returns 4 items, each with the same grand total, because the code runs once per item
It returns 1 item with the grand total
objective.explanation: In per-item mode the script runs for every input item, so it outputs 4 items. Each run reads all items and builds the same sum. To get one summary item, switch to 'Run Once for All Items' and return an array.

subjective.question: Explain how n8n passes data from one node to the next.
subjective.answer: n8n passes data as an array of items. Each item is an object with a json key that holds the fields, and an optional binary key for files such as PDFs, images or CSVs. A node receives this array, does its work, and outputs a new array of items for the next node. Even a single record is wrapped as an array with one item. This matters in practice. When I inspect a node's output in table, JSON or schema view, I am looking at those items. When I write expressions or Code node logic, I read item.json.field. If a node outputs zero items, the next nodes usually do not run. Thinking in items is the base for everything else in n8n.
keyPoints: Data is always an array of items
Each item is { json: {...}, binary?: {...} }
A single record is still an array of one item
Binary holds files; json holds fields
Zero output items usually stops the downstream nodes

subjective.question: What does per-item execution mean in n8n, and what mistake can it cause?
subjective.answer: Most n8n nodes run their operation once for every input item. If a Gmail node gets 25 items, it sends 25 emails, one per item, and each expression is evaluated using that item's data. This is powerful because you rarely need an explicit loop. It can also cause surprises. A common mistake is placing a 'send summary' Slack message after a node that outputs 100 rows, so the team gets 100 messages. The fix is to collapse items first with Aggregate or Summarize, or to turn on the node's 'Execute Once' setting, which uses only the first item. I always check the item count on a node's input before I add a node with side effects such as emails, payments or database writes.
keyPoints: Most nodes run once per input item
Expressions are evaluated per item
No explicit loop is usually needed
Risk of duplicate side effects such as 100 messages
Fix with Aggregate or Summarize, or the Execute Once setting

subjective.question: Compare {{ $json.field }} with {{ $('Node Name').item.json.field }}. When would you use each?
subjective.answer: $json is a shortcut to the current input item, which means the output of the node directly connected before the current node. It is the quickest option when the field I need comes from the previous step. $('Node Name') lets me reach any earlier node in the workflow by its name. Adding .item uses item linking to find the item in that node that corresponds to the item being processed now. For example, in Webhook → HTTP Request → Gmail, the Gmail node can read the API response with $json.status and read the customer's email with $('Webhook').item.json.email. One caution: if you rename a node, n8n updates references in the workflow, but it is still wise to give nodes clear names early.
keyPoints: $json reads only from the directly previous node
$('Node Name') reaches any earlier node
The .item accessor uses item linking
Combine both in a single node
Use clear node names

subjective.question: What are paired items (item linking) and why do they matter?
subjective.answer: Paired items are n8n's record of which input item produced each output item. When a node turns item 3 into a new item, n8n remembers that link. Then $('Earlier Node').item can trace back through the chain and return the matching earlier item, not just the first one. This is what lets a node use fields from several steps back for the correct record. Linking is clear for one-to-one nodes. It becomes unclear when items are merged, grouped, split or newly created, for example by a Code node that builds fresh items. Then you may see a paired item error or wrong data. Fixes include carrying needed fields forward, using .first(), .last() or .all(), or setting pairedItem in Code node output.
keyPoints: Tracks which input item produced each output item
Powers $('Node').item
Works cleanly for one-to-one transformations
Can break when grouping, merging or creating new items
Fix by carrying fields, using fixed positions, or setting pairedItem

subjective.question: When do you use .first(), .last() and .all() instead of .item on a node reference?
subjective.answer: I use .item when I want the earlier item that matches the current item through item linking. That suits record-by-record flows. I use .first() when the earlier node produces one item that every later item should share, such as a config lookup, an access token or a single settings row. .last() is useful when the final item matters, for example the latest page of a paginated result or the last status update. .all() returns every item from that node as an array.
