I use it when I need to count, search or sum, for example {{ $('Orders').all().length }}. Because .all() returns an array, I must map or index it. I cannot call .json on it directly.
keyPoints: .item follows item linking for the matching record
.first() for a single shared value such as config
.last() when the final item matters
.all() returns an array of all items
Do not call .json directly on the .all() result

subjective.question: Compare the two Code node modes and say how you read input in each.
subjective.answer: 'Run Once for All Items' is the default. The code runs a single time and sees every input item together. I read items with $input.all(), $input.first() or $input.last(), and I must return an array of items, each like { json: {...} }. This mode suits grouping, totals, de-duplication and sorting, because those need all the rows at once. 'Run Once for Each Item' runs the code separately for each item. Here I can use $json or $input.item.json, and I return one item object. It suits simple per-record changes such as building a full name or cleaning a phone number. A common error is using $json in all-items mode. It is not available there, so the code fails.
keyPoints: The default is Run Once for All Items
All-items mode: $input.all() and return an array
Each-item mode: $json or $input.item, return one item
Grouping needs all-items mode
$json is not available in all-items mode

subjective.question: When should you reach for the Code node, and when should you avoid it?
subjective.answer: I first try built-in nodes such as Edit Fields (Set), Filter, IF, Split Out, Aggregate, Summarize, Merge and Remove Duplicates. They are visible, easy for teammates to maintain, and keep item linking clean. I reach for the Code node when logic is hard to express with nodes. Examples are complex parsing, multi-condition grouping, custom sorting, building nested payloads, or calculations across many items. The Code node supports JavaScript and Python. The trade-offs are real. Code is harder for non-developers to read. Errors only appear when the workflow runs. New items can lose paired item links. On n8n Cloud you also cannot freely import external modules. My rule: use nodes first, and use code to fill the gaps, with short, commented blocks.
keyPoints: Prefer built-in nodes for clarity and maintenance
Use Code for logic nodes cannot express
Supports JavaScript and Python
Risks: readability and broken item linking
Keep code blocks short and commented

subjective.question: Explain how to wire Loop Over Items correctly and when it is actually needed.
subjective.answer: Most nodes already process every item, so I do not add Loop Over Items by default. I use it when I need control over batches. Typical cases are rate-limited APIs, services that accept a limited number of records per call, adding a Wait between calls, or nodes that only handle the first item. Wiring: set Batch Size, then connect the 'loop' output to the processing nodes, for example HTTP Request and then Wait. Connect the last processing node back into the Loop Over Items input. When every batch is done, the 'done' output fires with the combined results, and I continue the workflow from there. A common bug is forgetting the connection back to the loop, so only the first batch runs.
keyPoints: Not needed for normal per-item processing
Use it for rate limits, batch-size limits and adding waits
The 'loop' output goes to the processing nodes
The last node connects back to the loop input
The 'done' output continues after all batches

subjective.question: What is the difference between Split Out, Aggregate and Summarize? Give an example of each.
subjective.answer: Split Out takes an array field inside an item and makes one item per element. For example, one order with a lineItems array becomes one item per product. Aggregate does the opposite. It combines many items into a single item, either collecting specific fields into lists or putting all item data into one array. For example, it can gather 30 email addresses into one list for a single bulk API call. Summarize works like a spreadsheet pivot table. It calculates values such as count, sum, average, min or max, optionally grouped by fields to split by. For example, it can give the total order amount per customer. In short: Split Out expands, Aggregate collects, and Summarize calculates.
keyPoints: Split Out turns an array into many items
Aggregate turns many items into one item with lists
Summarize gives pivot-style counts and sums with grouping
Real example for each
Expand vs collect vs calculate

subjective.question: Walk through building the hands-on task: a CSV of orders transformed into per-customer totals.
subjective.answer: First, get the file. I use a trigger, then an HTTP Request node or a file-reading node, so the CSV arrives as binary data. Second, Extract From File, set to CSV, turns each row into an item with fields such as order_id, customer and amount. Third, I fix data types. CSV values usually arrive as strings, so I use Edit Fields to set amount as a number, for example {{ $json.amount.toNumber() }}, and I trim customer names. Fourth, a Summarize node with Sum on amount, split by customer, gives one item per customer. Finally, I check the output count against the number of unique customers and spot-check one total by hand. Then I send the result to a Google Sheet or Slack.
keyPoints: Get the CSV as binary data
Extract From File in CSV mode gives items
Convert strings to numbers and clean names
Summarize: Sum of amount split by customer
Verify counts and spot-check totals

subjective.question: Write the core of a Code node (JavaScript, default mode) that produces per-customer totals, and explain it.
subjective.answer: In 'Run Once for All Items' mode I would write: const totals = {}; for (const item of $input.all()) { const c = String(item.json.customer).trim(); const amt = Number(item.json.amount) || 0; totals[c] = (totals[c] || 0) + amt; } return Object.entries(totals).map(([customer, total]) => ({ json: { customer, total: Math.round(total * 100) / 100 } })); The loop reads every input item. Number() is essential because CSV values are strings, and without it + would join text. Trimming avoids treating 'Asha ' and 'Asha' as different customers. The return maps the totals object to an array of items, each with a json key, which is the format the next node expects. Rounding avoids floating-point noise in currency values.
keyPoints: Use default all-items mode with $input.all()
Convert amount with Number()
Normalise customer keys with trim
Return an array of { json: {...} } items
Round currency values

subjective.question: Why do data types matter when processing CSV data in n8n, and how do you handle them?
subjective.answer: Extract From File usually gives CSV values as strings, even when they look like numbers or dates. This causes quiet bugs. Adding strings joins them as text. Comparisons such as '100' > '20' compare text, not numbers. Filters on dates may fail. I handle this early, right after parsing. In Edit Fields I set the field type to Number or Boolean, or I use expressions such as {{ $json.amount.toNumber() }}. In a Code node I use Number() or parseFloat(). For dates I convert to a proper date, for example with Luxon's DateTime in expressions. I also watch for empty cells, commas inside numbers like '1,200', and currency symbols, and I clean these before converting.
keyPoints: CSV values usually arrive as strings
Risks: text joining and wrong comparisons
Convert early with Edit Fields or toNumber()
Use Number() or parseFloat() in code
Clean commas, symbols and empty cells

subjective.question: An expression referencing an earlier node returns the wrong record or a paired item error. How do you debug it?
subjective.answer: First, I check the item counts on each node between the source and the current node. If counts change, item linking may be unclear. Second, I open the expression editor and look at the live preview for several items, not only the first. Third, I look for nodes that create or reshape items, such as Code, Aggregate, Summarize or Merge, because they can break or blur paired items. Fixes depend on intent. If I need one shared value, I use .first(). If I need the correct record, I carry the field forward with Edit Fields before the reshaping node. In a Code node I can set pairedItem on the output items. Pinning test data helps me reproduce the issue quickly.
keyPoints: Compare item counts across nodes
Preview the expression for several items
Find nodes that reshape items
Use .first() or carry fields forward
Set pairedItem in Code output; pin test data

subjective.question: On self-hosted n8n, how do you allow the Code node to use npm modules or Node built-ins, and what are the risks?
subjective.answer: By default, the Code node cannot require external npm modules or most Node built-in modules. On self-hosted n8n, an admin enables them with environment variables. NODE_FUNCTION_ALLOW_BUILTIN lists built-ins such as crypto. NODE_FUNCTION_ALLOW_EXTERNAL lists installed npm packages such as lodash or moment. The external modules must also be installed where n8n runs, for example in a custom Docker image. Then n8n is restarted. The risks are about security and stability. Any workflow editor can run code with those modules, so allowing everything with a wildcard gives broad access to the server. I allow only specific modules that are needed, pin their versions, and keep the list documented. On n8n Cloud this kind of server control is generally not available.
keyPoints: Blocked by default
NODE_FUNCTION_ALLOW_BUILTIN for Node built-ins
NODE_FUNCTION_ALLOW_EXTERNAL for npm packages
Install the modules and restart n8n
Allow only what is needed; avoid wildcards

subjective.question: Explain n8n expression syntax and give practical examples, including referencing a field from any earlier node.
subjective.answer: Expressions sit inside double curly braces in a parameter set to Expression mode. They contain JavaScript, so I can use operators, string methods and ternaries. Examples: {{ $json.firstName + ' ' + $json.lastName }} joins names. For fields with spaces I use bracket notation: {{ $json['Customer Name'] }}. I can add defaults with {{ $json.city ?? 'Unknown' }}. For dates I use {{ $now.toFormat('yyyy-MM-dd') }}. To read from any earlier node I use {{ $('Webhook').item.json.body.orderId }} for the matching record, or {{ $('Settings').first().json.region }} for a single shared value. I always check the inline preview, and I drag fields from the input panel to avoid typos in paths.
keyPoints: {{ }} contains JavaScript
Bracket notation for fields with spaces
Defaults with ?? and dates with $now
$('Node').item or .first() for earlier nodes
Use the preview and drag-and-drop fields

subjective.question: The orders CSV stores amounts as text like '₹1,200.50' and some rows are blank. How would you clean this before summing per customer?
subjective.answer: Extract From File gives every value as a string, so I clean the data before any maths. In a Code node, or an Edit Fields expression, I remove the currency symbol and the thousands separators: String(v).replace(/[^0-9.-]/g, ''). Then I wrap the result in Number(). If the result is NaN or the field was empty, I decide on a rule. Usually I skip the row, or route it to an error branch with a Filter or IF node. Treating it as 0 silently is risky. I also trim and normalise the customer key, for example with trim() and toLowerCase(), so 'Asha ' and 'asha' fall into one group. Only then do I use Summarize or a reduce. I spot-check a few rows in the output panel to confirm the amounts are numbers, not strings.
keyPoints: CSV values arrive as strings
Strip symbols and commas, then use Number()
Handle blanks and NaN explicitly instead of silently
Normalise the grouping key
Verify the types in the output panel

subjective.question: When would you use the Edit Fields (Set) node instead of a Code node to reshape items?
subjective.answer: I use Edit Fields for most simple reshaping: renaming, adding computed fields with expressions, and dropping fields. It runs per item, and it is visual, so teammates can read it without knowing JavaScript. Its 'Include Other Input Fields' option controls whether you keep everything else or output only the fields you set. That makes it good for trimming payloads before an API call. It also keeps item pairing intact, because each output item maps to one input item. I switch to a Code node when I need logic across items, such as grouping, deduplicating with custom rules or complex parsing. I also switch when the expressions get so long they are unreadable. In short, Edit Fields handles per-item field work, and Code handles cross-item or algorithmic work.
keyPoints: Edit Fields handles rename, add and remove per item
Include Other Input Fields controls what passes through
It is readable and keeps pairing intact
Use Code for cross-item logic or complex parsing

subjective.question: A workflow is Schedule → Get Orders (sheet) → HTTP Request (fetch customer profile per order) → Email. The email must include the order ID and the customer's tier. How do you reference both, and why does it work?
subjective.answer: The HTTP Request node runs once per order item, so its output items stay paired with the order items. In the Email node, $json is the HTTP response, so I write {{ $json.tier }} for the tier. The order ID came from the sheet, so I write {{ $('Get Orders').item.json.orderId }}. That works because n8n follows the item links back from the current item to the matching order. The approach breaks if a node between them changes the item count without keeping links. Examples are an Aggregate, or a Code node that builds new items without pairedItem. In those cases I either carry orderId forward in the data or use a Merge node to join the data. I also check the HTTP node is not set to batch everything into a single request.
keyPoints: $json is the immediate previous node
$('Get Orders').item follows item linking
HTTP Request keeps 1:1 pairing per item
Count-changing nodes can break links
Carry fields forward or use Merge as a fallback

subjective.question: You must send a single summary email after processing 300 orders. Compare three ways to do it: Execute Once, Aggregate before the email, and .all() in the email expression.
subjective.answer: Execute Once makes the email node run once using only the first item. That is fine when the message is static, but you cannot list or total all orders from item data. Aggregate, or Summarize, collapses the 300 items into one item that holds an array or totals. The email node then runs once naturally, and the summary data is visible in the item. That makes debugging easy. Using {{ $('Orders').all() }} inside the email expression can also build a total or a list. But if the email node still receives 300 items, it will run 300 times unless Execute Once is also on. My preferred design is Summarize or Aggregate into one item, then email. It is explicit and testable.
keyPoints: Execute Once only uses the first item
Aggregate or Summarize yields one item with full data
With .all(), the node still runs per incoming item
Prefer collapsing to one item, then sending

subjective.question: Review this Code node (Run Once for All Items). It should return orders over 1000 with a flag. What is wrong, and how would you fix it?
subjective.answer: There are two issues. First, it pushes item.json, the plain object, into the array. The Code node expects items, so the safe form is out.push({ json: {...item.json, big: true} }). Current n8n versions often auto-wrap plain objects, but returning explicit items is clearer and portable. Second, it mutates the input item directly. That can confuse debugging and can affect references to earlier data, so I copy the object with spread instead. Also, amount from a CSV is probably a string. The string '999' compared with 1000 is coerced to a number by JavaScript, but a value like '1,200' becomes NaN and fails silently. So I use Number() after cleaning. Finally, the code drops rows, so I would add pairedItem if later nodes reference earlier ones with .item. A Filter node plus Edit Fields could replace this code entirely.
keyPoints: Return items shaped { json: {...} }
Avoid mutating input items
Convert string amounts explicitly
Add pairedItem when items are dropped or created
Consider Filter plus Edit Fields instead

subjective.question: Explain how binary data travels through an n8n workflow and how it relates to JSON.
subjective.answer: Every item has a json part and an optional binary part. Files are stored under a binary property name, 'data' by default. Examples are a downloaded CSV, an image or an email attachment. The property also holds metadata such as fileName, mimeType and fileExtension. Nodes that work on files, such as Extract From File, Write to Disk, Send Email attachments or HTTP Request uploads, ask for the binary property name. Expressions only see the JSON part, so you cannot read file contents with $json. You first convert the file, for example with Extract From File to turn CSV rows into JSON items. Some nodes drop binary data from their output, so you may need to keep it or re-reference it from the earlier node. On self-hosted setups, admins can configure binary data to be stored on the filesystem or external storage instead of in memory. This matters for large files.
keyPoints: An item has json plus binary
Binary data sits under a named property with metadata
Expressions read json, not file contents
Use Extract From File or Convert to File to switch formats
Storage mode matters for large files on self-hosted setups

subjective.question: A Filter node can return zero items, and the workflow then silently ends. How do you diagnose this, and what are the options and risks of fixing it?
subjective.answer: In the execution view, the workflow shows as successful, but the nodes after the Filter have no run. The Filter output panel shows 0 items. That is expected n8n behaviour, because nodes only run when they receive items. The options are these. First, enable Always Output Data on the Filter, so it emits one empty item and the chain continues. Second, use an IF node and handle the false branch explicitly. Third, keep the Filter's discarded-items output, if enabled, to log rejected rows. The risk with Always Output Data is that downstream nodes receive an empty item. They might send a blank email or write an empty row. I add an IF check such as {{ Object.keys($json).length > 0 }}, or a dedicated 'no data' branch. Explicit branching is usually clearer than relying on an empty item.
keyPoints: Zero items means downstream nodes do not run
Check the item counts in the execution view
Always Output Data emits one empty item
Guard against blank downstream actions
An IF node with explicit branches is often clearer

subjective.question: A CSV of orders is very large. Executions get slow or run out of memory. What design changes would you make in n8n?
subjective.answer: First, I reduce what each item carries. I use Edit Fields to keep only the needed columns early, and I avoid keeping large binary data after extraction. Second, I process in chunks. Loop Over Items with a sensible batch size can feed a sub-workflow through Execute Workflow. Each batch's data is then handled in a separate execution, and memory is not held for the whole file at once. Third, I push heavy aggregation to where it fits better. That might be a database query with GROUP BY, or a single efficient Code node reduce instead of many chained nodes. On self-hosted setups, I can also store binary data outside memory, raise the resources given to n8n, and use queue mode with workers. I also turn off saving full execution data for successful runs if it is not needed. I avoid quoting fixed limits, because they depend on the plan and the hardware.
keyPoints: Trim fields and binary data early
Batch and offload to sub-workflows
Push aggregation to a database or a single Code node
Self-hosted tuning: binary storage, resources, queue mode
Reduce saved execution data

subjective.question: What can you write inside {{ }} expressions, and when should logic move out of an expression?
subjective.answer: An expression is a single JavaScript expression evaluated per item. You can use operators, ternaries, string and array methods such as trim, split, map and join, and Luxon dates through $now and $today. You can also use n8n variables such as $json, $('Node'), $itemIndex and $execution. The examples here set a priority label, clean up a name, and compute a date seven days ago. Expressions cannot hold multi-statement logic such as loops with variables. A function wrapped in an IIFE is possible, but it becomes unreadable. I move logic out when the expression grows past one clear line, when it is repeated across many fields, or when it needs cross-item work. Then I use Edit Fields with simpler expressions, a Code node, or a Summarize or Aggregate node. I also guard against missing fields, for example $json.name ?? '', so the expression does not throw.
keyPoints: One JavaScript expression per field, evaluated per item
Ternaries, methods, Luxon and n8n variables are available
No multi-statement logic in practice
Move complex or cross-item logic to Code or other nodes
Guard against missing fields

subjective.question: Case study: every morning a supplier emails orders.csv as an attachment. You must ignore cancelled orders, compute per-customer totals, write them to Google Sheets, and post one Slack summary with the grand total. Design the workflow.
subjective.answer: I would start with an email trigger, such as Gmail or IMAP, set to download attachments. Extract From File then turns the binary CSV into one item per row. Next comes Edit Fields, where I type amount as a Number and trim the customer names. A Filter node drops rows where status equals 'cancelled'. I would add Remove Duplicates on orderId in case the export repeats rows. Summarize then sums amount, split by customer, and outputs one item per customer. Those items go straight to Google Sheets, which appends or updates one row per item. For Slack, I branch from Summarize into a second Summarize with no split field, which gives a single item holding the grand total. Slack then posts one message. I would also set Always Output Data or handle empty days, so a day with no orders still logs a result.
keyPoints: Extract From File turns the attachment into row items
Convert the types and filter out cancelled orders before aggregating
Summarize per customer, then a second Summarize for the single grand total
Slack receives exactly one item, so it sends one message
Handle empty days and duplicate rows

subjective.question: Troubleshooting: per-customer totals are suddenly two or three times too high. The only change was a new Merge node that adds customer details before Summarize. What is the likely cause and fix?
subjective.answer: The Merge node is most likely creating extra items. If it is set to 'Combine → All Possible Combinations', every order is paired with every customer row. If it matches on a key that is not unique, each order is duplicated once for every match. For example, the customer list may hold the same customer twice, or the match may be on a non-unique field like name. Summarize then sums the duplicated orders. To confirm, I compare the item count before and after Merge in the execution view. Orders in should equal orders out. To fix it, I use 'Combine → By Matching Fields' on a unique key such as customerId. I also remove duplicates from the customer list first, using Remove Duplicates on id. Another option is to move enrichment after Summarize, so I join 1 total to 1 customer instead of many orders to many rows.
keyPoints: Compare item counts before and after Merge
All Possible Combinations or a non-unique key multiplies items
Match on a unique key such as customerId
Deduplicate the lookup list, or enrich after aggregating

subjective.question: Put these steps in the correct order to process 1,000 contacts through a rate-limited API in batches of 25, then send one completion email: (a) connect the 'done' output to an Aggregate or Summarize, then the Email node; (b) add Loop Over Items with batch size 25; (c) connect the Wait node back to Loop Over Items; (d) add HTTP Request on the 'loop' output; (e) add a Wait node after HTTP Request. Explain why each step matters.
subjective.answer: The correct order is b, d, e, c, a. First, (b) add Loop Over Items with batch size 25, so each pass handles one chunk. Second, (d) put the HTTP Request on the 'loop' output, because that output carries the current batch. Third, (e) add a Wait node to pause between batches and stay under the rate limit. Fourth, (c) connect the Wait node back to the input of Loop Over Items. Without this link only the first batch runs. The node also collects results from each pass. Last, (a) use the 'done' output, which fires once with all collected items after the final batch. Put an Aggregate or Summarize there, so the Email node gets a single item and sends one email. If Email were connected straight to 'done' without aggregating, it would send one email per item.
keyPoints: Order: b, d, e, c, a
The 'loop' output carries each batch; 'done' fires once at the end
The loop-back connection is required, or only one batch runs
Wait controls the request rate
Aggregate before Email gives a single email

subjective.question: Spot the mistake: this Code node is meant to output one item per customer with a total. Downstream, the Google Sheets node writes just one strange row. What is wrong, and how do you fix it?
subjective.answer: The totals are correct, but the shape of the output is wrong. The code returns a single item whose json is an object keyed by customer name, such as { Asha: 320, Ravi: 90 }. n8n treats that as one item. Google Sheets therefore writes one row, with customer names as columns. n8n nodes work per item, so each customer should be its own item with fixed field names. The fix is: return Object.entries(totals).map(([customer, total]) => ({ json: { customer, total } })). Now each customer becomes an item with the same two fields, and Sheets writes one row per customer. This is a common Code node mistake. The output must be an array of { json } items, and its structure should match what the next node expects. Better still, a Summarize node would do this with no code.
keyPoints: Returning one item with dynamic keys gives a single row
Each customer should be a separate item
Use Object.entries(...).map(...) to build { json: { customer, total } } items
Keep field names fixed for downstream nodes
Summarize avoids the problem entirely

subjective.question: Which is better for per-customer totals in a team workflow: a Summarize node or a Code node? Argue both sides and give your choice.
subjective.answer: For plain per-customer sums or counts, I would choose Summarize. It is configured visually, so a teammate can see 'Sum of amount, split by customer' without reading code. It handles grouping by several fields and several aggregations at once, and it is less likely to break on edge cases. The Code node wins when the logic goes beyond simple aggregation. Examples are weighted totals, currency conversion with a lookup table, tiered discounts, or cleaning messy strings like '₹1,200.50' all in one pass. Code is also easier to unit-test mentally if the team is strong in JavaScript. Its downsides are maintenance, easy mistakes with the return shape and paired items, and the need to review it on every change. My rule: clean the types with Edit Fields, aggregate with Summarize, and use Code only for the part nodes cannot express. Keep that code small and commented.
keyPoints: Summarize is readable, configurable and low-risk
Code suits complex or conditional logic
Code adds maintenance, return-shape and paired-item risks
Prefer nodes and keep code small and focused

subjective.question: Compare two ways to throttle per-item API calls: the HTTP Request node's Batching option, and Loop Over Items with a Wait node. When is each the better choice?
subjective.answer: The HTTP Request node's Batching option is simplest when the only need is to space out the calls. You set items per batch and a batch interval, and the node handles the timing. There are no extra nodes and no loop wiring to get wrong. Loop Over Items with Wait is better when each batch needs several steps. Examples: call the API, transform the response, write to a database, and check for errors before the next batch starts. It is also better when you need a sequential step between batches, such as refreshing a token, or when other nodes in the batch must also be rate-limited. The trade-off is complexity. You must loop back correctly, collect results from 'done', and think about how item links behave across passes. I would start with the built-in batching option and move to a loop only when one node's setting cannot express the per-batch process.
keyPoints: Built-in batching suits rate-limiting a single node
A loop suits multi-node work per batch
A loop adds wiring and 'done' handling
Choose the simplest option that meets the requirement

subjective.question: Troubleshooting: after Extract From File reads a CSV, each item has a single field named 'customer;amount;date' with values like 'Asha;120;2026-03-01'. What is happening and how do you fix it?
subjective.answer: The file uses semicolons as separators, but the node is parsing it as comma-separated. Each whole line therefore becomes one value, and the header line becomes one long field name. This is common with exports from Excel in some regional settings. The fix is to open Extract From File's CSV options and set the delimiter to ';'. I then re-run the step and confirm that I see separate customer, amount and date fields. After that, I still convert amount to a Number in Edit Fields, because CSV values arrive as strings. If the first header appears with odd invisible characters, the file may have a BOM or a different encoding. I would check the encoding option or rename the field in Edit Fields. I would not split the strings in a Code node, because fixing the parser setting is cleaner and more robust.
keyPoints: The delimiter does not match (semicolon vs comma)
Set the delimiter in Extract From File options
Check the header row and encoding issues
Still convert numeric strings after parsing
Fix the parser rather than splitting strings in code

subjective.question: Spot the mistake: a learner wraps every node of a simple 'read sheet → add GST field → update sheet' workflow inside Loop Over Items with batch size 1 'to make sure each row is processed'. Review this design.
subjective.answer: The loop is unnecessary. n8n nodes already run once for each input item. An Edit Fields node that sets gst = {{ Number($json.amount) * 0.18 }} will process all 500 rows in one go. The update node will also write every item. Wrapping this in Loop Over Items with batch size 1 makes the workflow slower, because each pass adds overhead. It is also harder to read, and it creates new failure points: a missing loop-back connection, logic placed on the wrong output, and confusing item links between passes. A loop is justified only for real batch needs. Examples are API rate limits, payload size limits, or a sequence that must finish before the next batch starts. My review comment would be: remove the loop, chain read → Edit Fields → update directly, and check the item counts match.
keyPoints: Nodes iterate over items by default
The extra loop adds overhead and complexity
It brings wiring risks and item-linking confusion
Use loops only for rate limits, size limits or ordering needs

subjective.question: Case study: orders come in INR, USD and EUR. Finance wants totals per customer per currency, and a separate grand total in INR using a rates table held in another sheet. How would you build this?
subjective.answer: I would read the orders and use Edit Fields to set amount as a Number and normalise currency to upper case. For the per-currency report, Summarize sums amount, split by two fields: customer and currency. That gives one item per customer-currency pair, and I write those to the finance sheet. For the INR grand total, I read the rates sheet as a second branch. A Merge node set to 'Combine → By Matching Fields' then joins each order's currency to the rate's currency. After that, an Edit Fields node computes amountInr = {{ $json.amount * $json.rate }}. A second Summarize with no split field sums amountInr into one item. I would treat INR as rate 1 in the table, so it matches too. Finally, I would check the item count after Merge, because a missing currency would drop orders silently.
keyPoints: Summarize can split by several fields (customer and currency)
Use Merge by matching field to join the rates
Calculate the converted amount per item before summing
Include INR in the rates and validate item counts after Merge

subjective.question: Which is better for adding customer tier to 500 orders: a Merge node joining a customer list, or an HTTP Request per order to a profile API? Discuss the trade-offs.
subjective.answer: If the tiers can be fetched as one list, from a sheet, a database query or a bulk API endpoint, Merge by Matching Fields is usually better. It makes one or a few requests instead of 500. It avoids rate limits, runs faster, and is easy to see in the editor. The risks are joining on a key that is not unique, which duplicates items, and orders that have no match. I choose the Merge output mode with care to decide whether unmatched orders are kept. A per-order HTTP Request suits cases where the data must be live, or where no bulk endpoint exists. Then I would use the node's batching option to respect rate limits and add Retry on Fail. Downstream, $('Get Orders').item.json.orderId still works, because the HTTP node keeps item links. Overall: bulk fetch plus Merge for scale, and per-item calls only when necessary.
keyPoints: Merge means far fewer API calls and is faster
Watch for duplicate keys and unmatched orders
Per-item calls suit live data, but need batching and retries
Item links survive per-item HTTP calls

subjective.question: Spot the mistake: this Code node is in 'Run Once for Each Item' mode and is meant to add a grand total to a report. Execution is slow on 5,000 items and the output looks wrong. Explain the problem and the fix.
subjective.answer: In 'Run Once for Each Item' mode the whole script runs once per item. On 5,000 items, the reduce over all items runs 5,000 times, which is about 25 million additions. That explains the slowness. The output also has 5,000 items, each carrying the same grand total. That is probably not what the report needs. If the goal is one summary item, switch to 'Run Once for All Items' and return [{ json: { grand } }]. If every item really needs the grand total, still use 'Run Once for All Items'. Compute grand once, then return all.map(i => ({ json: { ...i.json, grand } })). This keeps the work linear. An even simpler route is Summarize with no split field for the total, followed by a Merge or an expression that uses .first() to attach it.
keyPoints: Per-item mode reruns the whole script for every item
The aggregation repeats N times (quadratic work)
Compute once in 'Run Once for All Items' mode
Return either one summary item or mapped items with the total

subjective.question: Troubleshooting: a workflow behaves differently depending on whether a node gets zero items or many. Explain how empty inputs, 'Always Output Data' and 'Execute Once' interact, with an example of misusing each.
subjective.answer: By default, a node that receives zero items does not run, so everything after it is skipped. 'Always Output Data' makes a node emit one empty item when it has no output. This keeps the chain alive. The risk is misuse. Put it on a Filter before a 'Create Invoice' node, and you may create a blank invoice on empty days. 'Execute Once' makes a node run only for the first input item. That is good for a single Slack notice after 200 orders. Misused on an HTTP Request that should update every order, it silently updates only the first order. My approach: use Always Output Data only where a downstream node can handle an empty item, such as a logging step. Use an If node to branch on whether real data exists. Prefer Aggregate over Execute Once when the single message must include data from all items.
keyPoints: Zero items means downstream nodes are skipped
'Always Output Data' emits an empty item and can trigger unwanted actions
'Execute Once' uses only the first item and can silently skip work
Guard with an If node; use Aggregate for summaries

subjective.question: In a Code node, how do you read data from a node that is not the direct parent? Explain the options for each mode and when each one is correct.
subjective.answer: In 'Run Once for Each Item' mode, $('Node Name').item gives the item from that node that is linked to the current item through paired-item data. This is right for per-row lookups, such as the original order behind an API response. In 'Run Once for All Items' mode there is no single current item, so .item is not available. Instead I loop over $input.all() with an index and call $('Node Name').itemMatching(i) to get the linked item for input i. In both modes, $('Node Name').first(), .last() and .all() ignore item links. first() suits a single settings item. all() suits building a lookup map. For large lookups I build a map once, for example from all() keyed by id, and read it inside the loop. This is faster and does not depend on item links surviving earlier Code nodes.
keyPoints: Per-item mode: $('Node').item follows the item links
All-items mode: use itemMatching(index)
first(), last() and all() ignore item links
Build a keyed map for large or link-free lookups

subjective.question: JavaScript or Python in the Code node: which would you choose for the CSV totals task, and why?
subjective.answer: I would choose JavaScript for this task. It is the main language of the Code node. Most of n8n's documentation, examples and community answers use it, and the same JavaScript syntax works in expressions. So what I learn carries over. Python is available and is fine for simple logic if the team knows it better. However, how Python runs depends on your n8n version and setup. Package availability is limited compared with a normal Python environment, and you should not expect libraries like pandas to be available by default. Python also uses different names for the built-in variables, which can confuse people who mix it with expression syntax. For summing amounts per customer, either language works in a few lines. But a Summarize node avoids the choice entirely. I reserve Code, in either language, for logic that nodes cannot express, and I check my instance's docs before relying on Python features.
keyPoints: JavaScript is primary, best documented and matches expression syntax
Python support and packages depend on the version and setup
Python's built-in variable names differ
Prefer Summarize for simple totals

subjective.question: Case study: a webhook receives an order with a lineItems array of products (sku, qty, unitPrice). You must store one row per product line in a database with the orderId, and reply to the webhook caller with the order total. Design it.
subjective.answer: I would set the Webhook node to respond using a 'Respond to Webhook' node, so I control the reply. Next, Split Out on body.lineItems turns one order into one item per product line. In its options I include the parent orderId field, or I add it afterwards with Edit Fields using {{ $('Webhook').item.json.body.orderId }}. This works because Split Out keeps item links. Edit Fields then calculates lineTotal = qty * unitPrice as a Number, and the database node inserts one row per item. For the reply, I branch after Edit Fields into Summarize, summing lineTotal with no split field, which gives one item. Respond to Webhook returns {{ $json.sum_lineTotal }} along with the orderId. I would check that qty and unitPrice are numbers, and handle an empty lineItems array so the caller still gets a response.
keyPoints: Split Out turns the array into per-line items
Carry orderId across through include options or item links
Calculate line totals as numbers before inserting
Summarize for the total; Respond to Webhook replies once
Handle empty arrays so the caller still gets a reply

subjective.question: Spot the mistake in these expressions used in an Edit Fields node after Extract From File (CSV). Explain each problem and give the corrected version.
subjective.answer: First, total: every CSV value is a string. qty * price is coerced to a number, but + shipping concatenates. So 2 * 50 + '10' gives '10010'. Use {{ Number($json.qty) * Number($json.price) + Number($json.shipping) }}, or type the fields as numbers first. Second, label: inserting $json prints [object Object]. Pick a field, such as {{ $json.orderId }}, or use JSON.stringify for debugging. Third, customer: a key with a space is invalid in dot notation. Use {{ $json['Customer Name'] }}. Fourth, region: Settings is a single-item node that is not linked to the CSV rows. .item may fail with a paired-item error, or return the wrong row. Use {{ $('Settings').first().json.region }}. Each fix makes the expression explicit about types, structure and which item it reads.
keyPoints: CSV strings cause concatenation with +; convert with Number()
An object in text prints [object Object]
Use bracket notation for keys with spaces
Use .first() for single-item settings nodes

steps.overview: This step takes you through the official n8n Course Level 1 on docs.n8n.io. You build a mini-workflow first, then the course's sample business workflow for the fictional company ABCorp: fetch orders, store them, filter, transform, summarise, notify the team and schedule the run. You then pass the final knowledge check to earn the Level 1 badge, which is the checkpoint for this step and the base for Level 2.
objectives: Navigate the n8n Editor UI: canvas, nodes panel, node details view, executions and workflow settings.
Build a multi-node workflow from a trigger through HTTP Request, Airtable, If, Edit Fields (Set), Code and Discord nodes.
Use credentials and expressions to pass data safely between nodes.
Schedule, activate, export and import a workflow as JSON.
Complete every course exercise and pass the final knowledge check to earn the Level 1 badge.

concepts.explanation: A trigger node starts a workflow. Examples are Manual Trigger, Schedule Trigger and Webhook. Action nodes do the work after the trigger, such as fetching, writing or sending data. A workflow that should run on its own needs a non-manual trigger and must be activated.

concepts.term: Items and the JSON data structure
concepts.explanation: Data moves between nodes as an array of items. Each item wraps its fields in a json key. A node usually runs once for each incoming item. So 30 orders entering a node means 30 runs, unless the node or Code mode processes all items together.

Double-click a node to open its NDV. It shows the input panel, the parameters and the output panel, and you can switch between Table, JSON and Schema views. You can drag fields from the input panel into a parameter to create an expression.

Expressions are written inside {{ }} and are evaluated for each item. For example, {{ $json.orderPrice }} reads a field from the current item. They let a node parameter use data from earlier nodes. The Discord message in the course uses expressions to insert the weekly totals.

Credentials store API keys, tokens or auth headers separately from the workflow, and they are encrypted. In the course you create credentials for the HTTP Request (header auth), Airtable and Discord. Credentials are not included when you export a workflow to JSON.
The If node checks a condition and sends each item to a true output or a false output. In the course it splits orders on orderStatus. Booked orders go one way and processing orders go the other.

This node adds, renames or keeps only selected fields. The course uses it to keep only fields such as orderID and employeeName for processing orders. You can set it to keep only the fields you define.

The Code node runs JavaScript or Python. In 'Run Once for All Items' mode you read every item with $input.all() and return an array of objects with a json key. The course uses it to count booked orders and sum their prices.

Use Test workflow or Test step to execute manually while you build. You can pin a node's output so later tests reuse it without calling the API again. Pinned data is used only in manual runs, never in production executions.

keyFacts: Course URL: docs.n8n.io → Courses → Level one. It is free and text-based. The badge is awarded after you pass the final quiz.
Sample workflow chain: Schedule Trigger → HTTP Request (get orders) → Airtable (insert) → If (orderStatus) → Edit Fields on one branch / Code (totals) → Discord (notify).
The course schedule is weekly: Mondays at 9:00.
A manual run does not make a workflow live. You must activate (publish) it before triggers like Schedule or Webhook fire in production.
Expression syntax is {{ }}. The current item is $json, and a named node's output is $('Node Name').item.json.
Code node output must be an array of objects, each with a json key. For example: return [{ json: { total: 5 } }].
An exported workflow is a JSON file containing nodes, connections and settings. Credentials are not included and must be re-created after import.
The If node has two outputs, true and false. Each output can connect to a different branch.
Workflow settings include the timezone. Schedule Trigger times follow the workflow or instance timezone.

example.caption: Code node ('Run Once for All Items') that counts booked orders and sums their value for the Discord message

pitfalls: Testing with the Manual Trigger and assuming the workflow is live. It only runs on schedule after you add the Schedule Trigger and activate it.
Leaving the Code node in 'Run Once for Each Item' mode. You then get one summary per order instead of a single total.
Returning plain values from the Code node instead of objects wrapped in a json key. This causes errors.
Hard-coding values that should be expressions, or referencing the wrong node name after renaming a node.
Pasting API keys into node parameters instead of using Credentials. Exported JSON can then leak secrets.
Forgetting that pinned data hides real API changes. Unpin before the final test.

project.title: n8n-level1-orders
project.summary: A local, offline copy of the n8n Course Level 1 business workflow. A mock orders API needs a header credential, and an n8n workflow fetches the orders, splits them with an If node, cleans the processing orders with Edit Fields (Set), and sums the booked orders in a Code node. docker-compose.yml runs n8n and the API, mock-api/server.js is the protected data source, workflows/orders-workflow.json is the exported workflow (trigger, action nodes, expressions, credentials, If, Set, Code and pinned data), and README.md maps each part to a lesson and lists the exercises.
project.run:
cp .env.example .env
docker compose up -d
docker compose exec n8n n8n import:workflow --input=/workflows/orders-workflow.json
curl -H "unique-id: $(grep ORDERS_API_KEY .env | cut -d= -f2)" http://localhost:3000/orders
open http://localhost:5678 (create the owner account, then add the 'Orders API header' credential)

files.code:
# Copy to .env. docker compose reads these values.

# Secret value that the mock API expects in the 'unique-id' header.
# In n8n you store this same value in a Header Auth credential, never in the node.
ORDERS_API_KEY=abc-corp-demo-key-123

# n8n uses this key to encrypt saved credentials. Keep it stable.
# If you change it later, n8n cannot decrypt the credentials it saved before.
N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY=change-me-to-a-long-random-string

# Timezone for Schedule Trigger and execution timestamps.
GENERIC_TIMEZONE=Asia/Kolkata

# Base URL the HTTP Request node reads via the expression {{ $env.ORDERS_API_URL }}.
# 'mock-api' is the docker compose service name, so n8n reaches it on the internal network.
ORDERS_API_URL=http://mock-api:3000

# Runs self-hosted n8n plus a tiny mock 'data warehouse' API.
services:
  n8n:
    image: docker.n8n.io/n8nio/n8n:latest   # official n8n image
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - "5678:5678"                          # editor UI: http://localhost:5678
    environment:
      - GENERIC_TIMEZONE=${GENERIC_TIMEZONE}
      - TZ=${GENERIC_TIMEZONE}
      - N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY=${N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY}
      - ORDERS_API_URL=${ORDERS_API_URL}
      # Lets expressions read $env.ORDERS_API_URL. Newer n8n versions block this by default.
      - N8N_BLOCK_ENV_ACCESS_IN_NODE=false
      - N8N_SECURE_COOKIE=false              # only for local http, never in production
    volumes:
      - n8n_data:/home/node/.n8n             # keeps workflows and credentials between restarts
      - ./workflows:/workflows:ro            # lets the CLI import our exported JSON
    depends_on:
      - mock-api

  mock-api:
    image: node:22-alpine
    working_dir: /app
    command: ["node", "server.js"]
    environment:
      - ORDERS_API_KEY=${ORDERS_API_KEY}
      - PORT=3000
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"                          # also exposed so you can test it with curl
    volumes:
      - ./mock-api:/app:ro

volumes:
  n8n_data:

# n8n-level1-orders

A local practice copy of the **n8n Course Level 1** business workflow (the ABCorp orders use case).
The official course uses its own hosted API and SaaS apps. Here a mock API stands in for them, so you can practise offline.
To earn the badge, you still complete the course on docs.n8n.io.

## Start
1. `cp .env.example .env`, then `docker compose up -d`.
2. Import the workflow: `docker compose exec n8n n8n import:workflow --input=/workflows/orders-workflow.json`
3. Open http://localhost:5678 and create the owner account.
4. **Credentials**: go to Overview > Credentials > Create > *Header Auth*. Set Name = `unique-id` and Value = your `ORDERS_API_KEY`. Save it as `Orders API header`.
5. Open the **Get orders** node and select that credential. The secret now lives in the encrypted credential, not in the workflow JSON.

## How each lesson maps to this project
| Lesson | Where to see it |
|---|---|
| Trigger vs action node | `Manual Trigger` starts the run. All other nodes are actions. |
| Items and JSON | The API returns an array, which n8n turns into one item per order. Each item is `{ json: {...} }`. |
| NDV | Double-click any node to see Input, Parameters and Output. Switch the view between Table, JSON and Schema. |
| Expressions | `{{ $env.ORDERS_API_URL }}`, `{{ $json.orderStatus }}`, and `.split(' ')[0]` in Edit Fields. |
| Credentials | The Header Auth credential sends the `unique-id` header. |
| If node | `Is processing?` sends processing orders to the true output and booked orders to the false output. |
| Edit Fields (Set) | Keeps only `orderID`, `employeeName` and `note`. Other fields are dropped. |
| Code node | Runs once for all items and returns one item with `totalBooked` and `bookedSum`. |
| Pinning | `Get orders` has pinned data, so test runs do not call the API. |

## Exercises
1. Click **Execute workflow** with the pinned data. The expected booked result is `totalBooked: 2, bookedSum: 2950`.
2. **Unpin** Get orders and run it again against the live API. The expected booked result is `totalBooked: 3, bookedSum: 3610`.
3. Use a wrong credential value. You should get a 401 error. Read the error in the NDV.
4. Add a Schedule Trigger (for example, every Monday 09:00 IST) next to the Manual Trigger, then activate the workflow.
5. In the Code node, round the average order value and add it to the output.

## Checkpoint
Finish every exercise in the official Level 1 course. Then pass its final knowledge check to earn the **Level 1 badge**.

revision.examFocus: This step maps to the n8n Course Level 1 final knowledge check. The quiz tests whether you understand core building blocks: triggers vs actions, items as JSON, expressions, credentials, If branching, Edit Fields vs Code, pinning, and activation. Questions are usually short scenarios from the course's sample order workflow, asking which node, setting or expression gives the correct result.

compare.difference: A manual test runs once in the editor while you watch. A scheduled workflow runs unattended only after it is activated.
compare.chooseA: Pick it when the question is about building, debugging or checking output step by step.
compare.chooseB: Pick it when the question says the workflow must run by itself every Monday at 9:00, or 'in production'.

compare.difference: Edit Fields adds, renames or keeps fields on each item without code. Code is for logic the built-in nodes cannot do, such as summing values across all items.
compare.chooseA: Pick it to add, rename or keep a few fields per item, with no calculation across items.
compare.chooseB: Pick it to aggregate, loop or transform with custom JavaScript or Python, such as a weekly total of order values.

compare.a: Code: Run Once for All Items
compare.b: Code: Run Once for Each Item
compare.difference: All Items runs your code once with every item available, so it can return one combined result. Each Item runs your code separately for every item, giving one output per input.
compare.chooseA: Pick it for totals, counts, averages or any single summary across orders.
compare.chooseB: Pick it when each order needs the same independent change and no item depends on others.

compare.difference: $json reads the item coming into the current node from the node directly before it. $('Node Name') reaches back to any earlier node by its exact name.
compare.chooseA: Pick it when the field comes from the node immediately before.
compare.chooseB: Pick it when the field came from an earlier node, for example the HTTP Request data used after an Airtable or If node.

compare.difference: Pinned data freezes a node's output so you can test downstream nodes without calling the API again. Live data shows what the service actually returns now.
compare.chooseA: Pick pinning to save API calls or rate limits while you build and test later nodes.
compare.chooseB: Pick live data, with pins removed, for the final test before activation or when the API response may have changed.

cues.cue: runs automatically every week / at a fixed time
cues.pick: Schedule Trigger, then activate (publish) the workflow
cues.why: Triggers fire on their own only in an active workflow; a manual test does not schedule anything.

cues.cue: one total / sum of all orders
cues.pick: Code node in Run Once for All Items mode
cues.why: Only this mode sees every item at once and can return a single summary item.

cues.cue: send items down different paths based on a value
cues.pick: If node (true and false outputs)
cues.why: Each If output connects to its own branch, for example processing vs booked orders.

cues.cue: use a value from a previous node dynamically
cues.pick: Expression in {{ }} with $json or $('Node Name')
cues.why: Expressions read data at run time, so values are never hard-coded.

cues.cue: store an API key or token securely
cues.pick: Credentials
cues.why: Credentials are encrypted and kept out of exported workflow JSON, so secrets do not leak when you share it.

cues.cue: keep only some fields / add a new field without code
cues.pick: Edit Fields (Set) node
cues.why: It is the no-code way to reshape each item.

cues.cue: avoid calling the API repeatedly while testing
cues.pick: Pin data on the HTTP Request node
cues.why: Downstream nodes reuse the frozen output, so the API is not called again.

cues.cue: workflow imported from a JSON file fails with auth errors
cues.pick: Re-create or re-select credentials in each node
cues.why: Exported workflow JSON never carries credential secrets.

scenario.situation: A company's workflow fetches weekly orders with HTTP Request, stores them in Airtable and splits them with an If node on orderStatus. On the 'booked' branch, a Code node should calculate the total value and number of booked orders, and Discord should post one message. When tested, Discord posts one message per order, each showing a single order's value. What should the builder change?
reasoning: Discord sends one message per incoming item, so the Code node must be emitting many items instead of one.
The Discord message itself is not the cause, so eliminate answers that only change it.
Adding a second If node does not combine items, so eliminate it.

Code that outputs one result per order points to Run Once for Each Item mode. Switch to Run Once for All Items, loop over $input.all(), and return one object such as [{ json: { totalBooked, bookedSum } }].
scenario.answer: Set the Code node to Run Once for All Items and return a single item wrapped in a json key. Discord then gets one item and posts one summary message.

memoryAids: T-A-B-C-D chain: Trigger (Schedule) → API (HTTP Request) → Base (Airtable) → Check (If) → Code/Edit Fields → Discord.
'Test is not Live': a green manual run means nothing until the Active/Publish switch is on.
Code return rule, 'Array of boxes labelled json': return [ { json: {...} } ].
cheatSheet: Every workflow starts with exactly one trigger per entry path; everything else is an action or logic node.
Data flows as items; each item is a JSON object, and most nodes run once per item.
NDV = Node Details View: input on the left, parameters in the middle, output on the right; drag input fields into parameters to build expressions.
Expressions use {{ }}; $json = current item; $('Exact Node Name').item.json = an earlier node's data.
Renaming a node breaks $('Old Name') references; update them after any rename.
If node: true output and false output, each wired to its own branch.
Edit Fields = no-code field changes; Code = cross-item logic or custom JS/Python.
For totals, use the Code node in Run Once for All Items mode with $input.all().
Secrets belong in Credentials, never in node parameters; credentials are not in exported JSON.
Unpin data before the final test so real API changes show up.
Schedule times follow the workflow timezone (Workflow settings), else the instance timezone; check this for 'Monday 9:00'.
Activate (publish) the workflow for Schedule or Webhook triggers to fire in production.
selfCheck: I can build the full course workflow from Schedule Trigger to Discord and explain what each node outputs.
I can write expressions with $json and $('Node Name').item.json, and fix them after a node rename.
I can write a Code node in Run Once for All Items mode that returns one correctly wrapped total.
I can choose between Edit Fields and Code, and between pinned and live data, for a given requirement.
I can explain why a workflow did not run on schedule, checking activation and timezone.
I can export and import a workflow and re-attach its credentials without exposing API keys.

objective.question: In n8n, which type of node starts a workflow execution?
options: A trigger node such as Schedule Trigger or Webhook
A Code node set to run once for all items
An If node placed at the start of the canvas
An action node such as HTTP Request
objective.explanation: Trigger nodes start executions, either on an event or on a schedule. Action nodes only do work after something has started the workflow. The If and Code nodes are processing nodes and cannot start a run.

objective.question: You built the Level 1 workflow with a Schedule Trigger set to Mondays at 9:00. You tested it manually and it worked. On Monday it did not run. What is the most likely cause?
options: The workflow was never activated (published), so the Schedule Trigger was not live
The Discord node must run before the Schedule Trigger
Schedule Trigger only works in n8n Cloud
The HTTP Request node had pinned data
objective.explanation: A manual run does not make a workflow live. The workflow must be activated (published) before Schedule or Webhook triggers fire in production. Pinned data only affects test runs, and Schedule Trigger works on both self-hosted and cloud.

objective.question: Which expression reads the orderID field of the current item?
options: { $json.orderID }
{{ item.orderID }}
${ json.orderID }
{{ $json.orderID }}
objective.explanation: n8n expressions use double curly braces, and $json refers to the current item's JSON. The other options use the wrong delimiters or a variable that does not exist.

objective.question: In the Discord node, you need the orderStatus value that came out of the node named 'HTTP Request', several nodes earlier. Which expression is correct?
options: {{ $node.HTTP Request.orderStatus }}
{{ $('HTTP Request').item.json.orderStatus }}
{{ $('HTTP Request').orderStatus }}
{{ $json['HTTP Request'].orderStatus }}
objective.explanation: $('Node Name').item.json returns the JSON of the item from a named node that is linked to the current item. $json only reads the directly previous node's output. The other forms are not valid n8n syntax.

objective.question: Which return statement is valid output for an n8n Code node?
options: return [{ total: 5 }];
return JSON.stringify({ total: 5 });
return [{ json: { total: 5 } }];
return { total: 5 };
objective.explanation: Code node output must be an array of objects, and each object needs a json key. A bare object, an array without json keys or a string does not follow the item structure taught in the course.

objective.question: A colleague sends you an exported workflow JSON file. After import, the Airtable and Discord nodes show errors. What should you do?
options: Delete the nodes, because imported nodes cannot be edited
Turn on pinning so the nodes skip authentication
Create the credentials again on your instance and select them in those nodes
Ask for a newer export, because credentials should have been included
objective.explanation: An exported workflow contains nodes, connections and settings, but it does not contain credentials. You must re-create the credentials and assign them after import. Pinning does not replace authentication for live runs.

objective.question: How many outputs does the If node have, and how are they used?
options: Two outputs, true and false, and each can connect to a different branch
Three outputs: true, false and error
Any number of outputs, one for each condition
One output, which carries a boolean field
objective.explanation: The If node sends items that match the condition to the true output and all other items to the false output. Each output can lead to its own branch. Routing to many outputs is what the Switch node does, not the If node.

objective.question: Your Schedule Trigger is set to 9:00 on Mondays, but the workflow runs at 3:30 IST instead of 9:00 IST. What should you check first?
options: The timezone in the workflow settings or the instance
Whether the HTTP Request node uses GET
The If node condition
The Discord webhook URL
objective.explanation: Schedule Trigger times follow the workflow or instance timezone. A 5.5-hour gap suggests UTC is being used instead of Asia/Kolkata. The other nodes do not control when the trigger fires.

objective.question: While building, you pin the output of the HTTP Request node. What is the main benefit?
options: Later test runs reuse the saved data, so you do not call the API every time
It activates the workflow automatically
Pinned data is encrypted, like credentials
The node calls the API faster in production
objective.explanation: Pinning keeps a node's output fixed during manual testing, so downstream nodes get stable data without calling the external service again. Pinned data is used only in test runs, not production executions, and it does not activate anything.

objective.question: How is data passed from one n8n node to the next?
options: As an array of items, where each item holds its data under a json key
As XML documents
As one flat JavaScript object per workflow
As a single string of CSV text
objective.explanation: n8n passes a list of items between nodes. Each item stores its fields in a json object, and can also have binary data. That is why the Code node must return the same shape.

objective.question: You only need orderID, employeeName and orderPrice for the next step, and you want to drop all other fields without writing code. Which node fits best?
options: Edit Fields (Set) node
Schedule Trigger
HTTP Request node
If node
objective.explanation: The Edit Fields (Set) node can add, rename or set fields, and it can keep only the fields you define. The If node only routes items, and the other two nodes fetch data or start the run.

objective.question: What does the Node Details View (NDV) show when you open a node?
options: The list of all workflows on the instance
Only the credential settings
The input data, the node's parameters and the output data
Only the node's documentation
objective.explanation: The NDV has an input panel, a parameters panel in the middle and an output panel. This lets you build expressions by dragging fields and check results right away.

objective.question: How do you earn the n8n Course Level 1 badge?
options: Publish a workflow to the community templates
Finish Level 2 first
Pass the final quiz at the end of the free text course on the docs site
Pay an exam fee and book a proctored test
objective.explanation: Level 1 is a free, text-based course on docs.n8n.io under Courses. The badge is awarded after you pass the final quiz. There is no fee, and you do not need Level 2 first.

objective.question: Which node order matches the Level 1 sample business workflow?
options: Schedule Trigger → HTTP Request → Airtable → If → Edit Fields / Code → Discord
Webhook → Discord → Airtable → If → Code
Schedule Trigger → Code → If → HTTP Request → Airtable
HTTP Request → Schedule Trigger → If → Airtable → Discord
objective.explanation: The workflow starts on a schedule, gets orders over HTTP, inserts them into Airtable, and branches on orderStatus. One branch uses Edit Fields and the other uses a Code node to calculate totals, and then Discord sends the notification. A trigger must always come first.

objective.question: The HTTP Request node returns 30 order items. The next node is an Airtable node that creates records, with field values mapped through {{ $json... }} expressions. What happens?
options: Airtable fails, because it accepts only one item
Only the first item is processed unless you add a Loop node
Airtable runs for each of the 30 items and creates 30 records
Airtable creates one record that holds all 30 orders
objective.explanation: Most n8n nodes process every incoming item automatically, and $json resolves to each item in turn. So 30 items produce 30 records. You do not need an explicit loop in this case.

objective.question: A Code node is set to 'Run Once for All Items'. The HTTP Request node before it outputs 30 order items. What does this code return?

code.code:
const booked = $input.all().filter(i => i.json.orderStatus === 'booked');
return [{ json: { bookedCount: booked.length } }];

options: One item whose bookedCount equals the number of booked orders
An error, because Code nodes cannot filter items
One item per booked order, each with bookedCount set to 1
30 items, each with a bookedCount field
objective.explanation: In 'Run Once for All Items' mode, $input.all() gives every incoming item, and the code returns one new item holding the count. Per-item output would need 'Run Once for Each Item' mode or a different return value.

objective.question: In the Discord node's Text parameter you type: Order $json.orderID is ready. The message arrives exactly as typed, with the text '$json.orderID' in it. Why?
options: The parameter is in Fixed mode and the reference is not wrapped in {{ }}, so n8n treats it as plain text
$json only works inside the Code node
The orderID field is empty, so n8n prints the variable name instead
The Discord credential lacks permission to evaluate expressions
objective.explanation: n8n only evaluates JavaScript inside {{ }} when the parameter is in Expression mode. Plain text is sent as-is. Permissions and empty fields would give errors or blanks, not the literal variable name.

objective.question: An item's JSON contains a field named 'order id', with a space in the name. Which expression reads it correctly?

code.code: { "order id": 1042, "employeeName": "Asha" }

options: {{ $json.order_id }}
{{ $json["order id"] }}
{{ $json->'order id' }}
{{ $json.order id }}
objective.explanation: Expressions are JavaScript, so a key with a space needs bracket notation. Dot notation breaks at the space, order_id is a different key, and -> is not valid JavaScript.

objective.question: Your If node checks whether orderPrice is greater than 500 using a Number comparison. The API sends orderPrice as a string such as "750", and the node fails with a type error. What is the cleanest fix inside the If node?
options: Pin the HTTP Request output so the types are fixed
Re-create the HTTP Request credential
Enable the If node option that converts types where required (loose type validation), or wrap the value with Number() in the expression
Switch the comparison to String 'contains'
objective.explanation: The If node validates types strictly by default. Letting it convert types, or converting the value yourself with Number(), makes the numeric comparison work. A string 'contains' check gives wrong logic, and pinning or credentials do not change data types.

objective.question: You add an Edit Fields (Set) node to create a new field called gstPrice. After running it, every output item contains only gstPrice, and orderID and employeeName are gone. What happened?
options: The option to include the other input fields is off, so only the fields you set are output
Pinned data overwrote the other fields
The expression for gstPrice failed silently
The Set node always deletes input fields
objective.explanation: The Edit Fields node can either keep only the fields you define or also pass through the other input fields. The option to include other input fields controls this. A failed expression would show an error or an empty value, not remove other fields.

objective.question: You pinned test data on the HTTP Request node and then activated the workflow. What happens when the Schedule Trigger fires in production?
options: The workflow fails because pinned data blocks activation
Production executions ignore pinned data, and the HTTP Request node calls the API as normal
n8n uses the pinned data only if the API call fails
The workflow uses the pinned data instead of calling the API
objective.explanation: n8n uses pinned data only in manual (development) executions. Production runs ignore it, so the node fetches live data. Pinned data is never used as a fallback.

objective.question: The orders API needs an API key sent in a header. Which HTTP Request setup is the best practice?
options: Put the key in the URL query string so it is easy to see
Keep the key in a Code node variable and reference it with an expression
Store the key in a Header Auth credential and select that credential in the node
Type the key into a header parameter in Fixed mode
objective.explanation: Credentials are stored encrypted and are not included when you export the workflow. Hard-coding the key in a parameter, the URL or a Code node leaks it in exports, logs and screenshots.

objective.question: Which expression puts today's date in yyyy-MM-dd format in a weekly report title?
options: {{ Date.format('yyyy-MM-dd') }}
{{ $today('yyyy-MM-dd') }}
{{ $json.now.format('yyyy-MM-dd') }}
{{ $now.toFormat('yyyy-MM-dd') }}
objective.explanation: $now is a Luxon DateTime built into n8n expressions, and toFormat() formats it. Date.format does not exist in JavaScript, $today is not a function, and $json only holds item data.

objective.question: You test only the Discord node by itself. Its expression uses $('HTTP Request').item.json.orderStatus, and the preview shows an error saying it cannot get data from that node. What is the most likely cause?
options: $('...') can only reference the node directly before
The Discord credential has expired
The node name must be in lowercase
The HTTP Request node has not run in the current execution, so no data is available to reference
objective.explanation: $('Node Name') can only read data from a node that has run in this execution, or that has pinned data. Run the earlier nodes first, or pin their output. Node names are case-sensitive but need not be lowercase, and $() can reach any earlier node.

objective.question: You are moving the Level 1 workflow from testing to production. Put these steps in the right order: A) Unpin the data on the HTTP Request node. B) Add a Schedule Trigger and connect it to the first action node. C) Run a full test and check every node's output. D) Save and activate (publish) the workflow.
options: D → B → A → C
A → D → C → B
C → D → B → A
B → A → C → D
objective.explanation: You add the real trigger first, then unpin the data so the final test uses the live API. You run that full test, and only after it passes do you save and activate. Activating before testing, or testing with pinned data, can push untested or stale logic into production.

objective.question: In the Schedule Trigger you choose Trigger Interval 'Custom (Cron)' and enter the expression below. When does the workflow run once it is active?
options: Every Monday at 09:00 in the workflow's timezone
Every 9 minutes, but only on Mondays
On the 1st of every month at 09:00
Every day at 09:00 except Monday
objective.explanation: The cron fields are minute, hour, day of month, month and day of week. So 0 9 * * 1 means minute 0, hour 9, any date, any month, on day-of-week 1 (Monday). The time is read in the workflow's configured timezone.

objective.question: Only booked orders should continue to the next step. All other orders should be dropped silently, with no branch for them. Which node is the better fit?
options: If node with the false branch connected to the Discord node
Edit Fields (Set) node with 'Include Other Input Fields' turned off
Code node, because conditions cannot be set without code
Filter node with the condition orderStatus is equal to booked
objective.explanation: The Filter node has one output and passes only the items that match, so it is the cleanest choice when you discard the rest. An If node also works, but it leaves an unused false branch. Edit Fields changes fields, not which items pass.

objective.question: The Airtable node uses 'Map Automatically'. Records get created, but the Order ID column is always blank. All other columns fill correctly. What is the most likely cause?
options: The item field is named orderID but the Airtable column is named orderId, and names must match exactly
The HTTP Request node data is pinned
Airtable only accepts one item per execution
The Airtable credential has read-only access
objective.explanation: Automatic mapping matches item field names to column names exactly, including case. A read-only credential would block the whole create operation, not one column. Pinned data would still supply an orderID value, so it would not cause one blank column.

objective.question: You renamed the HTTP Request node to 'Get Orders'. This Code node was typed by hand earlier. It now fails as soon as it runs. What is the cause and the fix?
options: The Code node cannot read data from earlier nodes; use $input.all() only
The return value must be a plain number
The node reference still uses the old name; change it to $('Get Orders')
The filter must use == instead of ===
objective.explanation: $('Node Name') must match the node's current name exactly. A reference to a name that no longer exists throws an error. The === comparison and the return format are already correct.

objective.question: Your flow is HTTP Request → Code (Run Once for All Items) → Discord. The Code node builds brand-new items from scratch. The Discord text uses {{ $('HTTP Request').item.json.employeeName }} and fails with an error about paired item data being unavailable. What is the best fix?
options: Carry employeeName into the Code node's output items and read it in Discord with {{ $json.employeeName }}
Rename the HTTP Request node so the reference refreshes
Switch the Discord node to 'Run Once for All Items'
Pin the HTTP Request output
objective.explanation: .item depends on item linking, and new items made in a Code node may not be linked back to the HTTP Request items. Passing the needed field through the Code output and reading it with $json avoids the problem. Pinning or renaming does not restore the missing link.

objective.question: A Code node is set to 'Run Once for Each Item'. It must add priceWithGST to each order and keep the existing fields. Which code is correct?
options: return { json: { priceWithGST: $input.item.orderPrice * 1.18 } };
return [ $input.item.json.orderPrice * 1.18 ];
return { json: { ...$input.item.json, priceWithGST: $input.item.json.orderPrice * 1.18 } };
return $json.orderPrice * 1.18;
objective.explanation: In 'Each Item' mode you return one object with a json key. Spreading $input.item.json keeps the original fields. Option 3 skips .json, so it reads undefined (giving NaN) and also drops the other fields. Options 1 and 4 return plain values, which are not valid items.

objective.question: This Code node runs on 30 orders, and only 12 of them are booked. It reports bookedCount: 30. What is the mistake?
options: A single = assigns 'booked' to every item, which is truthy, so every item passes; use ===
filter() does not work in the n8n Code node
The return value is missing the json key
$input.all() returns only the first item
objective.explanation: = is assignment, not comparison. It sets every orderStatus to 'booked' and returns a truthy string, so all 30 items pass the filter. Using === fixes it, and the return format is already valid.

objective.question: The API sends orderPrice as text, for example "120" and "80". This Code node outputs totalValue as "012080" instead of 200. Why?
options: The loop skips the first item
n8n turns every number into a string on output
+= with string values joins text together; convert with Number(item.json.orderPrice)
The mode should be 'Run Once for Each Item'
objective.explanation: Adding a string to a number in JavaScript joins them as text, so 0 + "120" becomes "0120". Converting each price with Number() or parseFloat() gives a true sum. The mode and the loop are not the problem.

objective.question: You want a Discord alert whenever the activated weekly order workflow fails. Which setup does this the n8n way?
options: Pin the error output on the HTTP Request node
Add a second Schedule Trigger that runs one minute later
Build a separate workflow that starts with an Error Trigger node and posts to Discord, then choose it as the Error Workflow in the main workflow's settings
Add an If node after every node to check for errors
objective.explanation: n8n runs the workflow chosen as the Error Workflow whenever a production execution fails. That workflow starts with the Error Trigger node, which receives details about the failure. The other options do not detect failures reliably.

objective.question: Your workflow is activated with a Monday 9:00 schedule. On Monday afternoon, where do you confirm whether it actually ran and what each node produced?
options: The Credentials page
The Schedule Trigger's output in the editor from your last manual test
The Executions list for that workflow
The pinned data panel on the HTTP Request node
