objective.explanation: Production runs are recorded in the Executions list. You can open a run there to see each node's data and any errors. The editor shows your manual test data, not the scheduled run.

objective.question: A client needs four things: (1) run every Monday at 9:00 IST; (2) no API key inside exported workflow JSON; (3) one Discord summary of booked orders; (4) processing orders saved to Airtable with only selected fields. Which design meets all four?
options: Schedule Trigger (workflow timezone Asia/Kolkata) → HTTP Request using a Header Auth credential → If on orderStatus → booked: Code (Run Once for All Items) → Discord; processing: Edit Fields → Airtable
Schedule Trigger → HTTP Request using a Header Auth credential → Code (Run Once for Each Item) → Discord → Airtable
Schedule Trigger in UTC → HTTP Request with the key typed in the URL → Filter → Airtable
Manual Trigger → HTTP Request with the key in a header parameter → If → Discord on both branches
objective.explanation: Option 2 schedules in IST, keeps the key in a credential, makes one summary with All Items mode and trims fields before Airtable. The others fail at least one requirement: a manual trigger, a key in a parameter or URL, per-item summaries, or the wrong timezone.

objective.question: The orders API needs a key in a header. Put these HTTP Request node steps in order: A) Set Authentication to 'Generic Credential Type'. B) Set Generic Auth Type to 'Header Auth'. C) Create a new credential and enter the header name and the key as the value. D) Save the credential and execute the node to check the response.
options: A → B → C → D
D → C → B → A
B → D → A → C
C → A → D → B
objective.explanation: You first tell the node to use a generic credential, then pick the Header Auth type. This lets you create the credential holding the header name and key. Executing the node last proves the credential works.

objective.question: The Code node before Discord outputs the item shown below. Which Discord Text value shows the booked count?
options: Booked: {{ $json.bookedCount }}
Booked: {{ $('Code').all().bookedCount }}
Booked: {{ bookedCount }}
Booked: {{ $json.json.bookedCount }}
objective.explanation: The json key is the item wrapper, and $json already points inside it. So $json.bookedCount is correct and $json.json.bookedCount is undefined. A bare name is not a defined variable, and .all() returns an array, not an object with a bookedCount field.

objective.question: Your workflow has a Manual Trigger and a Schedule Trigger, both connected to the HTTP Request node. You activate it. What happens?
options: It runs twice every Monday, once for each trigger
The Manual Trigger fires automatically each time you open the workflow
It runs on the schedule; the Manual Trigger is used only when you click to test in the editor
Activation fails because a workflow can have only one trigger
objective.explanation: A workflow can have more than one trigger. The Manual Trigger never fires by itself. It only starts runs you begin from the editor, while the active Schedule Trigger handles production runs.

objective.question: The If node sends 30 booked orders to this Code node. Discord then posts 30 messages, and each shows totalValue equal to the price of a single order. What is the cause?
options: The node runs once per item and returns one summary per order; switch to 'Run Once for All Items' and loop over $input.all()
The If node duplicates items
Number() rounds the price down
The Discord credential is wrong
objective.explanation: In 'Each Item' mode the code runs separately for every input item, so you get 30 small summaries. A single total needs 'Run Once for All Items', where you add up all the items and return one item.

subjective.question: Explain the difference between a trigger node and an action node in n8n, with examples from the Level 1 workflow.
subjective.answer: A trigger node starts a workflow. It waits for an event or a time, for example a Schedule Trigger, a Webhook or an app event. An action node does work after the workflow has started. It fetches, transforms or sends data. In the Level 1 workflow, the Schedule Trigger is the trigger and it fires every Monday at 9:00. The HTTP Request node that gets orders, the Airtable node that inserts records and the Discord node that posts a message are action nodes. The If, Edit Fields and Code nodes are core processing nodes. A workflow needs at least one trigger to run automatically. Also, triggers like Schedule or Webhook only fire in production after the workflow is activated (published). Before that, you run it manually for testing.
keyPoints: Trigger starts the execution; action nodes do the work
Schedule Trigger is the trigger in the sample workflow
HTTP Request, Airtable and Discord are action nodes
Triggers fire in production only after activation

subjective.question: Describe how n8n represents data as items. Why does this matter when you write expressions or code?
subjective.answer: n8n passes data between nodes as an array of items. Each item is an object with a json key that holds its fields, for example { json: { orderID: 1, orderStatus: 'booked' } }. An item can also carry binary data, such as files. Most nodes run once for each incoming item. So if the HTTP Request returns 30 orders, the Airtable node creates 30 records. This matters for expressions, because $json refers to the current item. It also matters for the Code node, because its output must keep the same shape: an array of objects with json keys. If you return a plain object, or forget the json wrapper, the next node will not get valid items. Understanding items also explains why counts in the output panel change after an If node splits the data.
keyPoints: Data is an array of items
Each item has a json key, and optionally binary data
Nodes usually run once for each item
$json is the current item
Code output must keep the items shape

subjective.question: How do you use the Node Details View (NDV) to build and debug a node?
subjective.answer: The NDV opens when you double-click a node. It has three parts. The input panel on the left shows the data that arrives from earlier nodes. The parameters panel in the middle is where you set the operation, credentials and fields. The output panel on the right shows the result after you run the node. To build, I drag a field from the input panel into a parameter, and n8n writes the expression for me. I can switch between Table, JSON and Schema views to check the structure. To debug, I run just that node and compare the input with the output. If an expression fails, the preview under the field shows the resolved value or the error. I can also pin the output, so downstream nodes get stable test data.
keyPoints: Three panels: input, parameters, output
Drag and drop fields to build expressions
Table, JSON and Schema views
Run a single node and check expression previews
Pin output to keep test data stable

subjective.question: What are n8n expressions? Explain the difference between $json and $('Node Name').item.json.
subjective.answer: Expressions let a parameter take a dynamic value instead of fixed text. They are written inside double curly braces and can hold JavaScript, for example {{ $json.orderPrice * 2 }}. $json is the JSON of the current item coming from the directly connected previous node. $('Node Name').item.json reaches back to a specific named node and returns the item linked to the current one. For example, in the Discord node after a Code node, I can use {{ $('HTTP Request').item.json.employeeName }} to get a field that the Code node did not pass on. Using the node name makes expressions clearer and safer when nodes in between change the data. One caution: if you rename a node, n8n usually updates the references, but you should still check your expressions.
keyPoints: Syntax is {{ }} and can contain JavaScript
$json is the current item from the previous node
$('Node Name').item.json is a linked item from a named node
Useful when intermediate nodes change the data

subjective.question: How does n8n handle credentials, and what happens to them when you export and import a workflow?
subjective.answer: Credentials hold the authentication details for a service, such as an Airtable token or a Discord webhook. n8n stores them separately from workflows and encrypts them. A node only references a credential by selecting it. When you export a workflow, the JSON file contains the nodes, connections and settings, but not the credentials. This is deliberate, so that secrets do not leak when files are shared. After import, the nodes that need authentication show a missing-credential error. You must create the credentials on the new instance and select them in each node. In real work, this means you can safely commit workflow JSON to Git. It also means you should keep a list of the credentials each workflow needs, so that deployment to another environment goes smoothly.
keyPoints: Credentials are stored separately and encrypted
Nodes only reference credentials
Exports hold nodes, connections and settings only
Re-create and assign credentials after import

subjective.question: In the sample workflow, how would you configure the If node to separate booked orders from other orders, and what happens on each branch?
subjective.answer: I add an If node after the Airtable insert. I set one condition: the value {{ $json.orderStatus }} as a string, with the operator 'is equal to' and the value 'booked'. Items that match go to the true output. All other items, such as processing orders, go to the false output. Each output connects to its own branch. In the course, one branch uses an Edit Fields node to keep or set only the fields we need. The other branch uses a Code node to calculate totals, for example the number of booked orders and their total value, which then goes to Discord. I run the node and check the item counts on both outputs, to confirm that every order lands on the right branch. I also check the data type, because comparing a number with a string can give an unexpected false.
keyPoints: Condition on {{ $json.orderStatus }} equals 'booked'
True and false outputs lead to different branches
Edit Fields on one branch, Code on the other
Check item counts on both outputs and the data types

subjective.question: When would you choose the Edit Fields (Set) node instead of the Code node?
subjective.answer: I use Edit Fields when the job is simple shaping of data. That means adding a field, renaming one, setting a fixed value, mapping a value with an expression, or keeping only certain fields. It needs no code, it is easy for teammates to read, and it shows clearly in the NDV. I use the Code node when the logic needs more than one item at once, or more complex JavaScript. Examples are summing totals across all items, grouping, loops, or custom calculations. In the Level 1 workflow, Edit Fields trims the order fields, and the Code node calculates the totals of booked orders. My rule is to start with built-in nodes and use Code only when they cannot express the logic cleanly. This keeps workflows easier to maintain.
keyPoints: Edit Fields for setting, renaming and keeping fields
No-code nodes are easier to read and maintain
Code node for aggregation and complex logic
Prefer built-in nodes first

subjective.question: Write the logic of a Code node that counts booked orders and sums their price, and explain its output format.
subjective.answer: I set the Code node to Run Once for All Items, so that I can see every item together. In JavaScript: const items = $input.all(); const booked = items.filter(i => i.json.orderStatus === 'booked'); const total = booked.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.json.orderPrice, 0); return [{ json: { bookedOrders: booked.length, bookedOrdersTotal: total } }]; The key point is the return shape. n8n expects an array of objects, and each object must have a json key. Here I return one item with two fields, so the Discord node can use {{ $json.bookedOrders }} and {{ $json.bookedOrdersTotal }}. If I returned a plain object, or an array without json keys, I would not get clean items. I also make sure orderPrice is a number, so the sum is not built as a string.
keyPoints: Run Once for All Items mode with $input.all()
Filter and reduce for the count and the total
Return [{ json: {...} }]
Check data types before arithmetic

subjective.question: What is data pinning in n8n? Give its benefits and one pitfall.
subjective.answer: Pinning saves a node's output so that later manual runs reuse it instead of running the node again. I pin from the output panel of the NDV. The benefits are clear. I do not call the API or the database again on every test, so I save rate limits, cost and time. I get stable data, which makes it easier to build expressions downstream. I can also edit pinned data to test edge cases, such as an order with a missing status. The pitfall is that pinned data applies only to test runs. Production executions use real data. So a workflow that looks fine with pinned data can fail live if the real API returns a different structure. I unpin, or run once with live data, before I activate the workflow.
keyPoints: Saves node output for reuse in test runs
Avoids repeated external calls
Edit pinned data to test edge cases
Not used in production, so test with live data before activating

subjective.question: Explain the difference between running a workflow manually and activating (publishing) it.
subjective.answer: A manual run, from the editor button or a single node, is for testing. It runs once, now, while I watch. It can use pinned data, and I see the results in the canvas. It does not make the workflow live. Activating (publishing) the workflow registers its triggers in production. After that, the Schedule Trigger fires at its set time and a Webhook listens on its production URL, even when nobody has the editor open. Production runs appear in the executions list. A common mistake is to test a workflow, see it work, and assume it will run every Monday at 9:00. It will not run until it is activated. Also, a Webhook node has separate test and production URLs, so you must use the production URL once the workflow is live.
keyPoints: Manual run is for one-off testing
Activation makes triggers fire in production
Pinned data affects test runs only
Webhooks have test and production URLs

subjective.question: Your weekly report workflow runs at the wrong hour for your Indian team. How do you troubleshoot it?
subjective.answer: First, I check the Schedule Trigger settings: the mode, Monday, hour 9 and minute 0. Then I check the timezone. Schedule Trigger times follow the workflow timezone, which is set in workflow settings. If that is not set, they follow the instance default. A self-hosted instance often defaults to UTC through its environment configuration. If the run happens at 3:30 IST, that is 9:00 UTC, which confirms a timezone mismatch. I set the workflow timezone to Asia/Kolkata, save it, and make sure the workflow is still active. Then I check the executions list after the next run. For teams in many regions, I document which timezone each workflow uses, so that nobody gets confused by schedule times.
keyPoints: Check the trigger fields first
Workflow timezone setting, with the instance default as fallback
Recognise a 5.5-hour offset as UTC versus IST
Confirm in the executions list

subjective.question: Walk through building the Level 1 sample business workflow from start to finish.
subjective.answer: I start with a Schedule Trigger set to weekly, Mondays at 9:00. Next, an HTTP Request node uses GET to fetch the orders data from the course endpoint. It returns items with fields such as orderID, orderStatus and orderPrice. I pin this output while building. Then an Airtable node, with its credential set up, creates a record for each order in the course table. After that, an If node checks whether orderStatus equals 'booked'. On one branch, Edit Fields keeps only the fields I need. On the other, a Code node calculates the number and total value of booked orders and returns [{ json: {...} }]. Finally, a Discord node posts a message using expressions like {{ $json.bookedOrdersTotal }}. I test each node, check the timezone, save, and activate the workflow.
keyPoints: Schedule, then HTTP Request, then Airtable, then If
Edit Fields on one branch, Code for totals on the other
Discord message built with expressions
Pin while building, then activate at the end

subjective.question: How would you safely share a workflow you built with a teammate on another n8n instance?
subjective.answer: I export the workflow, or copy the nodes, as JSON. The file contains the nodes, connections and settings, such as the timezone. It does not contain credentials, so secrets are not shared. Before exporting, I remove any hard-coded tokens or URLs from node parameters and expressions, because those would be exported. I also remove pinned data that holds real customer information. I send a short note with the file. It lists the credentials needed, such as Airtable and Discord, the expected timezone, and any node names that expressions refer to. My teammate imports the file, creates the credentials and selects them in each node, tests with a manual run, and then activates it. For team setups, keeping the JSON in version control helps track changes.
keyPoints: Export holds nodes, connections and settings, not credentials
Remove hard-coded secrets and sensitive pinned data
Document the required credentials and the timezone
Re-create credentials, test and activate on the target instance

subjective.question: Your Code node fails, or the next node shows no usable data. How do you debug the output shape?
subjective.answer: First, I read the error message in the Code node output. A common cause is the return value. The Code node must return an array of objects, each with a json key, like return [{ json: { total: 5 } }]. Returning { total: 5 }, or forgetting the json key, breaks the items structure. Next, I check the mode. In Run Once for Each Item, the code handles a single item at a time. In Run Once for All Items, I work with $input.all() and return an array. Mixing these up causes wrong results. Then I check the data. I open the input panel in JSON view to confirm the field names and types, for example whether orderPrice is a string. Finally, I add console.log, run only that node with pinned input, and compare the output with what the next node expects.
keyPoints: Return [{ json: {...} }]
Each Item versus All Items mode
Check field names and types in the input JSON
Use console.log and pinned input to test in isolation

subjective.question: Before activating a workflow like the Level 1 project, how do you test it properly?
subjective.answer: I test node by node. I run the trigger and the HTTP Request first, check the output in JSON view, and pin it. I check that each expression preview resolves correctly in the NDV. For the If node, I check that the item counts on the true and false outputs add up to the input count. I also test edge cases by editing pinned data, for example an unknown status or a missing price. I confirm that the Code node returns the correct items shape and correct totals. I check that the credentials work, by doing a real Airtable insert into a test table and posting to a test Discord channel. Then I unpin and run once with live data. Finally, I check the workflow timezone, activate it, and watch the first production execution in the executions list.
keyPoints: Test each node and check expression previews
Check that If branch counts match the input
Test edge cases with edited pinned data
Do a live run without pins before activating
Monitor the first production execution

subjective.question: Compare the Code node modes 'Run Once for All Items' and 'Run Once for Each Item'. When would you use each one in the Level 1 workflow?
subjective.answer: In 'Run Once for All Items' mode, the code runs one time. I read every incoming item with $input.all() and return an array of items. This is the right mode for aggregates, such as counting booked orders and summing their prices into one summary item for Discord. In 'Run Once for Each Item' mode, n8n runs the code once per item. I use $input.item and return a single item each time. This suits per-row transformations, such as adding a tax field to each order. Per-item mode is simpler for row logic, and n8n keeps item linking for me. All-items mode is needed whenever the result depends on several items together. If I pick the wrong mode, I get one output per input when I wanted a summary, or I cannot see the other items when I need them.
keyPoints: All Items: runs once, uses $input.all(), returns an array
Each Item: runs per item, uses $input.item
Aggregates such as the booked count need All Items
Per-row transformations suit Each Item

subjective.question: Explain the difference between $('HTTP Request').item, .first() and .all() in an expression. When would each give a wrong result?
subjective.answer: $('HTTP Request').item returns the item from that node that is linked to the item currently being processed. n8n uses paired-item tracking to find it. This is the usual choice when each output row must match its own source row. .first() always returns the first item of that node's output. It is right when the node produced one item, such as a config or token response. With 30 orders, though, every row would get order 1's data. .all() returns an array of all items. It is useful for lookups or totals, but if you put it straight into a text field you get an array, not a single value. .item can also fail when item linking is broken, for example after a Code node that builds new items without pairing information. In that case you must keep the pairing or use another way to reference the data.
keyPoints: .item uses paired-item linking to find the matching source item
.first() suits single-item outputs but repeats one value for many items
.all() returns an array, useful for aggregates
.item can break when custom code loses item linking

subjective.question: An API returns a single item whose JSON holds an array of 50 orders in the 'orders' field. Your If node must check each order. What do you do, and why?

code.code: [{ "json": { "page": 1, "orders": [ {"orderID": 1, "orderStatus": "booked"}, {"orderID": 2, "orderStatus": "processing"} ] } }]

subjective.answer: n8n nodes process items, not elements inside one item. Right now there is one item, so the If node would run once and could not route individual orders. I need to turn the array into separate items first. The simplest no-code option is the Split Out node with the field set to 'orders'. It outputs one item per order, and each order's fields become top-level, so $json.orderStatus works. The other option is a Code node in All Items mode that returns $input.first().json.orders.map(o => ({ json: o })). After the split, the If node evaluates every order and sends it to the true or false branch. I check the result in the NDV table view: there should be 50 items and orderStatus should be a top-level column.
keyPoints: Nodes iterate over items, not over nested arrays
Split Out turns array elements into separate items
A Code node alternative maps the array to { json } objects
Check the item count and the fields in the NDV after splitting

subjective.question: Your If node checks orderStatus equals 'booked', but every order goes to the false branch, even ones that look booked. How do you troubleshoot this?
subjective.answer: First, I open the If node's NDV and look at the input in JSON view, not just the table, so I can see the exact values. The common causes are a difference in case ('Booked' vs 'booked'), extra spaces ('booked '), the wrong field name such as order_status, or a value nested under another object, which makes $json.orderStatus undefined. I drag the field from the input panel into the condition so the path is correct, and I check the expression preview. For case or spaces, I enable the case-insensitive option if it is offered, or I compare against {{ $json.orderStatus.trim().toLowerCase() }}. I also confirm I chose a String comparison. Then I pin the input and re-run only the If node, and check the counts on the true and false outputs until they match what I expect.
keyPoints: Inspect the raw JSON in the NDV input panel
Check for case, spaces, wrong field names and nested paths
Drag fields in to get correct expressions, and check the preview
Pin the input and compare the branch counts

subjective.question: A teammate put the orders API key directly in the HTTP Request node's header field and then shared the workflow JSON on Slack. What is the risk, and how do you fix it properly?
subjective.answer: The key is now part of the workflow JSON. Anyone with the file or the Slack message can see it. It may also appear in version control and screenshots. Credentials are stored encrypted by n8n and are left out of exports, but plain parameter values are not. First, I treat the key as compromised and ask the API owner to rotate it. Then I create a Header Auth credential, or the API's own credential type, with the new key. I select it in the HTTP Request node's authentication settings and remove the hard-coded header. I re-test with a manual execution. Going forward, the team shares workflows without secrets. Each person sets up their own credentials after import, and access to shared credentials is controlled through n8n's credential sharing rather than copy-paste.
keyPoints: Parameter values are exported in plain text; credentials are not
Rotate the leaked key immediately
Move the secret into a credential such as Header Auth
Recipients create or receive credentials separately after import

subjective.question: What does this Code node do, and why does it output 0 for the total even though orders have prices? Fix it.
subjective.answer: The code runs in All Items mode. It loops over every incoming item and tries to add up the prices, then returns one summary item. The bug is that each n8n item wraps its data in a json key. So item.orderPrice is undefined, and the price is really at item.json.orderPrice. Adding undefined to a number gives NaN, which the output may show as null. If prices are strings, JavaScript joins them as text instead of adding them. The fix is: total += Number(item.json.orderPrice) || 0. If only booked orders should count, I first filter with item.json.orderStatus === 'booked'. I verify this in the NDV by opening the input in JSON view to confirm the exact path. Then I run the node and check that the single output item shows the expected number.
keyPoints: Items wrap data in the json key
The correct path is item.json.orderPrice
Convert with Number() to avoid string joining or NaN
Return one item as an array of { json }

subjective.question: The Discord node receives 12 booked-order items and posts 12 separate messages. The manager wants one summary message. How do you redesign this?
subjective.answer: Most action nodes run once per input item. Twelve items therefore means twelve Discord messages. The fix is to reduce the data to one item before the Discord node. In the Level 1 pattern, I put a Code node in All Items mode before Discord. It counts the booked items, sums their prices and returns a single item such as { totalBooked, bookedSum }. Another option is the Aggregate node, if I want to combine fields into lists without code. The Discord message then uses expressions like {{ $json.totalBooked }} and {{ $json.bookedSum }}. I confirm in the NDV that the node before Discord outputs exactly one item. If there are zero booked orders, I decide whether a message should still go out, and handle that case so the summary is not empty.
keyPoints: Action nodes execute once per input item
Aggregate to one item before Discord
Code node in All Items mode or the Aggregate node
Check that one item reaches Discord; handle the zero-orders case

subjective.question: Your activated weekly workflow failed last Monday and nobody noticed until Wednesday. How do you investigate the failed production run, and how do you reduce the chance of missing it again?
subjective.answer: I open the workflow's Executions list and filter for failed runs. I open the Monday execution to see which node failed, its error message, and the input data it received. Common causes are an expired or revoked credential, an API change in field names, or an empty response that a later expression did not expect. Where my instance supports it, I load that execution's data into the editor to debug with the real input. Otherwise I pin a copy of the failing input on the node and reproduce the problem manually. After fixing it, I re-run the workflow manually and confirm the outputs. To avoid silent failures, I set an error workflow in the workflow settings. It starts with the Error Trigger and sends an alert to Discord or email whenever a production execution fails.
keyPoints: Use the Executions list to find the failed node and its error
Reproduce with the real input data in the editor or pinned data
Check credentials, API changes and empty data
Set an error workflow with the Error Trigger for alerts

subjective.question: A company wants each new order to get a field 'priceWithGST' (orderPrice × 1.18, rounded to 2 decimals) before saving to Airtable. Show how you would do it without code, and explain how you would verify it.

code.code: {{ Math.round($json.orderPrice * 1.18 * 100) / 100 }}

subjective.answer: I add an Edit Fields (Set) node between the HTTP Request and Airtable nodes. In manual mapping, I add a field called priceWithGST of type Number. I set its value in Expression mode to the expression shown, which multiplies the price by 1.18 and rounds it to two decimal places. I turn on the option to include the other input fields, so orderID and employeeName still reach Airtable. Because the node runs per item, every order gets its own calculated value. To verify, I pin the HTTP Request output, run the Set node, and check several rows in the NDV output table against manual calculations. I also check an edge case, such as a price sent as a string; if needed I wrap the value in Number(). Then I map priceWithGST to the matching Airtable field.
keyPoints: Use Edit Fields with an expression-mode Number field
Include the other input fields so existing data is kept
Expressions run per item automatically
Verify with pinned data and spot-check the output in the NDV

subjective.question: Case study: A Pune retail client wants this every Monday at 9:00 IST. Fetch orders from their API with an API key. Ignore cancelled orders. Save processing orders to Airtable with a GST-inclusive price. Post one Discord summary of booked orders (count and total in ₹). The workflow must be safe to export. Design it and justify each choice.
subjective.answer: I would start with a Schedule Trigger and set the workflow timezone to Asia/Kolkata so 9:00 means IST. Next, an HTTP Request node uses a Header Auth credential. The key stays encrypted in Credentials, so an export holds only a reference to it. An If node or Switch then routes by orderStatus. Booked orders go one way, processing orders another, and cancelled orders match neither path. On the processing path, Edit Fields keeps orderID, employeeName and orderPrice, and adds priceWithGST using an expression. Airtable then creates the records. On the booked path, a Code node in 'Run Once for All Items' mode counts the orders and sums Number(orderPrice). It returns one item, and Discord posts one message such as 'Booked: {{ $json.bookedCount }}, ₹{{ $json.totalValue }}'. Before activating, I unpin all data and run a full test. I also set an Error Workflow for alerts.
keyPoints: Schedule Trigger plus workflow timezone Asia/Kolkata
Header Auth credential so exports hold no secret
Routing that drops cancelled orders
Edit Fields for GST and field trimming; Code node in All Items mode for one summary
Unpin, run a full test, activate, and add an Error Workflow

subjective.question: Every Monday, Airtable gets the same orders again, so last week's orders now appear three times. The workflow itself shows no errors. What is the cause, and how do you fix it?
subjective.answer: The workflow is doing exactly what it was built to do. The API most likely returns all orders, not only new ones, and the Airtable node always uses Create. So every run inserts everything again. There are three fixes, and I may combine them. First, ask the API for recent orders only, for example with a date query parameter built from {{ $now.minus({ days: 7 }).toISO() }}, if the API supports it. Second, change the Airtable operation to 'Create or Update' and match on the orderID column, so existing records get updated instead of copied. Third, remove duplicates before Airtable, for example with the Remove Duplicates node or by checking which IDs already exist. Then I would clean up the existing duplicates. Finally, I would test with two runs in a row and confirm that the second run adds no new rows.
keyPoints: No error shown means a logic problem, not a failure
The API returns the full dataset every time
Use Airtable 'Create or Update' matched on orderID
Filter by date or remove duplicates upstream
Verify with two runs in a row

subjective.question: For the booked-orders summary, compare using the Summarize node with using a Code node. Which would you choose in a team setting, and why?
subjective.answer: Both can produce one item with a count and a sum. The Summarize node needs no code. You pick aggregations such as Count on orderID and Sum on orderPrice, and you can group by a field. It is easy for non-developers to read and maintain, and it is less likely to break. The Code node is more flexible. It can convert string prices with Number(), apply custom rounding, add several conditions or format the output in one place. But it brings JavaScript risks, such as the wrong mode, string joining or a bad return shape. In a team, I would choose Summarize when the API sends clean numeric prices and the logic is just count and sum. I would move to Code only when the logic truly needs it, and I would comment the code and test it with pinned data first.
keyPoints: Summarize: no-code count, sum and grouping
Code: flexible but brings JavaScript and output-shape risks
Readability and maintenance matter in teams
Price data types can decide the choice
Use the simplest node that meets the need

subjective.question: The Discord weekly message shows a wrong booked total. Give the order of debugging steps you would follow, and say what you check at each one.
subjective.answer: First, I open the failing or suspect execution from the Executions list, so I see real production data and not my editor tests. Second, I check the HTTP Request output. Is the item count right, and is orderPrice a number or a string? Third, I check the If node. Do the true and false branches hold the items I expect? Check the case and spacing of orderStatus. Fourth, I open the Code node. Is the mode 'Run Once for All Items'? Is it summing Number(item.json.orderPrice)? Does it return a single item? Fifth, I check the Discord expression. Does it read the right field and the right node name? Then I copy the production data into the editor, pin it, fix the node and test again. Last, I unpin, run a full test and confirm the total by hand.
keyPoints: Start from the real execution in the Executions list
Follow the data node by node, from the source onward
Check counts, data types and If branch routing
Check the Code node mode, number conversion and return shape
Fix using pinned real data, then unpin and test again

subjective.question: Spot the mistake. This Code node should count booked orders and total their value, but it always reports bookedCount as 0 or 1. Explain and fix it.
subjective.answer: The return statement is inside the for loop. On the first pass, the code checks only the first item and then returns at once. So bookedCount is 1 if the first order is booked and 0 if it is not, and the other items are never read. The fix is to move the return statement below the loop's closing brace. Then the loop finishes adding up every item before one summary is returned. The rest is correct. The mode is All Items, === compares properly, Number() avoids joining strings, and the output is an array with a json key. After the fix, I would test with pinned data where I know the answer, for example 12 booked orders, and compare the result.
keyPoints: return inside the loop exits after the first item
Move return after the loop
Mode, comparison and Number() are already correct
The output shape is valid: an array of objects with json
Verify against pinned data with a known answer

subjective.question: Spot the problems in this extract from an exported workflow file that a teammate wants to publish on GitHub as a template.
subjective.answer: There are two leaks. First, the live API key sits in plain text in headerParameters. That happens when you type it into a node parameter instead of using Credentials. Anyone who reads the file can call the API. The key must be rotated now, and the node rebuilt with a Header Auth credential, so the export carries only a credential reference. Second, the pinData block holds real order data, including names and phone numbers. Pinned data goes into the export, so publishing it exposes personal data and may break privacy rules. Before sharing, I unpin the data, or replace it with fake sample data, and export again. Then I open the file and check that it contains no keys, tokens or real customer records before it goes public.
keyPoints: A hard-coded key in parameters is exported in plain text
Rotate the key and move it to a Header Auth credential
Pinned data is included in exports and can leak personal data
Unpin or use fake data before sharing
Review the JSON file before publishing

subjective.question: The workflow passed every test last month. Today the scheduled run fails at the HTTP Request node with a 401 Unauthorized error. In the editor, the node still shows a successful green output. What is going on, and how do you fix it?
subjective.answer: The green output in the editor is most likely pinned data, or old output from a past test. It does not prove the API works today. Production runs ignore pinned data and call the real API, which now returns 401. That points to an authentication problem. The API key may have expired or been rotated, the credential may have been edited, or the header name may have changed. To fix it, I open the failed run in the Executions list to see the exact error. Then I unpin the HTTP Request node and execute it live in the editor to reproduce the 401. Next, I update the Header Auth credential with a valid key and confirm the expected header name. Finally, I run the full workflow unpinned. To catch this early next time, I would add an Error Workflow that alerts on failures.
keyPoints: Pinned or old output hides live API problems
Production ignores pinned data
401 means an authentication problem: expired key, wrong header or edited credential
Reproduce unpinned, then update the credential
Add an Error Workflow alert

subjective.question: The Monday report reaches Discord twice every week, a few seconds apart. The Executions list for this workflow shows only one run each Monday. What could cause this, and how do you find it?
subjective.answer: This workflow ran once, so the second message is coming from somewhere else. The most likely cause is a second active copy, such as a duplicated workflow or an older version, that also posts to the same Discord channel. Another common cause is the same workflow active on two instances, for example an old self-hosted server and a new cloud workspace, both using the same webhook. To find it, I search the workflow list for active workflows that use that Discord credential or channel and check their Executions lists for Monday 9:00. I also ask whether any other instance is still running. If the Executions list had shown two runs, I would instead check the Schedule Trigger for two rules and whether two triggers are connected. The fix is to keep exactly one active workflow and deactivate or delete the copies.
keyPoints: One execution here means the duplicate comes from somewhere else
Check for duplicated or old active workflows
Check for the same workflow active on two instances
If two runs appear, check the Schedule rules and triggers
Keep one active workflow only

subjective.question: An Indian startup is choosing between n8n Cloud and self-hosting for its scheduled order workflows. What should they consider so that schedules and credentials keep working?
subjective.answer: With n8n Cloud, the hosting, uptime and upgrades are managed for you. The team still sets the workflow timezone to Asia/Kolkata. With self-hosting, the team owns more. The server must be running at schedule time, because a laptop that is asleep or a stopped container means missed runs. They should set the instance timezone, for example with GENERIC_TIMEZONE, or set it per workflow. Credentials are encrypted with the instance's encryption key. If that key is lost or changes during a migration, the saved credentials cannot be decrypted. So they must back up the key, set it explicitly and reuse it on the new server. Self-hosting also means they handle backups, updates, HTTPS and access control. In both cases, I would set an Error Workflow and check the Executions list after the first scheduled runs.
keyPoints: Cloud: managed uptime; still set the workflow timezone
Self-hosted: the server must be up at schedule time
Instance timezone setting such as GENERIC_TIMEZONE
Back up the encryption key or credentials cannot be decrypted
Error Workflow and Executions monitoring in both cases

subjective.question: Spot the mistake. The If node gets 30 orders with mixed statuses, but all 30 always go to the same branch. Here is the condition.

code.code:
If node condition
Value 1: {{ $('HTTP Request').first().json.orderStatus }}
Operation: String → is equal to
Value 2: booked

subjective.answer: .first() always returns the first item from the HTTP Request node. So the If node checks every one of the 30 items against the status of order number one. If the first order is booked, all 30 go to true. If it is not, all 30 go to false. The condition should check each item's own status, using {{ $json.orderStatus }}. The If node works on items directly after the HTTP Request node, so $json is the current item. {{ $('HTTP Request').item.json.orderStatus }} would also work, because .item follows item linking. To verify, I would run the node and check that the true and false counts match the known split in the data, for example 12 and 18. I would also look at a few items on each branch.
keyPoints: .first() always returns item 0
Every item is compared with the first order's status
Use $json.orderStatus or .item for the current item
$json works because each item is checked in turn
Check the branch counts against the known data

subjective.question: You need to test the Discord step many times while building, but every test posts to the real team channel. Compare your options and say which you would use.
subjective.answer: First, I would pin the output of the HTTP Request node or the Code node. That way I do not call the orders API again on every test, and the input stays the same between tests. Second, I would create a separate Discord credential that points to a private test channel or webhook, and select it during development. Then I switch to the production credential just before the final test. A third choice is to deactivate the Discord node while I work on earlier nodes. That stops any posting, but I cannot see how the message looks. Testing with no safeguard spams the team and confuses people. My preferred setup is pinned input plus a test channel, because I can see the real formatted message without disturbing anyone. Before going live, I unpin the data, switch credentials and run one full test.
keyPoints: Pin upstream data so tests repeat with the same input
Use a test-channel credential during development
Deactivating the node stops posting but hides the result
Switch to the production credential before the final test
Unpin before going live

subjective.question: A teammate tidied the workflow by renaming nodes, for example 'HTTP Request' became 'Fetch Orders' and 'Code' became 'Weekly Summary'. Now the Discord message shows errors or blank values. How do you diagnose and fix this?
subjective.answer: The likely cause is references that still use the old node names. This happens in Code node snippets typed by hand, in expressions pasted from another workflow, or where field names changed along with the nodes. First, I open the Discord node and look at each expression in the NDV preview. A wrong name shows an error saying the node is missing or cannot be found. Next, I search every node for $('HTTP Request') and $('Code'), especially inside Code nodes. I update them to the new names, or I replace them with $json when the data comes from the node directly before. For blank values with no error, I check that the field names still match the output of the referenced node. Then I run the workflow again and check every preview. To avoid this, I agree on final node names before writing many cross-node references.
keyPoints: $('Name') must match the current node name exactly
NDV previews show broken references
Check Code nodes and pasted expressions especially
Prefer $json for data from the node directly before
Blank values with no error point to field name mismatches

subjective.question: The weekly Discord report must start with the date range of the last 7 days in IST, for example '01 Jun 2026 – 08 Jun 2026'. Write the expression, and explain how you make sure the dates are correct for India.
subjective.answer: I would use $now, which is a Luxon DateTime, inside an expression: 'Report: {{ $now.minus({ days: 7 }).toFormat('dd LLL yyyy') }} – {{ $now.toFormat('dd LLL yyyy') }}'. Here minus subtracts seven days, and toFormat builds the text. dd is the two-digit day, LLL is the short month name and yyyy is the year. $now uses the workflow's timezone, so I set the workflow timezone to Asia/Kolkata in its settings. On a self-hosted instance, I also check the instance default. If the timezone is wrong, a run near midnight UTC can show the wrong day for an Indian team. To verify, I look at the NDV expression preview and compare it with today's date in IST. I would not type the dates by hand, because hard-coded dates are wrong the next week.
keyPoints: $now is a Luxon DateTime
minus({ days: 7 }) and toFormat('dd LLL yyyy')
Set the workflow timezone to Asia/Kolkata
Check the NDV preview
Never hard-code dates that change every week

subjective.question: Case study: Ops wants only booked orders above ₹5,000 saved to Airtable. All other orders are skipped. Discord must say how many orders were saved and how many were skipped. Prices sometimes arrive as strings. Design it.
subjective.answer: After the HTTP Request node, I add an If node with two conditions joined by AND. The first is orderStatus equals booked, as a string. The second is orderPrice greater than 5000, as a number, with loose type validation turned on, or using {{ Number($json.orderPrice) }}, so a string like "7500" compares correctly. The true branch goes to Airtable Create, perhaps through Edit Fields to trim the fields. For the counts, I add a Code node in 'Run Once for All Items' mode that reads the full list with $('HTTP Request').all(). It counts the items that pass the same rule and subtracts that from the total to get skipped. It returns one item with savedCount and skippedCount, and Discord posts {{ $json.savedCount }} and {{ $json.skippedCount }}. Keeping the rule identical in both places matters, so I test with pinned data that includes edge cases: exactly 5000, string prices and other statuses.
keyPoints: If node with AND: status equals booked and price greater than 5000
Handle string prices with Number() or loose type validation
True branch goes to Airtable
Code node in All Items mode counts saved and skipped from the full list
Test edge cases such as exactly 5000 and string prices

subjective.question: Which is better for the Level 1 business process: one workflow with an If node branching to Airtable and Discord, or two separate workflows that each fetch the orders? Justify your answer.
subjective.answer: For this process, I would choose one workflow with branches. Both outputs come from the same data, fetched at the same moment. One HTTP Request means one API call, so the Airtable records and the Discord summary always match. There is one schedule to manage, one Executions list to check and one place to update credentials. With two workflows, you call the API twice. The data could change between calls, so the numbers may not agree. You also have two schedules and two error setups to maintain. Separate workflows make sense when the parts have different schedules or owners, or when one part is reused by many processes. In that case, the shared part can become a sub-workflow called with Execute Workflow. Here, the single branched workflow is simpler and more consistent.
keyPoints: One fetch keeps both outputs consistent
Fewer API calls, schedules and monitoring points
Two workflows can disagree if the data changes between runs
Split only for different schedules, owners or reuse
Sub-workflows are the tool for reuse

subjective.question: Spot the mistakes. These five expressions appear in the Discord and Airtable nodes. The data has the fields orderID, employeeName, 'order id' and totalValue, and the nodes are named 'HTTP Request' and 'Code'. Which are wrong, and why?
subjective.answer: Expressions 1, 2 and 4 are wrong. In number 1, field names are case-sensitive. employeename does not match employeeName, so it shows blank or undefined. Number 2 uses 'http request', but the node is named 'HTTP Request'. Node references must match exactly, so this fails. Number 4 has no double curly braces, so n8n treats it as plain text and posts the words '$json.totalValue' instead of the number. It should be 'Total: {{ $json.totalValue }}'. Number 3 is correct, because bracket notation is the right way to read a field whose name contains a space. Number 5 is also correct: it formats today's date as yyyy-MM-dd, in the workflow's timezone. I would check each fix in the NDV preview, where it shows the resolved value.
keyPoints: Field names are case-sensitive
Node names in $() must match exactly
Expressions need {{ }} or they stay plain text
Bracket notation is correct for names with spaces
Check each fix in the NDV preview

steps.overview: This step teaches you to build n8n workflows that fail safely and tell you when they fail. You will use error workflows with the Error Trigger, node-level retry and error handling, timeouts, sub-workflows, and secured webhooks with controlled responses. These topics appear in the Level 2 course and knowledge check, and they are what separates a demo from a production automation.
objectives: Create an error workflow with the Error Trigger node and assign it to production workflows in Workflow Settings.
Configure Retry On Fail, On Error behaviour and timeouts on nodes and workflows.
Split a large workflow into reusable sub-workflows using the Execute Sub-workflow node and the 'When Executed by Another Workflow' trigger.
Secure a Webhook node with authentication and return a custom response using the Respond to Webhook node.
Force a failure with the Stop and Error node and verify that an alert shows the failing node.

concepts.explanation: A separate workflow that starts with the Error Trigger node. You link it to other workflows in Workflow Settings > Error workflow. When a linked workflow fails during an automatic (production) execution, n8n runs the error workflow and passes details of the failure. One error workflow can serve many workflows.

The Error Trigger receives JSON with execution and workflow details. Key fields are execution.id, execution.url, execution.error.message, execution.error.stack, execution.lastNodeExecuted, execution.mode, workflow.id and workflow.name. If the failure happens in the trigger node itself, the data arrives under a trigger object instead, and there is no execution id or url.

A node that deliberately throws an error with your own message or error object. Use it to fail a workflow when data is invalid, even if no node crashed. It is also the easiest way to test that your error workflow fires.

A node setting that re-runs a failed node automatically. You set Max Tries and Wait Between Tries (in milliseconds). Use it for temporary problems such as API rate limits, network blips or 5xx responses, not for bad input data.

A node setting with three choices: Stop Workflow (default), Continue, and Continue (using error output). Continue passes the error as normal output and moves on. Continue (using error output) adds a separate error branch, so you can route failed items to logging or alerts while good items continue.

Workflow Settings has a Timeout Workflow option that stops an execution after a set time. Many nodes, like HTTP Request, also have their own request timeout option. On self-hosted n8n, EXECUTIONS_TIMEOUT sets a default workflow timeout and EXECUTIONS_TIMEOUT_MAX caps what users can set.

A parent workflow calls a child workflow with the Execute Sub-workflow node (older name: Execute Workflow). The child starts with the 'When Executed by Another Workflow' trigger (older name: Execute Workflow Trigger), where you define its inputs. The parent can wait for the result or continue without waiting, and can run the child once for all items or once per item.

Every Webhook node has a Test URL (path contains /webhook-test/) and a Production URL (path contains /webhook/). The test URL works only while you listen for a test event in the editor. The production URL works only when the workflow is active (published).

The Webhook node supports Basic Auth, Header Auth, JWT Auth or None, each using an n8n credential. The Respond option can be Immediately, When Last Node Finishes, or Using 'Respond to Webhook' Node. The Respond to Webhook node lets you choose the body (JSON, text, items, binary, redirect or no data), the status code and headers.

keyFacts: The error workflow must start with an Error Trigger node; it does not need to be activated to run.
Error workflows run only for automatic executions, not when you click Execute Workflow manually in the editor.
A workflow that contains an Error Trigger can use itself as its error workflow, but a separate shared one is the common pattern.
Retry On Fail defaults: Max Tries 3, Wait Between Tries 1000 ms.
On Error has three options: Stop Workflow (default), Continue, Continue (using error output).
Set Workflow Settings > 'This workflow can be called by' to control which workflows may run a sub-workflow.
n8n documents that sub-workflow executions do not count toward the plan's execution limits.
Production webhook URLs need an active workflow; test URLs need the editor to be listening.
If you choose 'Using Respond to Webhook Node', the workflow must reach a Respond to Webhook node, or the caller gets an error or waits.
Use execution.lastNodeExecuted in the alert to show which node failed, and execution.url to link straight to the failed run.

example.caption: Code node inside the error workflow (after Error Trigger) that builds the alert text for Telegram or Gmail.

pitfalls: Testing the error workflow by running the failing workflow manually in the editor: error workflows do not fire for manual runs. Activate the workflow and trigger it for real, for example through its production webhook.
Forgetting to set the error workflow in each production workflow's settings: creating the Error Trigger workflow alone does nothing.
Using Retry On Fail for data errors such as a missing field: retries will fail every time and only delay the alert. Validate data and use Stop and Error instead.
Setting On Error to Continue and never checking the output: failures become silent, and the error workflow will not fire because the run counts as successful.
Calling the Webhook test URL from a production system: it stops working once you leave the editor. Use the /webhook/ production URL with authentication enabled.
Choosing 'Using Respond to Webhook Node' but having a branch that never reaches that node, so callers time out or get an error.

workflow.title: Build and verify a failure alert for production workflows

steps.label: Create the error workflow
steps.detail: Make a new workflow that starts with an Error Trigger node and save it as 'Global Error Alert'.

steps.label: Format the alert message
steps.detail: Add a Code or Set node that reads workflow.name, execution.lastNodeExecuted, execution.error.message and execution.url.

steps.label: Send the alert
steps.detail: Connect a Telegram or Gmail node that sends the formatted text to you.

steps.label: Link production workflows
steps.detail: In each production workflow open Workflow Settings, choose 'Global Error Alert' as the Error workflow and save.

steps.label: Add a forced failure
steps.detail: Insert a Stop and Error node with a clear message in a test copy of a production workflow.

steps.label: Run it in production
steps.detail: Activate the workflow and trigger it through its real trigger, such as the production webhook URL.

steps.label: Check the alert
steps.detail: Confirm the alert arrives, names the Stop and Error node as the failing node, and links to the execution.

project.title: n8n-reliable-orders
project.summary: A Dockerised n8n setup with three workflows. An authenticated orders webhook calls a validation sub-workflow, and any production failure triggers a global error workflow that posts an alert naming the failing node to a small local alert receiver. docker-compose.yml and alert-receiver/server.js give the runtime and the alert sink, error-alert.json shows the Error Trigger with Retry On Fail and a timeout, validate-order.json shows the Stop and Error node, orders-webhook.json shows Header Auth, Respond to Webhook, the errorWorkflow setting and the execution timeout, and README.md walks through the forced-failure checkpoint.
project.run:
cp .env.example .env   # then edit both secrets
docker compose up -d
docker compose exec n8n n8n import:workflow --separate --input=/workflows
# Open http://localhost:5678, create the 'Orders API key' Header Auth credential, select it in the Webhook node, then activate/publish 'Orders Webhook'
set -a; . ./.env; set +a
curl -i -X POST http://localhost:5678/webhook/orders -H "X-API-Key: $ORDERS_API_KEY" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"orderId":"A1","amount":500}'
curl -i -X POST http://localhost:5678/webhook/orders -H "X-API-Key: $ORDERS_API_KEY" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"orderId":"B2","amount":0}'
docker compose logs -f alert-receiver

files.code:
# n8n plus a tiny alert receiver on the same Docker network
services:
  n8n:
    image: docker.n8n.io/n8nio/n8n:latest
    ports:
      - "5678:5678"
    environment:
      - GENERIC_TIMEZONE=Asia/Kolkata
      - TZ=Asia/Kolkata
      # Production webhook URLs and the execution.url in alerts are built from this
      - WEBHOOK_URL=http://localhost:5678/
      - N8N_EDITOR_BASE_URL=http://localhost:5678/
      # Keeps saved credentials decryptable across container restarts
      - N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY=${N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY}
    volumes:
      - n8n_data:/home/node/.n8n
      # Workflow JSON files, imported with the n8n CLI
      - ./workflows:/workflows:ro
    depends_on:
      - alert-receiver

  alert-receiver:
    image: node:22-alpine
    command: node /app/server.js
    environment:
      - PORT=4000
    ports:
      - "4000:4000"
    volumes:
      - ./alert-receiver:/app:ro

volumes:
  n8n_data:

# n8n-reliable-orders

Step 5 hands-on task: a global error workflow that alerts you when a production workflow fails.

## What is inside
- `Orders Webhook`: a POST endpoint protected by Header Auth. It calls a sub-workflow, then replies 201 using Respond to Webhook. Settings: Error Workflow = `Error Alert`, timeout = 30 s.
- `Validate Order (sub-workflow)`: if `amount <= 0`, the Stop and Error node fails the run on purpose.
- `Error Alert`: Error Trigger -> Code node (reads `execution.lastNodeExecuted`, `execution.error.message`, `execution.url`) -> HTTP Request with Retry On Fail.
- `alert-receiver`: prints each alert. Replace it with Slack or email in real work.

## Setup
1. `cp .env.example .env`, then set both secrets.
2. `docker compose up -d`, then run the import command in the run steps.
3. In the n8n UI, create a credential of type **Header Auth**. Name it `Orders API key`. Set Name = `X-API-Key` and Value = your `ORDERS_API_KEY`.
4. Open `Orders Webhook`, select that credential in the Webhook node, save, then activate (publish) the workflow.

## Checkpoint: forced failure
- A valid order (`amount` 500) returns `201 {"ok":true,...}`.
- An invalid order (`amount` 0) makes n8n return an error response. `docker compose logs alert-receiver` then shows a line like:
  `[ALERT] ... n8n FAILURE | Orders Webhook | node: Validate Order | Invalid order B2: amount must be greater than 0`

## Exam and interview notes
- The Error Workflow is set per workflow (Settings > Error workflow). It does not need to be active itself.
- It fires only for production (automatic) executions. Manual test runs from the editor do not trigger it.
- The test URL (`/webhook-test/`) works only while you listen in the editor. The production URL (`/webhook/`) works only when the workflow is active.
- Retry On Fail suits flaky APIs. On Error (Continue / Continue using error output) suits items you can skip. Use the Stop and Error node when your business rules are broken.
- A request with no key or a wrong key gets an auth error (403) before any node runs.

# Copy to .env and change both values before first start

# Used by n8n to encrypt saved credentials. Keep it stable and secret.
N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY=change-me-to-a-long-random-string

# Shared secret for the Orders Webhook Header Auth credential (header X-API-Key)
# Paste the same value into the 'Orders API key' credential in the n8n UI
ORDERS_API_KEY=change-me-orders-key

# Ports used: n8n 5678, alert-receiver 4000
# The alert URL inside Docker is http://alert-receiver:4000/alert

revision.examFocus: This step maps to the error-handling part of the n8n Level 2 course and to the webhook and trigger basics from Level 1. The knowledge checks test whether you know which mechanism fires when: Error Trigger vs node-level settings, manual vs production runs, and test vs production webhook URLs. Expect scenario-style questions where one small setting, such as an unset error workflow or a manual run, explains why an alert never arrived.

compare.difference: Retry helps only with temporary faults such as timeouts, rate limits or a flaky API. Stop and Error deliberately fails the run with your own message when the data is wrong, so it does not wait for a retry that cannot succeed.
compare.chooseA: Pick Retry On Fail when the same request would probably succeed a few seconds later, for example a 429, 503 or network timeout.
compare.chooseB: Pick Stop and Error when your own validation finds bad or missing data and you want the error workflow to fire at once with a clear message.

compare.difference: Continue passes the error on as normal output, so later nodes cannot easily tell it apart from success. The error output option adds a separate error branch that you can route and handle.
compare.chooseA: Pick Continue only when a failed item truly does not matter and you accept the silent loss.
compare.chooseB: Pick the error output option when you want to log, notify or fix failed items on their own branch while good items carry on.

compare.difference: The error workflow is a workflow-wide safety net that runs only after an automatic run has failed. Node-level settings handle the failure inside the same run, so that run may never count as failed.
compare.chooseA: Pick an error workflow for central alerting across many production workflows.
compare.chooseB: Pick node-level handling when one known, expected failure needs a local fallback or cleanup.

compare.difference: The test URL works only while the editor is listening, and it shows the data on the canvas. The production URL works only when the workflow is active, and its runs appear in the Executions list.
compare.chooseA: Pick the test URL while building, so you can capture a sample request and map its fields.
compare.chooseB: Pick the production URL, with authentication, for any real external system calling n8n.

compare.b: HTTP Request to another workflow's webhook
compare.difference: Execute Workflow calls the sub-workflow inside n8n, with access control in workflow settings, and n8n states these runs do not count toward plan execution limits. A webhook call goes over HTTP, needs its own authentication and counts as a separate production execution.
compare.chooseA: Pick Execute Workflow to reuse logic between workflows on the same n8n instance.
compare.chooseB: Pick a webhook call when the caller is outside n8n or on a different instance.

cues.cue: alert when any production workflow fails
cues.pick: One shared workflow starting with Error Trigger, set as the Error Workflow in each production workflow's settings
cues.why: A single central handler is the documented pattern, but it works only where it has been linked in settings.

cues.cue: error workflow did not fire during testing
cues.pick: The run was manual from the editor, or the error workflow was never set in Workflow Settings
cues.why: Error workflows ignore manual runs and do nothing until they are linked.

cues.cue: API sometimes returns 429 or times out
cues.pick: Retry On Fail with a longer Wait Between Tries
cues.why: The fault is temporary, so spacing out the retries usually succeeds.

cues.cue: required field is missing or invalid
cues.pick: IF or Filter check, then a Stop and Error node
cues.why: Retrying bad data never succeeds and only delays the alert.

cues.cue: some items fail but the rest must still be processed
cues.pick: On Error: Continue (using error output)
cues.why: It splits failed items onto their own branch without stopping the good ones.

cues.cue: which node failed and a link to the run
cues.pick: {{ $json.execution.lastNodeExecuted }} and {{ $json.execution.url }} from the Error Trigger
cues.why: These fields give the failing node and a direct link to the failed execution.

cues.cue: caller needs a custom status code or body
cues.pick: Webhook Respond set to 'Using Respond to Webhook Node', with every branch ending in that node
cues.why: Only this node lets you set the response code, headers and body, and any branch that misses it leaves the caller waiting or erroring.

cues.cue: reuse the same logic in many workflows, only approved callers
cues.pick: Sub-workflow via Execute Workflow, with 'This workflow can be called by' restricted
cues.why: This gives reuse plus access control, without exposing a public endpoint.

scenario.situation: A team built a shared alert workflow that starts with an Error Trigger and sends a Slack message. They opened their order-sync workflow and set a bad API key. They clicked Execute Workflow in the editor, saw the HTTP Request node fail, but no Slack alert arrived. Order-sync is active and is triggered by a production webhook. What is the most likely reason, and how should they test it?
reasoning: Check how the run was started: it was started manually from the editor, and error workflows never fire for manual executions.
Rule out activating the alert workflow: an error workflow does not need to be active to run, so this is not the fix.
Check that order-sync's Workflow Settings name the alert workflow as its Error Workflow, because without that link nothing fires even for real runs.
Reject Retry On Fail as a fix: a bad API key is a permanent error, so retries only delay the failure.
Test correctly: call the production /webhook/ URL from outside the editor, then confirm the Slack message shows the failing node and the execution link.
scenario.answer: The alert did not fire because the run was manual. Confirm the Error Workflow setting in order-sync, then trigger it through its production webhook, and the Error Trigger will send the alert with lastNodeExecuted and the execution URL.","answer":"The run was manual, and error workflows ignore manual runs. Confirm that order-sync's Error Workflow setting points to the alert workflow, then trigger it through the production webhook URL to get the alert with the failing node and the run link.

memoryAids: LINK-LIVE-LOOK: Link the error workflow in Settings, run it Live (automatic, not manual), Look at lastNodeExecuted and the execution url in the alert.
Retry for Flaky, Stop for Faulty: temporary faults get Retry On Fail, bad data gets Stop and Error.
TEST needs the Editor, PROD needs Active: /webhook-test/ listens only while you watch, /webhook/ answers only when the workflow is active.
cheatSheet: The error workflow's first node must be Error Trigger, and the workflow does not need to be active.
Link the error workflow in every production workflow via Workflow Settings > Error Workflow.
Manual editor runs never trigger the error workflow. Test with a real trigger, such as a production webhook or a schedule.
Use Retry On Fail for temporary faults only. Raise Wait Between Tries for rate limits.
Use Stop and Error with a clear message for validation failures, so the error workflow fires at once.
On Error 'Continue' can hide failures. A run that continues counts as a success, so no error workflow fires.
Prefer 'Continue (using error output)' when failed items need their own branch.
Set timeouts so a hung request fails visibly: a request timeout on HTTP nodes, and a workflow timeout in Workflow Settings.
Sub-workflows: use Execute Workflow in the parent, restrict 'This workflow can be called by', and remember they do not count toward execution limits.
Webhook: use the test URL to build, and the production URL with Basic, Header or JWT auth for real callers.
'Using Respond to Webhook Node' means every path, including error paths, must reach a Respond to Webhook node.
Good alert fields: workflow.name, execution.lastNodeExecuted, execution.error.message, execution.url.
selfCheck: I can build an Error Trigger workflow, link it to a production workflow, and prove it fires with a real, non-manual failure.
I can decide between Retry On Fail, Stop and Error, Continue and Continue (using error output) for a given failure type.
I can write an alert message that shows the workflow name, failing node, error message and a clickable execution link.
I can explain why a webhook works in the editor but fails in production, or the other way round, and fix it.
I can configure a Webhook with authentication and a Respond to Webhook node so every branch returns a response.
I can split reusable logic into a sub-workflow and restrict which workflows may call it.

objective.question: You are building a shared alert workflow that should run whenever another workflow fails. Which node must this alert workflow start with?
options: Error Trigger
Execute Workflow Trigger
Schedule Trigger
Webhook
objective.explanation: An error workflow must begin with an Error Trigger node, which receives the failure data. The other triggers start workflows on HTTP calls, schedules or sub-workflow calls, not on failures.

objective.question: Your error workflow is set up correctly but is not activated. A production workflow that uses it fails on a schedule. What happens?
options: The error workflow runs, because it does not need to be activated
n8n activates the error workflow automatically and then runs it
The failed workflow retries three times instead
Nothing runs, because the error workflow is inactive
objective.explanation: An error workflow does not need to be activated to run. Activation is needed for trigger-based workflows like webhooks and schedules, not for the Error Trigger.

objective.question: You open a workflow in the editor, click Execute Workflow, and a node fails. Your error workflow does not send an alert. Why?
options: The Error Trigger must be pinned with test data first
The error workflow must be in the same folder
Manual runs always use Continue on error
Error workflows only run for automatic executions, not manual ones
objective.explanation: Error workflows run only for automatic executions, such as triggers and schedules. Manual runs from the editor show the error in the canvas instead.

objective.question: Where do you link a production workflow to your shared error workflow?
options: In the failing node's Settings tab
In the n8n environment variables only
In the production workflow's Workflow Settings, under Error Workflow
In the Error Trigger node parameters
objective.explanation: Each workflow chooses its error workflow in Workflow Settings. The Error Trigger does not list which workflows it watches.

objective.question: In your Slack alert you want to show which node failed. Which expression from the Error Trigger output should you use?
options: {{ $json.workflow.nodeName }}
{{ $json.error.node }}
{{ $execution.failedNode }}
{{ $json.execution.lastNodeExecuted }}
objective.explanation: The Error Trigger output includes execution.lastNodeExecuted, which is the node where the run stopped. The other paths are not part of the documented output.

objective.question: You want the on-call engineer to click once and open the failed run. Which field should you put in the alert?
options: execution.url
execution.mode
execution.retryOf
workflow.id
objective.explanation: execution.url is a direct link to the failed execution. workflow.id identifies the workflow, execution.mode shows how it ran, and retryOf is only set for retries.

objective.question: An order workflow receives a payload with a missing customer email. No node errors, but you want the run to be marked as failed and trigger the error workflow. What should you add?
options: A Stop and Error node on the invalid branch
Retry On Fail on the next node
A Wait node with a long timeout
A No Operation node
objective.explanation: Stop and Error deliberately throws an error with your message, so the execution fails and the error workflow runs. The other options do not fail the execution.

objective.question: You enable Retry On Fail on an HTTP Request node and do not change anything else. What are the defaults?
options: Max Tries 2, Wait Between Tries 500 ms
Max Tries 3, Wait Between Tries 0 ms
Max Tries 3, Wait Between Tries 1000 ms
Max Tries 5, Wait Between Tries 5000 ms
objective.explanation: The defaults are Max Tries 3 and Wait Between Tries 1000 ms. You can raise the wait for rate-limited APIs.

objective.question: A CRM update node sometimes fails for single records. You want failed items to go to a separate branch that logs them, while good items carry on. Which On Error setting fits?
options: Continue
Continue (using error output)
Retry On Fail with Max Tries 1
Stop Workflow
objective.explanation: Continue (using error output) adds an error output so you can route failed items to their own branch. Continue passes data on without a separate branch, and Stop Workflow halts the run.

objective.question: A node is set to On Error: Continue. It fails during a scheduled run. What is the most likely result?
options: The node retries forever
The workflow is deactivated
The workflow continues, and the error workflow does not run for that node failure
The execution stops and the error workflow runs
objective.explanation: With Continue, n8n carries on to the next node instead of failing the execution, so the error workflow is not triggered by that failure. Stop Workflow is the default behaviour that fails the run.

objective.question: A workflow sometimes hangs for hours because an external API never responds. Which setting best protects the instance at the workflow level?
options: Use the test webhook URL
Set On Error to Continue on the trigger
Turn on Always Output Data
Set a timeout in Workflow Settings so the execution is cancelled after a limit
objective.explanation: The workflow timeout setting stops executions that run past a set time. The other options do not limit run time.

objective.question: You built a reusable 'Send invoice' sub-workflow. You want only workflows in the same project to call it. Where do you control this?
options: Instance environment variables
The Error Trigger node
Sub-workflow's Workflow Settings > This workflow can be called by
Execute Workflow node > Options > Permissions
objective.explanation: The setting 'This workflow can be called by' in the sub-workflow's Workflow Settings controls which workflows may run it. The calling node has no permission setting.

objective.question: Your team worries that splitting a big workflow into sub-workflows will use up the plan's execution quota faster. What does n8n document?
options: Sub-workflow executions do not count toward the plan's execution limits
Sub-workflows count double
Only sub-workflows that fail are counted
Each sub-workflow run counts as a full execution
objective.explanation: n8n documents that sub-workflow executions do not count toward plan execution limits. Only the parent execution counts.

objective.question: A partner calls your production webhook URL and gets a 404 error, but the test URL works when you click 'Listen for test event'. What is the most likely cause?
options: Header Auth is missing
The Respond to Webhook node is missing
Retry On Fail is off
The workflow is not active
objective.explanation: Production webhook URLs only work when the workflow is active. Test URLs work only while the editor is listening.

objective.question: Your Webhook node uses Respond: 'Using Respond to Webhook Node'. On one IF branch there is no Respond to Webhook node. What happens when a request takes that branch?
options: The caller gets an error or waits, because no response node was reached
The webhook switches to the test URL
The request is retried on the other branch
n8n sends an empty 200 response automatically and silently
objective.explanation: With this option, the workflow must reach a Respond to Webhook node. If a branch skips it, the caller gets an error or waits for a response.

objective.question: Your alert workflow uses {{$json.execution.url}} to link to the failed run. For one failure the link is empty. The Error Trigger output for that failure is shown below. Why is the link empty?
options: The error happened in the trigger node, so n8n sends less data and there is no execution object
The workflow setting 'Save failed production executions' is off, which removes all error fields
The execution was a manual run from the editor, which never includes a URL
The error workflow was not activated, so n8n dropped the execution fields
objective.explanation: When the main workflow fails in its trigger node, the Error Trigger receives a smaller payload with a 'trigger' object and no execution ID or URL. Manual runs do not reach the error workflow at all, and the other options do not change the payload shape.

objective.question: An HTTP Request node calls a slow reporting API. Sometimes the API holds the connection open for many minutes. You want only this call to give up after 30 seconds so its error can be handled, while the rest of the workflow has no time limit. What should you configure?
options: Set the HTTP Request node option 'Timeout' to 30000 milliseconds
Add a Wait node set to 30 seconds before the HTTP Request node
Enable Retry On Fail with Wait Between Tries set to 30000 ms
Set the workflow setting 'Timeout Workflow' to 30 seconds
