project.title: support-agent-rag
project.summary: A self-hosted n8n support agent for a fictional product, CloudNotes. It answers questions from your own Markdown documents using RAG, and it calls a ticket tool only when the documents cannot solve the problem and the user agrees. docker-compose.yml and .env.example run n8n with a mock ticket API. docs/ holds the knowledge base. Workflow 1 loads, splits, embeds and stores the documents. Workflow 2 is the ticket tool, a sub-workflow that reads $fromAI() inputs and calls an HTTP API. Workflow 3 is the AI Agent root node, with a Chat Trigger and four sub-nodes: chat model, memory, vector store tool and Call n8n Workflow Tool.
project.run:
cp .env.example .env
docker compose up -d
docker compose exec n8n n8n import:workflow --separate --input=/workflows
open http://localhost:5678  # create owner account, add OpenAI credential to the 4 OpenAI sub-nodes
# Run workflow '1 - Ingest support docs' once, then open '3 - Support agent' and click 'Open chat'

files.code:
# support-agent-rag (n8n Step 6: AI agents)

A support chatbot that answers ONLY from `docs/` and creates a ticket only when needed.

## What each part teaches
- **Chat Trigger**: gives the agent a chat window and a `sessionId` for memory.
- **AI Agent (root node)**: a cluster node. Sub-nodes plug into it:
  - Chat model (OpenAI `gpt-4o-mini`), which does the reasoning.
  - Simple Memory (window buffer), which keeps the last 10 messages per session.
  - Tool `search_docs`: an In-Memory Vector Store in *retrieve-as-tool* mode (RAG).
  - Tool `create_ticket`: a Call n8n Workflow Tool. Its inputs are filled by `$fromAI()`.
- **RAG pipeline** (workflow 1): Read files, then Default Data Loader, then Recursive Character Text Splitter, then OpenAI Embeddings, then insert into vector store key `support_docs`.
- **Tool descriptions** decide WHEN the model calls a tool. Read them in workflow 3.

## Setup
1. `cp .env.example .env` and set a long random `N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY`.
2. `docker compose up -d`, then import the workflows (see the run commands).
3. In the n8n UI, create one **OpenAI** credential. Select it on:
   - the Embeddings node in workflow 1;
   - the Embeddings node and the Chat Model node in workflow 3.
4. Run **1 - Ingest support docs** once.
   - The in-memory store is cleared on every n8n restart, so run it again after each restart.
   - For production, use Pinecone, Qdrant, PGVector or Supabase.
5. Activate or open **3 - Support agent** and click **Open chat**.

## Checkpoint tests
| Message | Expected |
|---|---|
| How long do refunds take? | Answer from docs, using `search_docs` only |
| How do I export notes to PDF? | Answer from docs, no ticket |
| My sync has failed for 3 days, nothing in docs helps | Agent asks for your email, confirms, then calls `create_ticket` |

Check **Executions**. Open a run and look at the agent's tool calls. `create_ticket` must appear only in the third case.

## Notes
- The mock ticket API is `httpbin` at `TICKET_API_URL=http://tickets/post`. It echoes the payload back.
- Workflow 3 calls workflow 2 by its fixed ID `createTicket0001`. That ID is set in the JSON, so the link survives import.
- `N8N_RESTRICT_FILE_ACCESS_TO` limits the Read Files node to `/data/docs`.

# n8n + a mock ticket API, all local
services:
  n8n:
    image: docker.n8n.io/n8nio/n8n:latest
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - "5678:5678"            # n8n editor + chat at http://localhost:5678
    env_file: .env
    environment:
      - N8N_RESTRICT_FILE_ACCESS_TO=/data/docs   # Read Files node may only read here
      - N8N_BLOCK_ENV_ACCESS_IN_NODE=false       # allow {{ $env.TICKET_API_URL }} in workflow 2
      - TICKET_API_URL=http://tickets/post       # used by the create-ticket sub-workflow
    volumes:
      - n8n_data:/home/node/.n8n                 # credentials, workflows, executions
      - ./docs:/data/docs:ro                     # knowledge base for RAG
      - ./workflows:/workflows:ro                # exported JSON for n8n import:workflow
    depends_on:
      - tickets

  tickets:
    image: kennethreitz/httpbin                  # echoes POST /post, stands in for a helpdesk API
    restart: unless-stopped

volumes:
  n8n_data:

# Copy to .env. Never commit the real file.
# Encrypts saved credentials (your OpenAI key). Keep it stable across restarts.
N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY=replace-with-a-long-random-string

# Indian time for schedules and execution logs
GENERIC_TIMEZONE=Asia/Kolkata
TZ=Asia/Kolkata

# Editor URL used in links and webhook URLs
N8N_HOST=localhost
N8N_PORT=5678
N8N_PROTOCOL=http

# The OpenAI API key is NOT set here.
# Add it in the n8n UI as an 'OpenAI' credential, so it is stored encrypted.

# CloudNotes Support FAQ

## Refunds
- Refunds are allowed within 14 days of purchase for annual plans.
- Monthly plans are not refundable, but you can cancel any time.
- Approved refunds reach your bank or UPI account in 5 to 7 working days.

## Exporting notes
- Open a note, click the three-dot menu, choose Export, then PDF or Markdown.
- To export all notes, go to Settings > Data > Export workspace (ZIP file).

## Sync problems
- Check you are on the latest app version.
- Sign out and sign in again to refresh the sync token.
- Sync pauses when device storage is below 200 MB.
- If sync still fails after these steps, contact support. A ticket is needed.

## Account and billing
- Change your plan in Settings > Billing.
- GST invoices are emailed after each payment and are also in Settings > Billing > Invoices.
- Password reset: use 'Forgot password' on the login screen.

## Support hours
- Human support works Monday to Saturday, 9:00 to 18:00 IST.
- Tickets get a first reply within one working day.

revision.examFocus: The official n8n Level 1 and Level 2 text courses focus on core workflow skills such as nodes, expressions, data structures and error workflows. AI agents are covered mainly in n8n's Advanced AI documentation and are tested in practical builds and interviews. Expect two kinds of questions: which cluster sub-node to attach (model, memory, tool, vector store, embeddings), and why an agent misbehaves (wrong tool calls, lost memory, bad retrieval).

compare.b: Postgres or Redis Chat Memory / PGVector, Qdrant, Pinecone
compare.difference: The Simple nodes keep data in the n8n process's RAM. The external nodes persist data and share it across restarts and queue-mode workers.
compare.chooseA: Pick Simple nodes for a quick prototype or a demo on a single instance where losing data is acceptable.
compare.chooseB: Pick external stores whenever the question mentions production, restarts, scaling, multiple workers or queue mode.

compare.difference: The Workflow Tool runs a whole sub-workflow, so you get multiple steps, validation and error handling. The HTTP Request Tool makes one API call.
compare.chooseA: Pick the Workflow Tool when the action needs several steps, checks, logging or a friendly error message, such as creating a ticket.
compare.chooseB: Pick the HTTP Request Tool for one simple, read-only or low-risk API call, such as fetching order status.

compare.a: Vector store in 'retrieve as tool for AI Agent' mode
compare.difference: Retrieve mode is attached to the agent in the query flow. Insert mode sits in the ingest flow with a document loader, splitter and embeddings.
compare.chooseA: Choose retrieve-as-tool when the agent must look up knowledge during a chat.
compare.chooseB: Choose insert when loading or refreshing documents, on a manual or scheduled trigger.

compare.difference: The Chat Trigger supplies sessionId automatically. Other triggers need you to set the memory session key yourself.
compare.chooseA: Use the Chat Trigger for n8n's hosted or embedded chat, where memory works with default settings.
compare.chooseB: Use other triggers for external channels, and set the session key with an expression such as the chat ID or user ID.

compare.difference: The tool description tells the model what one tool does and when to call it. The system message sets overall role, rules and priority, for example 'search docs first'.
compare.chooseA: Fix the tool description when the agent calls the wrong tool, or calls a tool at the wrong time.
compare.chooseB: Fix the system message when the agent's overall behaviour, tone or order of steps is wrong.

cues.cue: agent opens tickets for simple questions
cues.pick: Rewrite the ticket tool description with explicit conditions, and add a matching rule in the system message
cues.why: The model decides tool use only from the descriptions and instructions it is given.

cues.cue: all users see each other's conversation
cues.pick: Set the memory session key with an expression based on the user or chat ID
cues.why: Without a unique key, every execution reads and writes one shared history.

cues.cue: similarity search returns irrelevant results or a dimension error
cues.pick: Use the same embedding model for insert and retrieve, then re-embed
cues.why: Vectors from different models or dimensions cannot be compared.

cues.cue: memory lost after restart / queue mode
cues.pick: Postgres or Redis Chat Memory
cues.why: Persistent stores survive restarts and are shared by all workers.

cues.cue: too many tokens / context limit / stale answers from a huge prompt
cues.pick: RAG with a vector store as a tool
cues.why: Only the relevant chunks are retrieved for each question.

cues.cue: answers miss information that sits across paragraphs
cues.pick: Tune chunk size and increase chunk overlap in the text splitter
cues.why: Overlap stops meaning being cut at chunk boundaries.

cues.cue: agent stops with max iterations reached
cues.pick: Make the tool return a clear success or error message; check tool descriptions
cues.why: Loops usually happen when tool output is empty, unclear or a failure the agent cannot interpret.

cues.cue: let the model fill in a tool parameter
cues.pick: $fromAI() in the tool's field
cues.why: It tells the agent to generate that value, using a key, a description and a type.

scenario.situation: A company runs n8n in queue mode with three workers. Its support agent is connected to a Telegram Trigger, an OpenAI chat model, Simple Memory, and a Simple Vector Store filled by a separate ingest workflow. Users complain that the bot forgets them, mixes up conversations, and sometimes says it has no documents. What is the best fix?
reasoning: Mixed-up conversations point to a missing or shared session key. The Telegram Trigger does not supply sessionId the way the Chat Trigger does.
Forgetting users and losing documents in queue mode point to in-memory nodes. Each worker has its own RAM, and restarts wipe it.
So adding more memory or a larger context window does not help. The storage is not shared, so that answer is wrong.
Changing the chat model does not fix storage or session problems either, so remove that option.
The correct fix has both parts: persistent shared stores plus a per-user session key.
scenario.answer: Replace Simple Memory with Postgres or Redis Chat Memory, keyed by an expression on the Telegram chat ID. Replace the Simple Vector Store with PGVector, Qdrant or Pinecone, and re-ingest the documents with the same embedding model.

memoryAids: Agent kit = M-M-T: Model (must have), Memory (optional), Tools (optional, but no tools means just a chatbot).
RAG ingest = L-S-E-I: Load, Split, Embed, Insert. RAG query = C-A-R: Chat, Agent, Retrieve-as-tool.
Same Model, Same Dimensions: embed and retrieve with one model, or re-embed everything.
cheatSheet: The AI Agent is a root node. Chat model, memory, tools and vector stores attach to it as sub-nodes.
API credentials go on the chat model or embeddings sub-node, never on the AI Agent node.
Max Iterations (default 10) is a safety cap on tool loops. It is not a fix for bad tools.
The Chat Trigger gives sessionId automatically. Any other trigger needs a session key expression.
Simple Memory and Simple Vector Store are for demos only. They are lost on restart and not shared across workers.
Keep ingest and query in separate workflows. Ingest runs on a manual or schedule trigger.
Changing the embedding model or its dimensions means rebuilding the index and re-embedding all documents.
Chunks too large give noisy matches. Chunks too small lose context. Overlap bridges the boundaries.
A good tool description states what the tool does, when to use it and when not to use it.
Use the Call n8n Workflow Tool for multi-step actions such as ticket creation, with error handling inside.
A tool sub-workflow should always return a clear text result, including on failure.
Sub-node expressions read only the first input item.
selfCheck: I can wire an AI Agent with a chat model, persistent memory, a retrieve-as-tool vector store and a ticket workflow tool.
I can build a separate ingest workflow that loads, splits, embeds and inserts documents with the same embedding model used for retrieval.
I can set a memory session key for a non-chat trigger such as Telegram or a webhook.
I can write a tool description and system message so the ticket tool runs only when the user asks for it or the documents cannot answer.
I can diagnose lost memory, shared conversations, irrelevant retrieval and max-iteration loops, and name the fix for each.
I can use $fromAI() to let the agent fill in ticket fields such as subject and priority.

objective.question: You add an AI Agent node to a new workflow. Which sub-node must you connect before the agent can run?
options: A Tool sub-node
An Output Parser sub-node
A Chat Model sub-node
A Memory sub-node
objective.explanation: The AI Agent needs a chat model to reason and reply, so the Chat Model connection is required. Memory, tools and output parsers are optional.

objective.question: An AI Agent has a chat model and Simple Memory connected but no tools. How does it behave?
options: It works as a chatbot that remembers the conversation but cannot take actions or fetch outside data
It calls any sub-workflow in the same project
It automatically uses the HTTP Request node to search the web
It fails validation and will not run
objective.explanation: Tools are optional, but without them the agent can only talk, using the model's knowledge and the conversation history. It cannot look up documents or create tickets.

objective.question: Your team is using OpenAI models. Where do you set the OpenAI credential in an agent workflow?
options: On the Chat Trigger node
On the OpenAI Chat Model sub-node and the Embeddings sub-node
In the workflow settings, once for all nodes
On the AI Agent node
objective.explanation: Provider credentials are set on the sub-nodes that call the provider, such as the chat model and embeddings sub-nodes. The AI Agent node has no provider credential of its own.

objective.question: During testing, a support agent keeps calling the same search tool again and again because the results never satisfy it. What setting stops this loop?
options: Max Iterations on the AI Agent node, which defaults to 10
Timeout on the Chat Trigger
Top K on the vector store
Context Window Length on the memory node
objective.explanation: Max Iterations caps how many reasoning and tool-call cycles the agent may run, with a default of 10. Context window length and Top K control memory size and the number of retrieved chunks, not loops.

objective.question: You replace the Chat Trigger with a Webhook trigger called by your website. Postgres Chat Memory now mixes up conversations between users. What is the fix?
options: Set the memory node's session key yourself, for example with an expression that reads the user or conversation ID from the webhook body
Increase Max Iterations
Add a second AI Agent node
Switch to Simple Memory
objective.explanation: The Chat Trigger supplies sessionId automatically, and memory reads it by default. With any other trigger you must define the session key yourself so that each conversation gets its own history.

objective.question: A self-hosted n8n instance runs in queue mode with several workers. The agent forgets earlier messages at random, and history disappears after restarts. It uses Simple Memory. What should you change?
options: Use Postgres Chat Memory or Redis Chat Memory
Turn off queue mode only for this workflow
Store the history in a Set node
Increase the context window length
objective.explanation: Simple Memory lives in the memory of one instance. It is not shared across workers and is lost on restart. Postgres or Redis memory persists outside n8n and works in production and in queue mode.

objective.question: You ingested documents into a Simple Vector Store. After the n8n server restarts, the agent says it cannot find any documents. Why?
options: Simple Vector Store keeps data in instance memory, so a restart erases it
The Chat Trigger session ended
Max Iterations was reached
The embeddings expired
objective.explanation: Simple Vector Store is in-memory and meant for testing. For persistent data use a real vector database such as PGVector, Qdrant or Pinecone.

objective.question: Your Qdrant collection was built with OpenAI text-embedding-3-small (1536 dimensions). You switch the embeddings sub-node to a model with a different dimension size, and inserts and queries fail. What is the correct fix?
options: Keep the old index and set Top K to 1
Change the chat model to match the embedding model
Create an index or collection that matches the new dimension size, then re-embed and re-insert all documents with the new model
Lower the chunk size in the text splitter
objective.explanation: Vector dimensions must match the index, and vectors from different models are not comparable. Changing the embedding model means you must re-embed the whole corpus into an index that matches the new size.

objective.question: What is the recommended structure for a RAG support bot in n8n?
options: A single Chat Trigger connected straight to the vector store with no agent
Embedding each user question and storing it as a document
An ingest flow (manual or scheduled trigger, load, split, embed, insert) and a separate query flow (Chat Trigger, AI Agent, vector store used as a retrieval tool)
One workflow that loads, embeds and inserts all documents on every chat message
objective.explanation: Ingestion is slow and runs only when documents change. Querying runs on every message. Keeping them in separate flows avoids re-embedding on every chat and keeps answers fast.

objective.question: Which vector store operation mode lets an AI Agent decide for itself when to search your documents?
options: Get Many
Retrieve Documents (As Tool for AI Agent)
Update Documents
Insert Documents
objective.explanation: In 'Retrieve Documents (As Tool for AI Agent)' mode, the vector store connects to the agent's Tool input. The agent then searches when its description fits the question. Insert is used for ingestion, and Get Many is for direct retrieval in a normal flow.

objective.question: Your agent creates support tickets even for simple questions that the documentation answers. What is the most effective first fix?
options: Write a clear tool description, for example 'Create a ticket only when the docs do not solve the issue or the user asks for a human', and support it in the system message
Raise Max Iterations to 50
Switch to a larger embedding model
Remove memory from the agent
objective.explanation: The agent chooses tools from their names and descriptions and from its system message. Clear rules about when to use, and when not to use, the ticket tool fix most wrong tool calls.

objective.question: In the ticket tool's 'Subject' field you write {{ $fromAI('subject', 'Short summary of the customer issue', 'string') }}. What does this do?
options: It lets the model generate the value for this parameter when it calls the tool
It encrypts the subject before sending it
It fetches the subject from the vector store
It reads the subject from the previous node's first item
objective.explanation: $fromAI() marks a tool parameter that the AI fills in at call time, using the key, description and type you give it. It does not read data from earlier nodes.

objective.question: You use the Call n8n Workflow Tool to run a 'Create Ticket' sub-workflow. How should that sub-workflow start?
options: With a Schedule Trigger
With a Webhook node set to POST
With the 'When Executed by Another Workflow' (Execute Workflow Trigger) node, defining the inputs it expects
With a Chat Trigger
objective.explanation: Sub-workflows called by the Call n8n Workflow Tool must start with the Execute Workflow Trigger. That node receives the inputs the agent passes to it.

objective.question: In the text splitter, what is the main purpose of chunk overlap?
options: It keeps context that crosses chunk boundaries, so a sentence or idea split between two chunks can still be retrieved meaningfully
It removes duplicate documents
It sets the vector dimension
It reduces the number of embeddings and the cost
objective.explanation: Overlap repeats some text between neighbouring chunks, so meaning is not cut at the boundary. It slightly increases the chunk count, so it does not reduce cost.

objective.question: Ten items flow into an AI Agent. A sub-node parameter uses {{ $json.customerId }}. What value does the sub-node use?
options: An array of all ten customerIds
The value is always empty
Only the customerId from the first input item
A different customerId for each of the ten items
objective.explanation: Sub-node expressions resolve only against the first input item, unlike normal nodes, which resolve per item. If each item needs its own value, process items one at a time, for example in a loop or a sub-workflow.

objective.question: Your AI Agent worked with the Chat Trigger. You replace the trigger with a Webhook node that receives {"message": "..."} in the request body. The agent now fails because it finds no prompt. What is the correct fix?
options: Rename the webhook body field to 'prompt' so the agent detects it automatically
Add a Simple Memory sub-node so the agent can read the incoming message
Enable 'Return Intermediate Steps' so the agent exposes the input text
Set the agent's prompt source to 'Define below' and map the prompt to {{ $json.body.message }}
objective.explanation: With the 'Connected Chat Trigger Node' prompt source, the agent expects the Chat Trigger's chatInput field. With any other trigger, you must define the prompt yourself and map it to the incoming data. Renaming fields, adding memory or exposing intermediate steps does not tell the agent where the user's text is.

objective.question: A support agent uses Simple Memory with Context Window Length set to 5. What does this setting control?
options: How many recent past interactions are sent to the model with each new message
How many minutes a conversation is kept before it expires
How many tool calls the agent may make per message
The maximum number of chat sessions the memory can hold at once
objective.explanation: Context Window Length limits how much recent history is passed to the chat model on each turn, which controls both context and token cost. It does not cap sessions, set an expiry time or limit tool calls. Tool calls are limited by Max Iterations.

objective.question: You set a Pinecone Vector Store node to the mode 'Retrieve Documents (As Vector Store for Chain/Tool)'. You want an AI Agent to use it for answering questions. How do you connect it?
options: Connect it to a Vector Store Question Answer Tool, then connect that tool to the agent
Connect it to the agent's Chat Model input in place of the LLM
Put it in the main flow before the agent so retrieved documents arrive as items
Connect the vector store directly to the agent's Memory input
objective.explanation: In this mode, the vector store feeds a chain or a tool such as the Vector Store Question Answer Tool. That tool then becomes one of the agent's tools. A vector store is not a memory or a chat model. Placing it in the main flow would retrieve documents once, not when the agent decides it needs them.

objective.question: While ingesting, you added a 'product' metadata field to every chunk with the Default Data Loader. Users of Product A sometimes get answers taken from Product B documents. What is the best fix?
options: Use a separate chat model for each product
Lower Max Iterations so the agent searches less often
Apply a metadata filter on product in the vector store retrieval options
Increase the chunk overlap so chunks carry more context
objective.explanation: A metadata filter limits similarity search to chunks that match a metadata value, such as product = A. Vector stores like PGVector, Qdrant and Pinecone support this. Overlap, model choice and iteration limits do not stop the search from returning chunks from the wrong product.

objective.question: An agent calls a 'Create Ticket' sub-workflow through the Call n8n Workflow Tool. What does the agent receive as the tool's result?
options: The data output by the last node that runs in the sub-workflow
Nothing; the tool runs asynchronously and returns immediately
The full execution log of the sub-workflow
Only a success or failure flag
objective.explanation: The tool returns the output of the sub-workflow's final node to the agent. Design that node to return something useful, such as the ticket ID and status, so the agent can confirm to the user. It does not return only a flag or the full execution log.

objective.question: A downstream node needs the agent's reply as JSON with the fields 'answer' and 'needsTicket'. Free-text prompting alone gives inconsistent output. What should you do?
options: Add a Code node after the agent that uses regex to extract the fields
Add a second memory sub-node that stores the JSON template
Set the chat model temperature to 0 and hope the format stays stable
Enable 'Require Specific Output Format' on the agent and connect a Structured Output Parser with the schema
objective.explanation: The output parser gives the model a schema and validates the agent's output against it, so you get reliable structured fields. Regex parsing and a low temperature are fragile. Memory has nothing to do with output format.

objective.question: An agent gives a wrong answer. You want to see which tools it called, with what inputs, and what each tool returned. Which option on the AI Agent node helps most?
options: Return Intermediate Steps
Context Window Length
Always Output Data
Max Iterations
objective.explanation: Return Intermediate Steps adds the agent's tool calls and observations to its output, so you can debug its reasoning path. The execution logs panel shows similar detail. Max Iterations and Context Window Length control behaviour, not visibility. Always Output Data is a general node setting.

objective.question: You made a Chat Trigger publicly available in Hosted Chat mode to demo the support bot. You realise anyone with the URL can use it and spend your LLM credits. Which built-in option restricts access without extra infrastructure?
options: Switch the vector store to insert mode
Rename the workflow so the URL changes
Lower the Simple Memory context window
Set the Chat Trigger's Authentication to Basic Auth or n8n User Auth
objective.explanation: The Chat Trigger has an Authentication option that supports Basic Auth and n8n User Auth. These restrict who can chat. Memory and vector store settings do not control access. A renamed workflow does not add any authentication.

objective.question: A ticket tool parameter contains the expression below. What is the role of the fourth argument, 'medium'?

code.code: {{ $fromAI('priority', 'Ticket priority: low, medium or high', 'string', 'medium') }}

options: It is a default value used when the model does not provide one
It tells the model to use a medium-sized chat model
It is the description shown to the user in the chat
It limits the model to producing at most a medium-length string
objective.explanation: The $fromAI() signature is key, description, type and defaultValue. The fourth argument is a fallback value used if the model does not supply that parameter. It does not control length, model choice or what the user sees.

objective.question: During an Insert Documents run, in what order does your data actually pass through the parts of a RAG ingest setup in n8n?
options: File → Vector store → Embeddings → Text Splitter → Default Data Loader
File → Text Splitter → Vector store → Embeddings → Default Data Loader
File → Default Data Loader (reads text, adds metadata) → Text Splitter (creates chunks) → Embeddings (turns chunks into vectors) → Vector store (saves vectors)
File → Embeddings → Text Splitter → Default Data Loader → Vector store
objective.explanation: The loader turns the file into documents and uses the splitter to chunk them. The embeddings model then converts each chunk into a vector, and the vector store saves it. Embedding before splitting, or saving before embedding, is not possible.

objective.question: A weekly schedule re-ingests all product manuals into the same Pinecone namespace. After a month, the agent returns the same paragraph three or four times and sometimes quotes outdated text. What is the best fix?
options: Remove the old vectors before inserting, for example with the Clear Namespace option on a full rebuild or by deleting a document's old chunks by ID before re-inserting it
Switch to Simple Vector Store, which removes duplicates automatically
Raise the retrieval Limit so newer chunks also appear
Increase chunk overlap so duplicate chunks merge together
objective.explanation: Each insert adds new vectors. It does not replace the old ones, so repeated runs pile up duplicate and stale chunks. Clearing or deleting the old vectors before re-inserting fixes this. Overlap and Limit do not remove anything, and Simple Vector Store is not persistent.

objective.question: The ticket tool fails as soon as the agent tries to use it. What is wrong with this parameter?

code.code: {{ $fromAI('customer email', 'Email address of the customer', 'string') }}

options: The key contains a space; $fromAI() keys may only use letters, numbers, underscores and hyphens (1–64 characters), for example 'customer_email'
$fromAI() only works inside Code nodes
The description must be shorter than 10 characters
'string' is invalid; the type must be 'email'
objective.explanation: The first argument is the parameter name the model fills in. It must follow the documented key rules, and spaces are not allowed. 'email' is not a valid type, the description has no 10-character limit, and $fromAI() is meant for tool parameters.

objective.question: An internal FAQ widget must only answer questions from HR policy documents. It takes no actions, needs no conversation history, and the team wants the simplest and most predictable setup. Which design fits best?
options: An AI Agent with all policies pasted into the system message
A Basic LLM Chain with no retrieval
A Question and Answer Chain with a Vector Store Retriever connected to the policy vector store
An AI Agent with five tools and Postgres Chat Memory
objective.explanation: When there are no actions and no tool choice to make, a Question and Answer Chain always retrieves and then answers. That makes it simpler and more predictable than an agent. Pasting documents into the prompt wastes tokens, and a Basic LLM Chain without retrieval cannot see your documents.

objective.question: The agent calls the Create Ticket tool, but every ticket in the sub-workflow arrives with null subject, description and email. What is the cause?

code.code:
Sub-workflow trigger: When Executed by Another Workflow
  Input data mode: Define using fields below
  Fields: subject (String), description (String), email (String)

Agent tool: Call n8n Workflow Tool
  Workflow: Create Ticket
  Workflow Inputs:
    subject:     (empty)
    description: (empty)
    email:       (empty)

options: The workflow inputs are empty; fill each one with a $fromAI() expression, or let the model define the value, so the agent supplies it
The sub-workflow is not active
The chat model has no permission to call sub-workflows
The sub-workflow must use 'Accept all data' for tools to work
objective.explanation: The sub-workflow declares its inputs, but the tool never maps values to them, so they arrive as null. Mapping each input with $fromAI(), or the 'let the model define' option, lets the agent fill them in. Sub-workflows called this way do not need to be active.

objective.question: Users report two identical tickets for one problem. Intermediate steps show the agent called Create Ticket twice. The sub-workflow ends with an HTTP Request node, and the helpdesk returns an empty 201 response body. What is the best fix?
options: Remove memory from the agent
End the sub-workflow with a Set node that returns a clear confirmation such as 'Ticket T-1042 created', and tell the agent in the system message to create at most one ticket per issue
Set the chat model temperature to 0
Set Max Iterations to 1
objective.explanation: The agent only sees what the last node returns. An empty result looks like a failure, so the agent tries again. A clear success message with the ticket ID stops the retry. Max Iterations 1 would break normal tool use, and temperature does not fix the missing feedback.

objective.question: Both workflows run on the same n8n instance with no restart in between. The ingest completes, yet the agent's document tool always returns nothing. What is the cause?

code.code:
Ingest workflow:
  Simple Vector Store
    Operation: Insert Documents
    Memory Key: support_docs

Chat workflow:
  Simple Vector Store
    Operation: Retrieve Documents (As Tool for AI Agent)
    Memory Key: supportDocs

options: The retrieve mode must be 'Get Many'
The embeddings sub-node is not needed for retrieval
The memory keys differ ('support_docs' vs 'supportDocs'), so retrieval reads an empty store
Simple Vector Store cannot be shared between workflows
objective.explanation: Simple Vector Store separates data by its Memory Key. A different key points to a different, empty store. The same key works across workflows on one instance, and embeddings are still needed to embed the query.

objective.question: Your agent uses the Vector Store Question Answer Tool. You want lower cost, and you want the agent to see the raw chunks with their source metadata so it can cite documents. Which change is better?
options: Connect the vector store node directly in 'Retrieve Documents (As Tool for AI Agent)' mode with Include Metadata turned on
Use the HTTP Request Tool to call the vector database
Paste the documents into the system message
Keep the Question Answer Tool and add a second chat model
objective.explanation: The Question Answer Tool runs its own chat model call and returns a summary, which adds cost and hides the chunks. The 'As Tool' mode returns the matching chunks and their metadata straight to the agent. The other options waste tokens or add needless complexity.

objective.question: A hospital's support bot has these requirements: patient queries must not leave its own servers, n8n is self-hosted, chat history must survive restarts, and answers must come from internal documents. Which stack meets all the requirements?
options: Ollama Chat Model, Embeddings Ollama, PGVector on an internal Postgres, Postgres Chat Memory
Ollama Chat Model, Embeddings Ollama, Simple Vector Store, Simple Memory
Anthropic Chat Model, Embeddings Ollama, Qdrant Cloud, Redis Chat Memory
OpenAI Chat Model, OpenAI Embeddings, Pinecone, Simple Memory
objective.explanation: Local Ollama models with Postgres-based vector storage and memory keep all data on the hospital's servers and survive restarts. The other stacks either send data to external APIs or cloud services, or use Simple stores that lose data on restart.

objective.question: You switch the agent to a small local model served through Ollama. The agent never calls the document or ticket tools, and some runs fail with an error saying the model does not support tools. What is the cause?
options: The model you picked does not support tool (function) calling, which the AI Agent needs; choose a model that supports tools
Max Iterations is too low
Memory must be removed when you use local models
Ollama models cannot be used with n8n
objective.explanation: The AI Agent depends on the model's native tool calling. Models without this feature cannot call tools. Many Ollama models do support tools, and iterations or memory are not the cause here.

objective.question: Testing shows that the correct chunk is often ranked 6th to 8th by similarity, but the tool's Limit is 4, so the agent misses it. Which change improves this most directly?
options: Retrieve a larger candidate set and turn on Rerank Results with a reranker sub-node, such as Cohere, so the most relevant chunks are placed first
Switch the embeddings model only for queries
Add the documents to the system message as a backup
Lower the chunk size to 50 characters
objective.explanation: A reranker re-scores the candidates with a stronger relevance model, so the right chunk moves to the top. Tiny chunks lose context, and different embedding models for insert and query break the search. Pasting documents into the prompt wastes tokens.

objective.question: Inside the Create Ticket sub-workflow, the helpdesk HTTP Request node sometimes fails with a 503 error. The run then stops, and the user gets a generic error. You want the agent to receive a friendly message it can pass on. Which configuration achieves this?
options: Raise Max Iterations on the agent
Enable 'Always Output Data' on the trigger node
Turn off Retry On Fail
Set On Error to 'Continue (using error output)' on the HTTP node and connect the error branch to a Set node that returns 'Ticket system unavailable, please try later'
objective.explanation: The error output sends failures down a separate branch, which can return a clear message as the tool result. You can still combine it with Retry On Fail. More iterations only allow more retries, and 'Always Output Data' on the trigger does not catch HTTP failures.

objective.question: What is the correct order for adding a Create Ticket tool that uses the Call n8n Workflow Tool?
options: Create the sub-workflow with 'When Executed by Another Workflow' and defined input fields → build the ticket logic and a final node that returns a clear result → add a Call n8n Workflow Tool to the agent and select the sub-workflow → map the inputs with $fromAI() → write a precise tool name and description
Map the inputs with $fromAI() → create the sub-workflow → delete the trigger
Create the sub-workflow with a Webhook trigger → activate it → add an HTTP Request Tool
Add the tool to the agent → write the system message → create the sub-workflow → add the trigger
objective.explanation: The sub-workflow and its declared inputs must exist before the tool can select it and map its inputs. The description then tells the agent when to use the tool. A Webhook plus an HTTP Request Tool is a different pattern, and a sub-workflow cannot run without its trigger.

objective.question: Which text splitter does n8n recommend as the default choice for most general documents?
options: Recursive Character Text Splitter
No splitter; insert whole files
Character Text Splitter
Token Splitter
objective.explanation: The Recursive Character Text Splitter splits on paragraphs, then sentences, then words, so it keeps related text together. It is the recommended default. Whole files produce poor, oversized embeddings.

objective.question: A Google Drive node downloads PDF manuals as files. How should you configure the Default Data Loader so it can read them?
options: Type of Data: Binary, so it reads the file content, with the PDF format or automatic detection
Convert the PDFs to images first
No loader is needed; connect the embeddings directly
Type of Data: JSON, and point it to the file name field
objective.explanation: Downloaded files travel as binary data, so the loader must be set to read binary input. JSON mode would only read the item's fields, such as the file name. The vector store always needs a document loader to insert data.

objective.question: You embed the Chat Trigger's chat widget on https://help.example.in. The widget shows no replies, and the browser console shows a CORS error. What should you change?
options: Add https://help.example.in to the Chat Trigger's Allowed Origins (CORS) option
Turn off authentication on the chat model
Increase the agent's Max Iterations
Switch the Chat Trigger to Hosted Chat mode
objective.explanation: The Chat Trigger only accepts browser requests from allowed origins. Adding your site's domain fixes the CORS block. Hosted mode avoids embedding instead of fixing it, and the other two settings do not affect CORS.

subjective.question: Explain cluster nodes in n8n. How do the AI Agent root node and its sub-nodes relate to each other?
subjective.answer: In n8n, AI features are built as cluster nodes. A cluster has one root node and the sub-nodes plugged into it. The AI Agent is a root node. It controls the reasoning loop: it reads the input, decides what to do, calls tools and writes the final reply. Sub-nodes give it abilities. The Chat Model sub-node is required, because it is the brain. Memory sub-nodes keep the conversation history. Tool sub-nodes, such as the HTTP Request Tool, the Call n8n Workflow Tool or a vector store in tool mode, let the agent act and fetch data. An output parser can enforce structured output. Sub-nodes do not run on their own in the main flow; the root node calls them. Two details matter in practice. Credentials go on the sub-nodes, for example the chat model. Sub-node expressions resolve only against the first input item.
keyPoints: Cluster = one root node plus attached sub-nodes
AI Agent is the root and runs the reasoning and tool loop
Chat model is required; memory, tools and parsers are optional
Credentials are set on the sub-nodes
Sub-node expressions use the first item only

subjective.question: Walk me through how you would build a support agent in n8n that answers from company documents and can create a ticket.
subjective.answer: I build two workflows plus one sub-workflow. First comes the ingest flow. It has a manual or schedule trigger, then a node to fetch the files, for example from Google Drive. Next a vector store node in Insert Documents mode, with a Default Data Loader, a Recursive Character Text Splitter and an embeddings sub-node, stores everything in PGVector or Qdrant. Second comes the query flow. A Chat Trigger feeds an AI Agent. The agent gets a chat model, Postgres Chat Memory and two tools. One tool is the same vector store in 'Retrieve Documents (As Tool for AI Agent)' mode, using the same embedding model. The other is a Call n8n Workflow Tool that points to a 'Create Ticket' sub-workflow. That sub-workflow starts with the Execute Workflow Trigger and calls the helpdesk API. The system message tells the agent to answer only from the documents, and to create a ticket only when the documents do not solve the issue or the user asks for a human.
keyPoints: Separate ingest and query flows
Same embedding model for insert and retrieve
Vector store attached as a retrieval tool
Ticket action as a Call n8n Workflow Tool sub-workflow
System message and tool descriptions control behaviour

subjective.question: How does an AI Agent decide which tool to call? How do you make sure the ticket tool is used only when needed?
subjective.answer: The agent sends the model the user message, the system message, the memory and a list of the tools with their names, descriptions and parameter schemas. The model then decides whether to call a tool, which one, and with what arguments. So the tool description is effectively the instruction. For the ticket tool, I give it a clear name like 'create_support_ticket'. The description says when to use it and when not to: 'Use only after searching the knowledge base finds no answer, or when the user explicitly asks for a human. Do not use for general questions.' In the system message I repeat the order: search the docs first, answer if found, and offer or create a ticket only if not. I also give the knowledge base tool a clear description. Then I test with simple questions, questions the docs do not cover and explicit escalation requests. I check the execution log to see which tools were called.
keyPoints: The model chooses tools from name, description and schema
Descriptions should say when and when not to use the tool
System message sets the order: docs first, ticket last
Test with positive and negative cases
Check tool calls in the execution logs

subjective.question: How does conversation memory know which conversation it belongs to? What changes when you do not use the Chat Trigger?
subjective.answer: Memory nodes store history under a session key. When the workflow starts from the Chat Trigger, the trigger outputs a sessionId for each chat. Memory nodes read it by default, so every chat gets its own history with no extra setup. If I start the agent from a Webhook, a Telegram trigger or a form, there is no automatic sessionId. In the memory node I then change the session ID setting to define it myself, using an expression that points to a stable unique value. Examples are the Telegram chat ID, a user ID or a conversation ID sent by the website. If I get this wrong, for example by using a fixed value, all users share one history. That leaks context between customers and confuses the agent. I also choose a context window length that keeps enough recent turns without making prompts too long.
keyPoints: Memory is keyed by a session ID
Chat Trigger supplies sessionId automatically
Other triggers need a custom session key expression
A wrong key mixes users' histories
Context window length limits how much history is sent

subjective.question: Compare Simple Memory and Simple Vector Store with their production alternatives. When is each appropriate?
subjective.answer: Simple Memory and Simple Vector Store keep their data in the memory of the n8n instance. They need no setup, so they are great for learning, demos and quick tests. But the data is lost when n8n restarts. In queue mode, different executions may run on different workers that do not share that memory, so behaviour becomes unreliable. For production I use persistent stores. For chat history I use Postgres Chat Memory or Redis Chat Memory. Postgres suits teams that already run a database and want durable, queryable history. Redis is fast and suits short-lived sessions. For documents I use a real vector database: PGVector if we already run Postgres, Qdrant if we want a strong self-hostable option, or Pinecone if we prefer a managed service. Moving from test to production is mostly a matter of swapping the sub-nodes and adding credentials. The agent design stays the same.
keyPoints: Simple stores live in instance memory
Data is lost on restart and unreliable in queue mode
Use Postgres or Redis for chat memory
Use PGVector, Qdrant or Pinecone for vectors
Swapping sub-nodes keeps the agent design unchanged

subjective.question: Describe a production-ready RAG ingest flow in n8n and explain the role of each node.
subjective.answer: The ingest flow runs separately from the chat flow. It starts with a Schedule Trigger for regular syncs, or a manual trigger for one-off loads. A file event trigger such as a Google Drive trigger also works. Next, nodes fetch the source content, for example by downloading files or reading pages through HTTP. Then a vector store node, such as PGVector or Qdrant, in Insert Documents mode does the storing. Three sub-nodes attach to it. The Default Data Loader turns binary or JSON input into documents and can add metadata like source and title. The text splitter, usually the Recursive Character Text Splitter, breaks documents into chunks with a set size and overlap. The embeddings sub-node converts each chunk into a vector. I add metadata so I can filter results or cite the source later. I also plan for updates, for example by clearing the collection and re-inserting, or by deleting old chunks for a changed file, so I do not create duplicates.
keyPoints: Separate flow with a schedule or manual trigger
Fetch source data, then Insert Documents mode
Data loader, text splitter and embeddings sub-nodes
Add metadata for filtering and citations
Handle updates to avoid duplicate chunks

subjective.question: How do chunk size and chunk overlap affect retrieval quality? How would you tune them?
subjective.answer: Chunk size controls how much text each vector represents. Chunks that are too large mix several topics. Their embedding becomes vague, and they fill the model's context with irrelevant text. Chunks that are too small lose context; a single line may match the query but lack the surrounding explanation. Overlap repeats part of the previous chunk at the start of the next one. A sentence or step that crosses a boundary is then not cut in half. Overlap increases the number of chunks a little, which adds storage and embedding cost. To tune, I start with a moderate size and a small overlap. I build a test set of real support questions with known answers and check whether the correct chunks come back in the top results. Then I adjust the size, the overlap and the number of retrieved chunks. Structured documents like FAQs often work best when split on natural sections.
keyPoints: Large chunks give vague matches and waste context
Small chunks lose surrounding meaning
Overlap preserves context across boundaries
Overlap adds some cost through more chunks
Tune with a real question test set

subjective.question: Why must embedding dimensions match the vector index? What happens if you change the embedding model?
subjective.answer: An embedding model turns text into a vector with a fixed number of dimensions. OpenAI text-embedding-3-small, for example, produces 1536. A vector index or collection is created for one dimension size, and the database expects every vector to have exactly that length. If I insert or query with a model of a different size, the operation fails. Even if two models have the same size, their vectors live in different spaces. Comparing a query from one model with documents from another gives meaningless similarity scores. So the ingest flow and the query flow must use the same embedding model. If I change the model, I create a new index with the correct dimensions, re-embed and re-insert all documents, and only then switch the query flow to the new model. I usually keep the old index until the new one is tested, so I can roll back.
keyPoints: Index dimension is fixed, e.g. 1536 for text-embedding-3-small
A mismatched size causes errors
Different models' vectors are not comparable
Ingest and query must use the same model
Changing the model means re-embedding everything

subjective.question: What is $fromAI() and how would you use it in a ticket-creation tool?
subjective.answer: $fromAI() is an n8n expression function used in tool parameters. It tells n8n that the AI model should provide this value when it calls the tool. I give it a key, a description, and optionally a type and a default value. For a ticket tool, say an HTTP Request Tool calling our helpdesk API, I might set the subject to $fromAI('subject', 'One-line summary of the issue', 'string'). The description would be $fromAI('description', 'Full details including steps already tried', 'string'), and the priority would be $fromAI('priority', 'low, medium or high based on business impact', 'string'). The model sees these keys and descriptions as the tool's input schema and fills them from the conversation. Fixed values such as the API key, the queue ID or the requester source stay hard-coded, so the model cannot change them. Clear descriptions give cleaner, more consistent tickets.
keyPoints: Marks a parameter for the model to fill at call time
Takes a key, description, optional type and default
Becomes part of the tool's input schema
Keep secrets and fixed values hard-coded
Good descriptions improve argument quality

subjective.question: When would you use the Call n8n Workflow Tool rather than the HTTP Request Tool for creating tickets?
subjective.answer: The HTTP Request Tool is fine when a single API call does the job and the request is simple. The agent fills in a few parameters and n8n sends the call. I prefer the Call n8n Workflow Tool when ticket creation needs more logic. Examples: looking up the customer in the CRM, checking for an existing open ticket, setting priority rules, creating the ticket, posting to Slack and returning a clean confirmation. The sub-workflow starts with the Execute Workflow Trigger, which defines the inputs the agent must pass. It can use normal nodes, error handling and retries, and its last node's output goes back to the agent as the tool result. This keeps the agent simple and the business logic testable on its own. The sub-workflow can also be reused by other workflows. The sub-workflow also controls exactly which fields reach the helpdesk.
keyPoints: HTTP Request Tool for simple single API calls
Workflow Tool for multi-step logic and checks
Sub-workflow starts with Execute Workflow Trigger
The last node's output returns to the agent
Testable, reusable and supports error handling

subjective.question: What does Max Iterations do on the AI Agent node? How would you debug an agent that hits the limit?
subjective.answer: Max Iterations caps how many reasoning and tool-call cycles the agent can run for one input. The default is 10. It is a safety net: if the agent gets confused, it cannot loop forever, burn tokens or hammer an API. If an agent hits the limit, I open the execution and look at the agent's logs to see each tool call, its inputs and its outputs. Common causes are these. A tool returns an error or empty result, so the agent keeps retrying. Two tools have overlapping descriptions, so the agent swaps between them. The system message asks for something no tool can give. The retrieval tool returns irrelevant chunks, so the agent keeps searching. I fix the root cause: clearer tool descriptions, better tool outputs with useful error messages, better retrieval settings, or an instruction to stop and escalate. I raise the limit only when a task truly needs more steps.
keyPoints: Caps agent loop cycles; default 10
Prevents runaway cost and API abuse
Inspect agent logs for each tool call
Common causes: tool errors, vague descriptions, poor retrieval
Fix the root cause before raising the limit

subjective.question: Your support agent sometimes gives answers that are not in the documents. How do you make it stay grounded?
subjective.answer: First I check whether retrieval works at all. I look in the execution log to see whether the agent called the knowledge base tool, and what chunks came back. If it skipped the tool, I make the tool description clearer and add a rule to the system message: 'Always search the knowledge base before answering product questions. Answer only from the retrieved content. If the answer is not there, say so and offer to create a ticket.' If the tool ran but returned weak chunks, I fix the ingest side: chunk size and overlap, metadata, the number of results returned, and making sure the same embedding model is used. I can ask the agent to mention the source document, which makes guessing easier to spot. A lower model temperature also helps reduce creative answers. Finally, I test with questions that are deliberately out of scope and confirm the agent declines instead of inventing answers.
keyPoints: Check in the logs whether the retrieval tool was called
A strict system message: answer only from retrieved content
Fix retrieval quality on the ingest side
Ask for sources; lower the temperature
Test with out-of-scope questions

subjective.question: Explain the 'first item only' behaviour of sub-node expressions and how to work around it.
subjective.answer: Normal n8n nodes run once per input item, so an expression like {{ $json.email }} gets a different value for each item. Sub-nodes are different. Expressions in sub-nodes, such as a memory session key, a tool URL or a vector store filter, resolve only against the first input item. If ten items reach an AI Agent and the memory session key uses $json.userId, all ten use the first user's ID. That can mix histories or send wrong data. The workaround is to make sure each agent run sees one relevant item at a time. I can use Loop Over Items with a batch size of one before the agent. Or I can move the agent into a sub-workflow called once per item. In chat use cases this rarely matters, because the Chat Trigger sends one message per execution. It matters a lot in batch jobs, such as classifying many emails with an agent.
keyPoints: Normal nodes resolve expressions per item
Sub-node expressions use only the first item
Risk: wrong session keys, filters or URLs in batches
Workaround: Loop Over Items or a per-item sub-workflow
Mostly a concern in batch, not chat, workflows

subjective.question: How would you choose between PGVector, Qdrant and Pinecone for a self-hosted n8n support bot?
subjective.answer: All three work as vector store nodes in n8n, so the choice is mostly operational. PGVector is a Postgres extension. If we already run Postgres, for example as the n8n database or for chat memory, it adds no new system. Backups and access control are familiar. It suits small to medium document sets. Qdrant is a dedicated vector database that can be self-hosted easily with Docker. It offers good performance and metadata filtering, and data stays on our own servers, which helps with data residency requirements for Indian clients. Pinecone is fully managed, so there is nothing to run. It suits teams that want minimal operations and accept a cloud service and its pricing. Whatever I pick, I avoid Simple Vector Store in production, especially in queue mode. I make sure the index dimension matches the embedding model, and I plan re-indexing when documents or models change.
keyPoints: PGVector reuses existing Postgres; simple operations
Qdrant is self-hostable with strong filtering and data control
Pinecone is managed with low operational effort
Never use Simple Vector Store in production
Index dimension must match the embedding model

subjective.question: How would you test the checkpoint: the agent answers from documents and calls the ticket tool only when needed?
subjective.answer: I prepare a small test set with three groups. Group one: questions clearly answered in the documents. I expect the knowledge base tool to be called, a correct answer and no ticket. Group two: questions the documents do not cover. I expect the agent to say it could not find the answer and then offer or create a ticket. Group three: explicit requests like 'I want to talk to a human'. I expect a ticket with sensible fields. I run each through the Chat panel. In the execution view I check the agent logs: which tools ran, in what order, and with what arguments, including the $fromAI values. I confirm that the ticket sub-workflow ran only in groups two and three, and that tickets actually appear in the helpdesk. I also test follow-up messages, to check that memory carries context within the same session. I rerun the set after any prompt, tool description or chunking change.
keyPoints: Test set: covered, uncovered and escalation cases
Verify tool calls and order in the execution logs
Ticket tool runs only for uncovered or escalation cases
Check ticket fields and helpdesk records
Retest after any prompt or retrieval change

subjective.question: Review this system message for a support agent. What would you improve, and why?

code.code:
You are a helpful assistant. Answer any question the user asks.
Use your tools if you want. Be creative.

subjective.answer: This prompt invites hallucination and random tool use. 'Answer any question' and 'be creative' push the model to invent answers. 'Use your tools if you want' gives no rule for when to search or create a ticket. I would define a clear role: a support agent for our product. I would give it an explicit order of steps. First, always search the knowledge base tool for product questions. Answer only from the retrieved content. If nothing relevant is found, say so. Create a ticket only when the user reports a problem the documents cannot solve, or asks for a human. Before creating a ticket, collect the required details and confirm with the user. I would also add tone, a scope limit (refuse unrelated topics) and the output style. The tool descriptions should match these rules.
keyPoints: Remove wording that invites invented answers
Give an explicit rule: search documents first and stay grounded
Define precise conditions for creating a ticket and confirm first
Set scope, refusal behaviour and tone
Keep the prompt consistent with the tool descriptions

subjective.question: Explain the options for exposing an n8n chat agent to users through the Chat Trigger: hosted versus embedded chat, authentication and response modes.
subjective.answer: The Chat Trigger can be made publicly available. In Hosted Chat mode, n8n serves a ready-made chat page at the trigger's URL. This is good for demos and internal users. In Embedded Chat mode, you build your own interface or use n8n's chat widget on your website, and it calls the trigger's URL. For access control, the trigger supports Authentication options such as Basic Auth and n8n User Auth. The embedded widget should only be allowed from your own domains. For the reply, the default is to respond when the last node finishes. You can instead use response nodes to control exactly what is sent back. Recent versions also support streaming the agent's reply as it is generated. The session ID from the trigger links the chat to memory. Remember that the workflow must be active for the production URL to work.
keyPoints: Hosted Chat gives a ready page; Embedded Chat is for your own site or widget
Use the Authentication options to restrict access
Choose a response mode: last node finishes, response nodes or streaming
The session ID links the chat to memory
Activate the workflow to use the production URL

subjective.question: Design the 'Create Ticket' sub-workflow called by the agent so that it is safe and reliable. What inputs, checks and outputs would you include?
subjective.answer: The sub-workflow starts with the 'When Executed by Another Workflow' trigger. I define explicit input fields such as subject, description, priority and sessionId, so the agent's tool has a clear schema. Next, a validation step checks that required fields are present and that priority is one of the allowed values. If validation fails, it returns a clear error message so the agent can ask the user for the missing details. To avoid duplicates, I check whether an open ticket already exists for this session or user with a similar subject. Then I create the ticket in the helpdesk with a stored credential. I set Retry On Fail on that API call. The last node returns a small JSON object, such as ticketId, status and a short message. The agent reads this to confirm to the user. Errors are also logged or sent to an error workflow.
keyPoints: Use the 'When Executed by Another Workflow' trigger with defined inputs
Validate inputs and return readable errors to the agent
Check for duplicate tickets
Add retries and credential-based API calls
Return a concise result, such as ticket ID and status, from the final node

subjective.question: Documents were ingested successfully, but the agent keeps saying it cannot find relevant information. Give a structured troubleshooting checklist.
subjective.answer: First, I confirm the data exists. I run the vector store in Get Many mode, or check the database, to see chunks in the expected index, collection or table. Second, I check that the ingest and retrieval nodes point to the same index or collection name and namespace. Third, I confirm both sides use the same embedding model, because different models produce incompatible vectors. Fourth, I inspect the chunks. If they are too large, too small or full of noise, such as PDF headers, similarity search suffers. Fifth, I check the retrieval limit (top K) and any metadata filter that may exclude results. Sixth, I read the tool name and description. If the description is vague, the agent may not call the tool at all. I use the execution logs or intermediate steps to see whether the tool was called, with what query, and what came back. Finally, I test the same question directly against the vector store.
keyPoints: Verify the chunks actually exist in the target index or collection
Use the same index or namespace and the same embedding model on both sides
Inspect chunk quality and splitter settings
Check the limit and metadata filters
Confirm the agent calls the tool, using the logs, and test retrieval directly

subjective.question: Your product documentation changes every week. How would you keep the agent's knowledge base current in n8n without leaving stale answers?
subjective.answer: I would build a separate ingest workflow, triggered on a schedule or by a change event, such as a new file in Google Drive or a CMS webhook. Each chunk gets metadata such as document ID, source URL and version or updated date. When a document changes, I delete or replace all existing vectors for that document ID before inserting the new chunks. Otherwise, old and new versions both get retrieved and the agent contradicts itself. Not every vector store node supports deletion the same way, so I may need the store's API or SQL for PGVector. I process only changed documents to save embedding cost. I log each run and alert on failures. Including the source URL in the metadata also lets the agent cite where an answer came from, so users can check it.
keyPoints: Use a separate ingest workflow triggered by a schedule or change event
Add metadata with document ID, source and version
Remove old vectors before inserting the updated ones
Process only changed documents to control cost
Monitor runs, and use source metadata for citations

subjective.question: Your agent workflow is becoming expensive. Which n8n settings and design choices would you use to reduce token usage without hurting answer quality much?
subjective.answer: First, I look at what goes into each model call. Memory's Context Window Length controls how much history is sent, so I keep it small enough for the use case. Retrieval sends chunks to the model, so I tune chunk size and the vector store limit. A few focused chunks usually beat many large ones. I keep the system message concise and avoid long tool descriptions that repeat themselves. Max Iterations caps runaway tool loops, which can multiply cost. I choose a smaller, cheaper chat model for routine questions and reserve a stronger model for hard cases. I might route between them with an earlier classification step. For ingestion, I embed only new or changed documents. Finally, I review execution logs to see token-heavy runs and fix the prompts or tools that cause them.
keyPoints: Tune Context Window Length in memory
Tune chunk size and the retrieval limit
Keep prompts and tool descriptions concise
Cap loops with Max Iterations and choose the right model size
Avoid re-embedding unchanged documents and review the logs

subjective.question: What security risks come with a support agent that reads your documents and can create tickets, and how would you reduce them in n8n?
subjective.answer: The main risk is prompt injection. A user, or text inside a document, can tell the agent to ignore its rules, reveal its system prompt, or call tools with harmful inputs. Tools are where real damage happens, so I give each tool the least privilege it needs. The ticket tool can only create tickets, not delete or read other customers' data. Trusted values, such as the customer's ID or email, come from the authenticated session or the trigger data, not from $fromAI(). The sub-workflow validates every input. Credentials stay in n8n's credential store and are never placed in prompts. I secure the Chat Trigger with authentication and rate limits at the proxy. For high-impact actions, I add human approval. I also avoid ingesting confidential documents into a public bot, and I log tool calls for auditing.
keyPoints: Prompt injection from users or from document content
Give tools least privilege and validate their inputs
Take identity values from trusted data, not from the model
Protect credentials and the chat endpoint
Add human approval for risky actions and audit the logs

subjective.question: How do you handle errors in an n8n agent workflow, such as a failing helpdesk API, a model outage or a tool timeout?
subjective.answer: I handle errors at several layers. Inside tools, I set Retry On Fail on HTTP and helpdesk calls for transient errors. In sub-workflows, I catch failures and return a clear message, such as 'Ticket system unavailable, please try later'. The agent can then tell the user honestly instead of crashing or making up a ticket number. For the model, the AI Agent supports a fallback chat model, so a second provider can take over if the primary one fails. I set Max Iterations so the agent cannot loop forever on failing tools. At the workflow level, I attach an Error Workflow that alerts the team, for example on Slack or by email, with the execution details. For the chat user, I make sure some response is always returned, even on failure.
keyPoints: Retry On Fail for transient tool errors
Return readable error results to the agent instead of failing silently
A fallback chat model for provider outages
Max Iterations to stop loops
An Error Workflow for alerting, and always reply to the user

subjective.question: Review this HTTP Request tool configuration that an agent uses to create tickets. What is risky, and how would you fix it?
subjective.answer: There are three problems. First, the API key is hardcoded in the body. It should live in an n8n credential, such as Header Auth, so it is not exposed in the workflow JSON or in exports. Second, the customer email comes from $fromAI(). The model could invent an email or be tricked into using someone else's. Identity should come from trusted data, such as the authenticated session or trigger payload, mapped with a normal expression. Third, priority has no allowed values and no default. I would describe the allowed values, low, medium or high, give 'medium' as the default argument, and validate the value. Even better, I would move this logic into a sub-workflow called with the Call n8n Workflow Tool. That makes validation, duplicate checks and a clean ticket ID response easy. Only subject and description need to come from the model.
keyPoints: Move the hardcoded API key into n8n credentials
Take the customer identity from trusted data, not $fromAI()
Constrain priority with allowed values, a default and validation
Consider a sub-workflow for validation and a clean response
Let the model fill only the fields it should decide

subjective.question: Case study: an Indian telecom wants a Telegram support bot. Users write in Hindi, English or Hinglish, while the documents are in English. The bot must open a ticket for network outages and hand over to a human on request. Design it in n8n.
subjective.answer: I would start with a Telegram Trigger feeding an AI Agent. I would use a multilingual chat model and Postgres Chat Memory, with the session key set to the Telegram chat ID so users stay separate. Documents are ingested into PGVector with a multilingual embeddings model, so Hindi queries still match English chunks. The system message tells the agent three things: reply in the user's language, answer only from retrieved documents, and open a ticket only for outages or explicit requests. The Create Ticket sub-workflow takes the issue, the location and the chat ID. It validates them, calls the helpdesk, and returns the ticket ID. A separate human handover tool posts the conversation to the support team's Slack channel and marks the session as handed over. I would test with mixed-language questions.
keyPoints: Telegram chat ID as the memory session key
Multilingual embeddings so Hindi queries match English documents
System message rules for language, grounding and ticket conditions
Separate ticket and human handover tools with validation
Test with mixed-language cases

subjective.question: Troubleshooting: the support agent works perfectly in the editor's chat panel. However, the public chat URL you shared with customers gives no response. What would you check?
subjective.answer: First, I would check that I shared the production URL and not the test URL. The test URL only works while the editor is listening. Second, the workflow must be activated (published, in newer versions). Otherwise the production endpoint is not registered. Third, I would confirm that 'Make Chat Publicly Available' is on, and that the mode is Hosted Chat if the customers use the n8n page. If authentication is set, the customers need the credentials. Fourth, I would open the Executions list. If production runs appear and fail, the cause is often a credential, or a sub-workflow the tool cannot reach. If no runs appear, the request never reached n8n, so I would check the reverse proxy, the WEBHOOK_URL setting on self-hosted instances, and CORS for embedded widgets.
keyPoints: Test URL versus production URL
The workflow must be active or published
Public availability, mode and authentication settings
Use the Executions list to separate 'never arrived' from 'failed'
Reverse proxy, webhook URL and CORS on self-hosted instances

subjective.question: Comparison: should one AI Agent hold ten tools, or should a main agent delegate to specialised sub-agents, such as billing and technical? Which is better for a growing support bot, and why?
subjective.answer: With a few tools, one agent is simpler, cheaper and easier to debug. As tools grow towards ten or more, the model's choices become less reliable. Descriptions overlap, the prompt grows, and wrong tool calls rise. At that point, I prefer a main router agent that delegates to specialised agents. In n8n, I would build each specialist with the AI Agent Tool node or as a separate agent workflow called through the Call n8n Workflow Tool. Each specialist gets a short system message, a few tools and its own retrieval scope. The trade-offs are more model calls, more latency and harder tracing. So I split only along clear domains, and I give each sub-agent a precise description so the router knows when to use it. I measure tool-choice accuracy before and after the change.
keyPoints: A single agent is simpler and cheaper with few tools
Many tools reduce tool-selection accuracy and grow the prompt
Sub-agents via the AI Agent Tool node or agent workflows
Trade-offs: cost, latency and harder debugging
Split along clear domains and measure the result

subjective.question: Put in order the steps to migrate a running support bot from Simple Vector Store to PGVector without breaking it for users.
subjective.answer: First, I prepare Postgres with the pgvector extension and create a PGVector credential in n8n. Second, I copy the ingest workflow and swap Simple Vector Store for PGVector in Insert mode. I keep the same embeddings model, and I choose a new table name. Third, I run a full ingest and check the row count against the expected number of chunks. Fourth, I copy the chat workflow, connect PGVector in 'Retrieve Documents (As Tool for AI Agent)' mode, and use exactly the same embeddings model. Fifth, I run my test questions: answers from the documents, the ticket cases, and no-answer cases. I compare the results with the old bot. Sixth, I switch production to the new chat workflow and deactivate the old one. Finally, I point the scheduled re-ingest at PGVector and remove the Simple stores.
keyPoints: Prepare pgvector and the credential first
Same embeddings model for insert and retrieve
Full ingest, then verify the row count
Run the test question set before switching
Switch production, then update the scheduled ingest

subjective.question: Spot the mistake: users say the bot never remembers what they said one message ago. Here is the memory configuration.

code.code:
Trigger: Webhook (POST /support)
AI Agent -> Postgres Chat Memory
  Session ID: Define below
  Key: {{ $now.toISO() }}
  Context Window Length: 10

subjective.answer: The session key is the current timestamp. Every message therefore gets a brand-new session ID, and the memory loads an empty history each time. The context window length does not matter, because nothing is ever stored under the same key twice. The key must identify the conversation and stay stable across messages. Examples are a user ID, a conversation ID, or a sessionId that the website sends in the webhook body, such as {{ $json.body.sessionId }}. The front end should generate this ID once per conversation and resend it with every message. I would also check that the ID cannot be guessed or chosen by another user. Otherwise one user could read another user's history. After the fix, I would confirm in the Postgres table that rows for one session collect under a single key.
keyPoints: $now creates a new session on every message
The key must be stable per conversation
Send the sessionId from the client in the webhook body
Avoid guessable IDs to protect user privacy
Verify that rows are grouped under one key in the table

subjective.question: Case study: the ticket tool needs the customer's email. Tickets are being created with invented addresses such as user@example.com. How do you stop this?
subjective.answer: The model fills required $fromAI() parameters even when the user never provided them, so I fix this in three layers. First, if the user is logged in, I do not ask the model for the email at all. I pass it from the trigger data, such as the authenticated session, into the sub-workflow as a fixed value, which is the most reliable option. Second, if the email must come from the chat, the description and the system message say: 'Ask the user for their email; never guess it.' Third, the Create Ticket sub-workflow validates the email format and rejects obvious placeholders. It returns a clear message such as 'Email missing or invalid, ask the user', so the agent asks the user instead of retrying blindly. I would add test cases where the user gives no email.
keyPoints: Models fill required parameters even without real data
Pass trusted values from trigger or session data, not $fromAI()
Clear instruction to ask and never guess
Validate in the sub-workflow and return a corrective message
Test the case where no email is given

subjective.question: Comparison: Postgres Chat Memory or Redis Chat Memory for a production support bot? Which would you pick and why?
subjective.answer: Both are persistent and shared, so both work in queue mode, unlike Simple Memory. Redis is very fast and supports a session TTL, so old conversations expire automatically. That suits high-volume chat where history only needs to last a few hours or days. Postgres is durable and easy to query with SQL. It can also be backed up like any other table. That suits cases where you want to audit conversations, analyse common issues, or keep history for compliance. If the n8n setup already runs Postgres, for example for PGVector or as n8n's own database, Postgres Chat Memory adds no new infrastructure. My usual choice for a support bot is Postgres, because I need auditability and already have it. I would choose Redis if latency or automatic expiry matters more, or if Redis is already in the stack for queue mode.
keyPoints: Both are persistent and work across workers
Redis: speed and TTL-based expiry
